ayurveda.remedy: Vasa (Adhatoda vasica) leaf extract/formulations
ayurveda.note: [Human RCT] Clinical review of Vasa formulations on Shwasa Roga (Tamaka Shwasa is the classical entity most closely correlated with asthma) — same source already cited for bronchitis.

ayurveda.remedy: Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum)
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review] Reviewed bronchodilator activity specifically evaluated in asthma patients, compared with salbutamol in one included study — though the review itself flags that rigorous human safety data remain limited.

ayurveda.remedy: Warm, light diet; avoiding cold/heavy/mucus-forming foods (Kapha-aggravating per classical dietetics)
ayurveda.note: Traditional dietary approach for a Kapha-predominant respiratory presentation.

yoga.note: [Human RCT] Randomised controlled trial IN ASTHMA PATIENTS specifically — not extrapolated from elsewhere, unlike most Yoga4U entries.
yoga.video: The Breathing Technique That Saved My Life — Buteyko Breathing

yoga.note: [Human RCT] Single-blind RCT in asthma patients: improved asthma control, pulmonary function and quality of life.
yoga.video: Pranayama breathing technique for asthma control

yoga.note: General autonomic/respiratory-mechanism support, alongside prescribed preventer therapy.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique

evidence.quote: Most people with dengue recover within 1-2 weeks, but it's important to watch for warning signs as the fever comes down -- that's when severe dengue can develop.
evidence.recovery: 1-2 weeks
evidence.seekCareIf: Severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums/nose, blood in vomit or stool, breathing difficulty, or unusual restlessness/lethargy -- especially as the fever settles (day 3-7) -- need same-day medical review.
evidence.source: WHO Dengue and severe dengue fact sheet

conventional.remedy: Paracetamol for fever and pain
conventional.note: WHO: paracetamol is the recommended antipyretic/analgesic in dengue. NSAIDs (ibuprofen, aspirin, diclofenac) must be avoided -- they increase bleeding risk.

conventional.remedy: Plenty of oral fluids
conventional.note: WHO: adequate fluid intake helps prevent dehydration and supports recovery; monitor urine output as a simple hydration check.

conventional.remedy: Rest and watch closely through the critical period
conventional.note: WHO: the highest-risk window is typically as the fever subsides (day 3-7), even if you start to feel better -- keep monitoring for warning signs through this period.

ayurveda.remedy: Papaya leaf extract (Carica papaya)
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] A meta-analysis of RCTs found a significant pooled increase in platelet count with papaya leaf extract in dengue, though individual trial quality varies -- it supports, and does not replace, medical monitoring of platelet count.

ayurveda.remedy: Guduchi / Giloy (Tinospora cordifolia)
ayurveda.note: [Preclinical / mechanistic, limited human trials] Reviewed for anti-dengue and immune-modulating activity (berberine content); most evidence is preclinical or small uncontrolled studies rather than robust RCTs.

ayurveda.remedy: Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) as a general supportive tea
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Reviewed for general antiviral/immunomodulatory activity; no dengue-specific clinical trial evidence exists.

evidence.quote: Malaria is treatable and curable with prompt antimalarial medicine -- the biggest risk comes from delayed diagnosis and treatment, not from the illness itself once properly treated.
evidence.recovery: Days to 1-2 weeks with correct antimalarial treatment
evidence.seekCareIf: Confusion or drowsiness, repeated vomiting preventing you from keeping medicine down, jaundice, dark urine, reduced urine output, or breathing difficulty need emergency assessment -- these can signal severe (often falciparum) malaria.
evidence.source: WHO Malaria fact sheet

conventional.remedy: Confirmed diagnosis and antimalarial treatment -- not optional
conventional.note: WHO: malaria requires species-confirmed antimalarial treatment (e.g. artemisinin-based combination therapy for P. falciparum); it is not a self-treatable illness, but supportive care alongside treatment does help comfort and recovery.

conventional.remedy: Paracetamol for fever, plenty of fluids
conventional.note: Standard supportive care for fever and to prevent dehydration during rigors/sweats, alongside -- never instead of -- antimalarial treatment.

conventional.remedy: Rest between doses
conventional.note: Malaria's cyclical fever/rigor pattern is exhausting; rest between fever episodes supports recovery while treatment takes effect.

ayurveda.remedy: Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) tea for general comfort
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Traditionally used general supportive tea for fever; general antimicrobial/immunomodulatory activity reviewed, but no evidence it treats malaria itself -- confirmed antimalarial drug treatment remains essential.

ayurveda.remedy: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) for nausea
ayurveda.note: [Human RCT, extrapolated] Ginger has RCT-level evidence for nausea in other settings (e.g. pregnancy, chemotherapy); reasonable extrapolation for malaria-associated nausea, not a treatment for the infection itself.

evidence.quote: With appropriate antibiotics, most people with typhoid fever improve within a few days, though full recovery can take a few weeks.
evidence.recovery: Days to a few weeks with antibiotic treatment
evidence.seekCareIf: Severe abdominal pain or a rigid/distended abdomen (possible bowel perforation), confusion, or bleeding need emergency assessment -- these are recognised typhoid complications.
evidence.source: CDC Typhoid Fever -- Clinical Overview

conventional.remedy: Antibiotics as prescribed, completed in full
conventional.note: Typhoid requires antibiotic treatment (e.g. ceftriaxone or azithromycin per local resistance patterns) -- stopping early risks relapse and resistance.

conventional.remedy: Small, frequent, easily digestible meals and fluids
conventional.note: Supports nutrition and hydration while appetite and gut function recover; avoid raw/unwashed food and untreated water during and after recovery.

conventional.remedy: Rest through the fever
conventional.note: Standard supportive care while antibiotics take effect over the first few days.

ayurveda.remedy: Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) tea for general comfort
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Traditionally used general supportive tea for fever; no typhoid-specific clinical trial evidence -- antibiotic treatment remains essential.

ayurveda.remedy: Coriander (dhania) seed water
ayurveda.note: [Traditional use, evidence gap stated honestly] Widely used in Indian home care as a cooling fluid during fever; no clinical trial evidence specific to typhoid or fever reduction generally.

evidence.quote: Most cases of leptospirosis are mild and resolve with antibiotic treatment, but severe disease (Weil's disease) with jaundice, kidney involvement or bleeding needs hospital care.
evidence.recovery: Days to 2-3 weeks with antibiotic treatment; longer if severe
evidence.seekCareIf: Jaundice, reduced urine output, breathing difficulty, or bleeding (gums, skin, coughing/vomiting blood) need emergency assessment -- these signal severe disease (Weil's disease).
evidence.source: CDC Leptospirosis -- Clinical Care

conventional.remedy: Antibiotics as prescribed (doxycycline, penicillin or ceftriaxone)
conventional.note: Started early, antibiotics shorten the illness and reduce complication risk.

conventional.remedy: Plenty of fluids and rest
conventional.note: Standard supportive care; monitor urine output as a simple check for the renal involvement leptospirosis can cause.

conventional.remedy: Avoid further exposure to flood water or contaminated water
conventional.note: Reduces reinfection risk and protects others -- wear protective footwear if wading through flood water or paddy fields is unavoidable.

ayurveda.remedy: Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) tea for general comfort
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Traditionally used general supportive tea for fever; no leptospirosis-specific evidence -- antibiotic treatment remains essential.

evidence.quote: Most people recover from the acute fever within a week or two, though the joint pain can persist for weeks to months in some -- this is a recognised, usually self-limiting pattern.
evidence.recovery: 1-2 weeks for the fever; joint pain can persist weeks to months in a minority
evidence.seekCareIf: Bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, or confusion need urgent assessment -- these are not typical of chikungunya and should prompt reconsidering dengue or another cause.
evidence.source: WHO Chikungunya fact sheet

conventional.remedy: Paracetamol for fever and pain
conventional.note: WHO: paracetamol is preferred; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin until dengue has been excluded, since the two mosquito-borne illnesses circulate together and share early symptoms.

conventional.remedy: Rest in the acute phase, gentle movement as pain allows during recovery
conventional.note: Standard supportive care; gradual return to normal activity as joint pain settles.

conventional.remedy: Plenty of fluids
conventional.note: Standard supportive care for any febrile illness.

ayurveda.remedy: Turmeric / curcumin (Curcuma longa)
ayurveda.note: [Human RCT meta-analysis, extrapolated] A meta-analysis of RCTs shows curcumin reduces pain and inflammation across several types of arthritis -- extrapolated here to chikungunya's joint pain, since no chikungunya-specific trial exists.

ayurveda.remedy: Guggulu (Commiphora mukul) as a traditional anti-inflammatory
ayurveda.note: [Preclinical / mechanistic, evidence gap stated honestly] Long traditional use for joint pain in Ayurveda; robust human RCT evidence specific to viral arthritis is lacking.

evidence.quote: Scrub typhus responds dramatically to doxycycline, often within 24-48 hours -- most people recover fully with prompt treatment.
evidence.recovery: Days with antibiotic treatment; can be prolonged and severe if delayed
evidence.seekCareIf: Breathlessness, confusion, or signs of organ involvement (chest pain, reduced urine output) need urgent assessment -- untreated scrub typhus can progress to multi-organ involvement.
evidence.source: CDC Rickettsial Diseases -- Scrub Typhus Clinical Care

conventional.remedy: Doxycycline as prescribed, started promptly
conventional.note: Response is typically rapid and dramatic; often started empirically in endemic areas while confirmatory tests are pending, given how effective and time-critical treatment is.

conventional.remedy: Rest and plenty of fluids
conventional.note: Standard supportive care alongside antibiotic treatment.

conventional.remedy: Check skin folds, groin and armpits for the bite eschar
conventional.note: Finding and monitoring the eschar (a small painless scab) helps confirm the diagnosis and track local healing as you recover.

ayurveda.remedy: Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) tea for general comfort
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Traditionally used general supportive tea for fever; no scrub-typhus-specific evidence -- antibiotic treatment remains essential and highly effective here.

evidence.quote: Lifestyle changes -- less salt, more activity, weight loss, less alcohol -- can lower blood pressure as much as a single medication in many people, and work alongside any medication you're prescribed.
evidence.recovery: Ongoing management, not a cure -- blood pressure control is usually lifelong
evidence.seekCareIf: A reading above 180/120 with chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual disturbance or confusion is a hypertensive emergency -- seek immediate medical care, do not wait for a routine appointment.
evidence.source: NICE Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management

conventional.remedy: DASH-pattern diet (fruit, vegetables, whole grains, low-fat dairy, less salt)
conventional.note: [Systematic review of RCTs] A meta-analysis of 30 RCTs found the DASH diet reduced systolic BP by ~3-7 mmHg and diastolic BP by ~2.5-3.5 mmHg -- comparable to a single antihypertensive drug class.

conventional.remedy: Salt restriction specifically
conventional.note: NICE: reducing dietary salt intake lowers blood pressure -- particularly relevant in Indian diets, where pickles, papad and added salt make intake typically very high.

conventional.remedy: Regular aerobic exercise, weight loss if overweight, and limiting alcohol
conventional.note: NICE: each independently lowers blood pressure and reduces overall cardiovascular risk.

conventional.remedy: Home blood pressure monitoring
conventional.note: NICE: home/ambulatory monitoring gives a more reliable picture than isolated clinic readings and helps confirm the diagnosis and track control.

ayurveda.remedy: Arjuna (Terminalia arjuna) bark
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Long-studied for cardiovascular support in Indian traditional medicine; reviews of clinical studies report modest favourable effects on blood pressure and cardiac function, though trial quality and standardisation vary -- not a substitute for prescribed antihypertensives.

ayurveda.remedy: Garlic (Allium sativum)
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review of RCTs] A meta-analysis found garlic supplementation reduced systolic BP by ~5 mmHg and diastolic BP by ~2.5 mmHg versus placebo, with a larger effect (~8/7 mmHg) in the hypertensive subgroup specifically.

yoga.note: [Systematic review of RCTs, low-certainty evidence] A 2025 meta-analysis of 30 RCTs found yoga reduced systolic BP by ~8 mmHg and diastolic BP by ~5 mmHg versus control, though the authors rated the evidence quality as very low -- a genuine but not yet definitively proven benefit.

evidence.quote: Type 1 diabetes requires insulin from diagnosis -- it cannot be managed by diet and lifestyle alone. What self-management adds is better day-to-day control and fewer complications, alongside insulin, not instead of it.
evidence.recovery: Lifelong condition -- the goal is stable, well-controlled blood glucose, not a cure
evidence.seekCareIf: Vomiting, abdominal pain, fruity-smelling breath, rapid breathing or drowsiness need emergency assessment -- these suggest diabetic ketoacidosis.
evidence.source: ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines

conventional.remedy: Insulin therapy exactly as prescribed -- not optional
conventional.note: Basal-bolus insulin is essential from diagnosis; never stop or skip insulin, even when unwell or eating less -- sick-day rules usually mean MORE insulin, not less.

conventional.remedy: Carbohydrate counting and consistent meal timing
conventional.note: Supports matching insulin dose to food intake for more stable glucose control -- best learned through structured diabetes education.

conventional.remedy: Regular blood glucose (or continuous glucose) monitoring
conventional.note: Essential for safe insulin dosing and for catching highs/lows before they become dangerous.

conventional.remedy: Know your hypo (low blood sugar) treatment and carry fast-acting sugar
conventional.note: Standard safety practice for anyone on insulin -- treat suspected hypoglycaemia immediately with fast-acting carbohydrate.

ayurveda.remedy: Not a substitute for insulin -- general dietary discipline only
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Classical dietary measures used alongside diabetes management (regular mealtimes, avoiding excess simple sugars) support overall glycaemic stability, but no herbal or dietary measure replaces insulin in type 1 diabetes -- doing so is dangerous.

yoga.remedy: Regular moderate physical activity, including yoga, once glucose is stable
yoga.note: [Guideline-consistent, mechanistic] Physical activity improves insulin sensitivity and general wellbeing; time activity carefully around insulin dosing and meals, and check glucose before/after -- exercise can cause both hyperglycaemia and delayed hypoglycaemia in type 1 diabetes.

evidence.quote: Even a modest weight loss of 5-10% produces real, measurable improvements in blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol -- you don't need to reach an 'ideal' weight to benefit.
evidence.recovery: Ongoing management -- sustainable change matters more than rapid loss
evidence.seekCareIf: Rapid unexplained weight gain with other symptoms (extreme tiredness, cold intolerance, purple stretch marks, muscle weakness) should be assessed for an underlying cause rather than treated as simple obesity.
evidence.source: NICE Obesity: identification, assessment and management

conventional.remedy: A structured, sustainable calorie-reduced diet
conventional.note: NICE: dietary change is the foundation of weight management -- sustainable moderate reduction outperforms very restrictive crash diets for long-term results.

conventional.remedy: Regular physical activity (150+ minutes/week moderate intensity)
conventional.note: NICE: combined with dietary change, physical activity improves weight loss maintenance and metabolic health independent of weight change.

conventional.remedy: Behavioural support (goal-setting, self-monitoring, relapse planning)
conventional.note: NICE: structured behavioural support materially improves the success of weight management programmes compared with diet/exercise advice alone.

ayurveda.remedy: Traditional dietary discipline (Agni-supportive eating -- regular mealtimes, avoiding late/heavy meals)
ayurveda.note: [Traditional use, evidence gap stated honestly] Classical Ayurvedic dietary discipline aligns with modern advice on meal timing and portion control; no controlled trial evidence specific to weight outcomes.

ayurveda.remedy: Guggulu (Commiphora mukul)
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Traditionally used for weight/lipid management; a controlled study found no clear cholesterol benefit and reported gastrointestinal side effects -- not well-supported as a weight-loss aid specifically, and discuss with a doctor before use.

yoga.remedy: Regular yoga practice combined with diet change
yoga.note: [Systematic review of RCTs, mixed by comparator] A meta-analysis of 30 trials found no overall effect of yoga alone on weight/BMI/waist circumference across all comparisons, but a significant BMI reduction specifically in overweight/obese participants, and a weight benefit when yoga was compared directly against no exercise -- best framed as a useful adjunct to diet and activity, not a stand-alone weight-loss method.

evidence.quote: Dietary and lifestyle change can lower LDL cholesterol by 10-15% on its own, and adds to the benefit of any statin you're prescribed.
evidence.recovery: Ongoing management -- lipid levels are monitored periodically, not 'cured'
evidence.seekCareIf: Very high triglycerides (discovered on a blood test) can cause acute pancreatitis -- severe abdominal pain in this context needs urgent assessment.
evidence.source: NICE Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction

conventional.remedy: Soluble fibre (oats, psyllium, legumes)
conventional.note: [Meta-analysis of RCTs] A meta-analysis found psyllium/soluble fibre as an adjunct to statins meaningfully enhances LDL-cholesterol lowering.

conventional.remedy: Reduce saturated fat, replace with unsaturated fats (olive oil, nuts, oily fish)
conventional.note: NICE: dietary fat quality (not just total fat) meaningfully affects LDL cholesterol and cardiovascular risk.

conventional.remedy: Plant sterols/stanols (fortified foods)
conventional.note: [Meta-analysis of RCTs] A meta-analysis found plant sterol/stanol intake of 0.6-3.3 g/day reduces LDL cholesterol by 6-12% on average, as an adjunct to diet -- not a substitute for statin therapy where indicated.

conventional.remedy: Regular aerobic exercise
conventional.note: NICE: improves the overall lipid profile (raises HDL, lowers triglycerides) independent of weight change.

ayurveda.remedy: Guggulu (Commiphora mukul)
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Traditionally used for lipid management; a controlled study found no significant LDL benefit versus placebo -- not a substitute for statin therapy where indicated.

ayurveda.remedy: Garlic (Allium sativum)
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed evidence] Meta-analyses show modest total cholesterol reduction with garlic supplementation, though effect on LDL specifically is inconsistent across trials.

yoga.note: [Systematic review of RCTs] A meta-analysis of 53 RCTs (13,191 participants) found yoga significantly improved total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides -- an adjunct to, not a replacement for, dietary change and prescribed lipid-lowering therapy.

evidence.quote: Lifestyle intervention is the single most effective treatment for metabolic syndrome -- it addresses all its components (weight, blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol) together, rather than treating each in isolation.
evidence.recovery: Ongoing management -- the goal is reducing the components below diagnostic thresholds and lowering overall cardiovascular/diabetes risk
evidence.seekCareIf: Chest pain, breathlessness or other cardiovascular symptoms need their own urgent assessment, separate from routine metabolic syndrome management.
evidence.source: IDF Consensus Worldwide Definition of the Metabolic Syndrome

conventional.remedy: Combined dietary change and physical activity
conventional.note: Addresses central obesity, blood pressure, glucose and lipids together -- the best-evidenced single intervention for the syndrome as a whole (see the Obesity, Hypertension and Dyslipidaemia entries for the specific evidence behind each component).

conventional.remedy: Weight loss of 5-10% of body weight
conventional.note: Produces measurable improvement across all metabolic syndrome components, not just weight itself.

ayurveda.remedy: Traditional dietary discipline and Agni-supportive eating patterns
ayurveda.note: [Traditional use, evidence gap stated honestly] Aligns with the general dietary principles known to help each component; no trial evidence specific to the composite metabolic syndrome diagnosis.

yoga.note: [Systematic review of RCTs, mixed by outcome] A meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (794 participants) found yoga was superior to usual care for waist circumference and systolic BP specifically, but found no significant effect on diastolic BP, triglycerides, HDL, fasting glucose, or overall resolution of the syndrome -- a genuine but partial benefit, not a substitute for treating each component directly.

evidence.quote: Even a modest 5-10% weight loss (if overweight) can restore regular ovulation and periods in many women with PCOS, and lifestyle measures improve symptoms regardless of weight.
evidence.recovery: Ongoing management -- PCOS is a long-term condition, though symptoms and fertility can improve substantially with treatment
evidence.seekCareIf: Very heavy or prolonged bleeding, or bleeding after a long gap of no periods, should be assessed rather than assumed to be routine PCOS-related irregularity.
evidence.source: International Evidence-based Guideline for PCOS (2023)

conventional.remedy: Weight management (if overweight) through diet and exercise
conventional.note: International PCOS Guideline: even modest weight loss improves ovulation, cycle regularity and metabolic markers.

conventional.remedy: Combined oral contraceptive for cycle regulation and symptom control
conventional.note: International PCOS Guideline: first-line for managing irregular periods, acne and excess hair growth when contraception is also wanted or not contraindicated.

conventional.remedy: Low-glycaemic-index dietary pattern
conventional.note: Supports insulin sensitivity, a core driver of PCOS; complements but does not replace medical management.

ayurveda.remedy: Myo-inositol supplementation
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review of RCTs, informs international guideline] A meta-analysis of RCTs found myo-inositol improves insulin resistance, androgen levels and ovulation/pregnancy rates in PCOS -- this evidence directly informed the 2023 International PCOS Guideline update.

ayurveda.remedy: Cinnamon (Cinnamomum spp.)
ayurveda.note: [Human RCT] A randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial found cinnamon powder improved insulin resistance in PCOS; a separate trial found improved menstrual cyclicity over 6 months. Evidence base is smaller and less consistent than for myo-inositol.

yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs] A meta-analysis found yoga improves menstrual regularity, hirsutism, and metabolic/hormonal markers in PCOS, including in a large adolescent RCT where a holistic yoga programme outperformed conventional exercise.

evidence.quote: Regular physical activity is one of the few lifestyle factors consistently linked to better outcomes in prostate cancer, alongside whatever treatment or surveillance plan you're on.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage and treatment -- localised disease under active surveillance has an excellent long-term outlook
evidence.seekCareIf: New back pain, unexplained weight loss, or worsening urinary symptoms while on active surveillance should be reported promptly, not assumed to be routine BPH-type progression.
evidence.source: Movember/PCF dietary and lifestyle guidance for prostate cancer

conventional.remedy: Regular moderate-to-vigorous physical activity
conventional.note: [Observational, strong signal; RCT evidence on QoL/biomarkers rather than mortality] Men with higher activity levels show lower prostate-cancer-specific and all-cause mortality in observational cohorts; RCTs confirm favourable effects on insulin, inflammation and quality of life, though RCT-level mortality data is still limited.

conventional.remedy: Adherence to the active surveillance or treatment schedule
conventional.note: Regular PSA checks and follow-up are how low-risk disease is safely monitored without over-treatment -- do not skip appointments even when feeling well.

conventional.remedy: A varied, plant-forward diet
conventional.note: Consistent with general cardiovascular/cancer-risk-reduction dietary advice; no specific food or supplement has been shown to treat existing prostate cancer.

ayurveda.remedy: General supportive measures only
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for treating prostate cancer itself -- general wellbeing practices (diet, stress reduction) may support quality of life alongside, not instead of, oncology-directed treatment.

yoga.remedy: Regular yoga practice for quality of life during treatment
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs] A meta-analysis of yoga in cancer patients and survivors found improvements in quality of life, fatigue and psychological wellbeing -- supportive care, not a cancer treatment.

evidence.quote: Nutrition support alongside oncology treatment measurably improves how well people tolerate surgery and chemotherapy for gastric cancer -- this is standard, evidence-based supportive care, not an alternative to treatment.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage at diagnosis and treatment -- early referral for endoscopy matters a great deal
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent oncology assessment already -- if not yet under specialist care, seek that without delay rather than trying self-care first.
evidence.source: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in Cancer

conventional.remedy: Small, frequent, energy-dense meals
conventional.note: ESPEN: supports adequate intake when early satiety and appetite loss make normal-sized meals difficult -- a core part of standard supportive oncology nutrition care.

conventional.remedy: Early referral to an oncology dietitian
conventional.note: ESPEN: individualised nutrition support improves treatment tolerance and outcomes -- ask for this referral early rather than waiting for weight loss to become severe.

conventional.remedy: Psychological/emotional support alongside treatment
conventional.note: Standard supportive oncology care -- ask the treating team about counselling or support-group resources.

ayurveda.remedy: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) for treatment-related nausea
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed/modest evidence] Reviews of RCTs found ginger may modestly reduce acute chemotherapy-induced vomiting at low doses (under 1g/day), but did not clearly reduce nausea itself -- a possible adjunct for symptom comfort, not a cancer treatment.

yoga.remedy: Gentle yoga practice for quality of life during treatment
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs] Improves quality of life, fatigue and psychological wellbeing in cancer patients broadly -- supportive care during treatment, adapted to what the treating team advises is safe for your specific situation.

evidence.quote: Pancreatic enzyme replacement and nutrition support are core, evidence-based parts of standard care for pancreatic cancer -- alongside, never instead of, oncology treatment.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage and resectability at diagnosis
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent oncology assessment already -- if not yet under specialist care, seek that without delay.
evidence.source: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in Cancer

conventional.remedy: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (as prescribed) with meals
conventional.note: ESPEN: corrects the malabsorption that drives much of the weight loss and diarrhoea in pancreatic cancer -- a prescribed medical therapy, not a supplement choice.

conventional.remedy: Small, frequent, energy- and protein-dense meals
conventional.note: ESPEN: supports nutritional status through treatment; oncology dietitian input is recommended early.

conventional.remedy: Manage itching from jaundice with prescribed treatment
conventional.note: Cholestatic itch responds to treating the underlying obstruction and, in the interim, prescribed antipruritic medication -- not a self-care matter alone.

ayurveda.remedy: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) for treatment-related nausea
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed/modest evidence] As with other cancers, ginger may modestly help acute chemotherapy-induced vomiting at low doses -- a possible comfort measure only.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy treats pancreatic cancer itself
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Given how time-critical treatment is for this cancer, do not delay oncology care to try alternative remedies.

yoga.remedy: Gentle yoga practice, only as advised by the treating team
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, general cancer evidence] Supportive quality-of-life benefit shown broadly in cancer patients; pancreatic cancer patients are often more unwell at diagnosis, so check with the oncology team before starting.

evidence.quote: Dietary change is one of the most effective things you can do for chronic kidney disease -- sodium restriction, appropriate protein intake and blood pressure control together can meaningfully slow progression.
evidence.recovery: Ongoing management -- the goal is slowing progression and reducing cardiovascular risk, not reversal
evidence.seekCareIf: Rapidly rising creatinine, new or worsening breathlessness, confusion, or a big drop in urine output need urgent medical assessment.
evidence.source: KDIGO 2024 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Evaluation and Management of CKD

conventional.remedy: Sodium restriction (<2g/day)
conventional.note: [Guideline] KDIGO 2024 recommends strict salt restriction to under 2g sodium/day to reduce blood pressure and improve fluid control.

conventional.remedy: Appropriate (not excessive) dietary protein
conventional.note: [Guideline] KDIGO 2024 recommends around 0.8g protein/kg/day in CKD stages 3-5, and specifically advises against high protein intake (>1.3g/kg/day), which can accelerate progression.

conventional.remedy: Individualised potassium and phosphate management
conventional.note: [Guideline] KDIGO 2024: potassium/phosphate advice should be individualised with a renal dietitian based on blood levels and CKD stage, not applied as a blanket restriction to everyone.

conventional.remedy: Blood pressure and blood sugar control
conventional.note: Treating the underlying driver (hypertension/diabetes) is the single most effective way to slow CKD progression -- see this app's Hypertension and T2DM self-care entries.

ayurveda.remedy: Punarnava (Boerhavia diffusa)
ayurveda.note: [Preclinical / mixed small clinical studies, evidence gap stated honestly] Long traditional use for oedema and kidney support; nephroprotective effects shown in preclinical models and small polyherbal clinical studies, but not yet robust standalone RCT evidence -- discuss with your nephrologist before use, since some herbal products can worsen kidney function.

yoga.remedy: Gentle regular physical activity, including yoga
yoga.note: [Guideline-consistent, general CKD/dialysis population evidence] Supports cardiovascular health and quality of life in CKD; intensity should be discussed with your nephrology team, especially in advanced disease.

evidence.quote: Most children with nephrotic syndrome (minimal change disease) respond well to steroid treatment and go on to do well long-term -- this is usually a very treatable condition, not a lifelong kidney-failure diagnosis.
evidence.recovery: Variable -- many respond well to steroids within weeks; some relapse and need longer-term management
evidence.seekCareIf: Fever, abdominal pain, or a swollen/tender calf need urgent assessment -- infection and blood clots are recognised complications of nephrotic syndrome.
evidence.source: KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline on Glomerular Diseases

conventional.remedy: Sodium restriction to manage swelling
conventional.note: Reducing dietary salt helps limit fluid retention alongside diuretic treatment if prescribed.

conventional.remedy: Take corticosteroids exactly as prescribed, for the full course
conventional.note: Steroids are the mainstay first treatment, especially in children -- stopping early risks relapse; never adjust the dose without medical advice.

conventional.remedy: Watch for and promptly report infection
conventional.note: Nephrotic syndrome increases infection risk (loss of immune proteins in the urine) -- fever should be assessed promptly, not managed as a routine cold.

ayurveda.remedy: Punarnava (Boerhavia diffusa)
ayurveda.note: [Preclinical / mixed small clinical studies, evidence gap stated honestly] Traditionally used for oedema; some supportive preclinical/small clinical data, but not a substitute for steroid treatment, and some herbal products can affect kidney function -- discuss with your nephrologist first.

yoga.remedy: Gentle activity once swelling and steroid side effects allow
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No condition-specific trial evidence for yoga in nephrotic syndrome; general gentle activity is reasonable once medically stable, per your treating team's advice.

evidence.quote: Structured exercise and yoga programmes are now standard, evidence-based parts of supportive breast cancer care -- shown to improve quality of life, fatigue and psychological wellbeing during and after treatment.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage at diagnosis and receptor status -- early diagnosis and treatment substantially improve outcomes
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent breast-clinic assessment already -- if you have a new lump or breast change and are not yet under specialist review, seek that without delay.
evidence.source: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in Cancer + yoga/breast cancer evidence base

conventional.remedy: Do not delay the triple-assessment pathway
conventional.note: Early diagnosis substantially changes treatment options and outcomes -- this is the single most important 'self-care' step for a new breast lump.

conventional.remedy: Nutrition support through surgery/chemotherapy/radiotherapy
conventional.note: ESPEN: adequate protein and energy intake supports treatment tolerance and recovery -- ask for an oncology dietitian referral.

conventional.remedy: Regular moderate exercise as tolerated during and after treatment
conventional.note: Well-established supportive-care benefit for fatigue, cardiovascular health and psychological wellbeing in breast cancer specifically -- discuss timing/intensity with your oncology team.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy treats breast cancer itself
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Given how much early treatment changes outcomes in breast cancer, do not delay or substitute urgent specialist assessment for alternative remedies. General wellbeing practices may support quality of life alongside treatment.

yoga.remedy: Regular yoga practice during and after treatment
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, breast-cancer-specific] A meta-analysis specifically in breast cancer patients/survivors found large reductions in distress, anxiety and depression, and moderate improvements in fatigue and quality of life -- one of the best-evidenced supportive yoga applications in oncology.

evidence.quote: A low-glycemic-load diet has repeatedly, independently been shown in randomised trials to reduce acne lesion counts -- diet genuinely matters here, alongside standard topical/oral treatment.
evidence.recovery: Usually improves over weeks to a few months with consistent treatment; can persist or relapse, especially around hormonal changes
evidence.seekCareIf: Scarring, nodulocystic lesions, or acne not responding to standard topical treatment after 2-3 months warrants review for prescription-strength or oral therapy.
evidence.source: Smith RN et al., A low-glycemic-load diet improves symptoms in acne vulgaris patients: a randomized controlled trial, Am J Clin Nutr 2007

conventional.remedy: A low-glycemic-load diet (less refined sugar/white bread/white rice, more whole grains and legumes)
conventional.note: [Randomised controlled trial, independently replicated] The original RCT and several later trials found fewer inflammatory acne lesions on a low-glycemic-load diet compared with a typical higher-glycemic diet.

conventional.remedy: Reducing milk/dairy intake, especially skimmed milk
conventional.note: [Two independent meta-analyses of observational studies] Consistent, dose-dependent association between dairy (particularly skimmed milk) intake and acne -- not proven to be causal by RCTs, but a reasonable, low-risk dietary trial.

conventional.remedy: Zinc supplementation as an adjunct (discuss dose with a doctor/pharmacist)
conventional.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis, small/heterogeneous trials] Acne patients often have lower serum zinc, and zinc treatment showed a significant reduction in inflammatory lesion counts as an adjunct -- not a substitute for standard topical/oral treatment.

conventional.remedy: Gentle cleansing (avoid harsh scrubbing) and non-comedogenic products
conventional.note: Standard dermatological self-care advice -- over-washing and scrubbing can worsen inflammation without improving acne.

ayurveda.remedy: Turmeric (curcumin) -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap] No randomised controlled trial of turmeric/curcumin for acne was found in the literature -- only preclinical/mechanistic rationale and a 2026 narrative review that itself describes the clinical evidence as preliminary. May be used traditionally alongside, not instead of, evidence-based treatment.

ayurveda.remedy: Dietary approach shared with classical practice: favour fresh, minimally processed food over refined sugar and excess dairy
ayurveda.note: This overlaps with the low-glycemic-load and dairy-reduction evidence above (see Conventional) -- a rare case where classical dietary advice and modern trial evidence point the same way.

yoga.remedy: General stress-management practice -- evidence gap for yoga specifically, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No yoga trial for acne exists. The closest real intervention trial is a small, non-blinded pilot of a cognitive (not yoga-based) stress-management technique, which showed improved acne staging -- weak/emerging support for stress-management in general, not proof that yoga itself changes acne.
yoga.video: 1 Minute Breathing Exercise for Anxiety and Stress

yoga.note: Stress is a recognised acne aggravator in clinical experience even without acne-specific yoga trial evidence -- a low-risk supportive practice alongside, not instead of, the treatments above.
yoga.video: 1 Minute Meditation for Quick Stress Relief

evidence.quote: Complete alcohol abstinence is the single most important intervention in cirrhosis, regardless of the original cause -- associated with reduced decompensation and improved transplant-free survival.
evidence.recovery: Highly variable -- depends on the underlying cause and whether it's compensated or decompensated; treating the cause and complications can meaningfully slow progression
evidence.seekCareIf: Confusion or drowsiness (encephalopathy), vomiting blood or black stools (variceal bleeding), or rapidly worsening abdominal swelling/jaundice need urgent same-day assessment.
evidence.source: EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines: Management of Alcohol-Related Liver Disease, J Hepatol 2018

conventional.remedy: Complete alcohol abstinence
conventional.note: [Guideline] The single most important intervention regardless of the original cause of cirrhosis -- reduces decompensation risk and improves transplant-free survival.

conventional.remedy: Sodium restriction to about 2,000 mg/day if ascites is present
conventional.note: [Guideline] AASLD practice guidance recommends moderate sodium restriction (~88 mmol/2,000 mg per day) as a core part of managing ascites, alongside prescribed diuretics.

conventional.remedy: Hepatitis A vaccination, if not already immune
conventional.note: [Guideline] The CDC/ACIP specifically recommends Hepatitis A vaccination for people with chronic liver disease, including chronic hepatitis B and C -- a second liver infection on top of existing chronic disease can be far more serious.

conventional.remedy: Regular coffee consumption (2-3 cups/day, if otherwise tolerated)
conventional.note: [Multiple meta-analyses of observational studies] A consistent, dose-dependent association between coffee intake and lower risk of liver fibrosis progression and hepatocellular carcinoma has been shown across several independent meta-analyses -- not RCT-proven causation, but a reasonable, low-risk habit to continue or adopt.

ayurveda.remedy: Milk thistle / silymarin -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Cochrane systematic review] A Cochrane review of milk thistle in alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C liver disease found NO significant effect on mortality, complications, or liver histology, despite widespread traditional and commercial use. May be used alongside, but should not be relied on instead of, guideline-directed treatment.

yoga.remedy: Gentle activity as tolerated -- evidence gap for a cirrhosis-specific trial, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No condition-specific yoga trial for cirrhosis was identified. Gentle activity within energy limits is reasonable once medically stable, but intensity should be discussed with your hepatology team, especially with ascites or muscle wasting (sarcopenia is common in cirrhosis).

evidence.quote: Chronic hepatitis B is manageable, often for life, with regular monitoring and antiviral therapy when active -- the goal is controlling the virus and preventing progression to cirrhosis or liver cancer, not necessarily curing it.
evidence.recovery: Usually a long-term, managed condition rather than a curable one -- regular 6-monthly monitoring is central to good outcomes
evidence.seekCareIf: New jaundice, confusion, abdominal swelling, or vomiting blood suggest decompensation and need urgent assessment.
evidence.source: CDC/ACIP recommendations for Hepatitis A vaccination in chronic liver disease, MMWR 2020

conventional.remedy: Attend all scheduled monitoring appointments (viral load, LFTs, 6-monthly ultrasound/AFP if cirrhotic)
conventional.note: Regular monitoring is how progression or the need to start antiviral therapy is caught early -- the condition is usually silent even when active.

conventional.remedy: Avoid alcohol
conventional.note: Alcohol accelerates liver damage on top of chronic viral infection -- a standard, low-risk precaution regardless of current liver test results.

conventional.remedy: Hepatitis A vaccination, if not already immune
conventional.note: [Guideline] The CDC/ACIP specifically recommends Hepatitis A vaccination for people with chronic liver disease, including chronic hepatitis B and C -- a second liver infection on top of existing chronic disease can be far more serious.

conventional.remedy: Screen and vaccinate household/close contacts
conventional.note: Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids -- household contacts should be tested and, if susceptible, vaccinated.

ayurveda.remedy: Milk thistle / silymarin -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Cochrane systematic review] A Cochrane review of milk thistle in alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C liver disease found NO significant effect on mortality, complications, or liver histology, despite widespread traditional and commercial use. May be used alongside, but should not be relied on instead of, guideline-directed treatment.

yoga.remedy: General stress-management practice -- evidence gap for hepatitis B specifically, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No condition-specific trial evidence exists. A general low-risk supportive practice alongside, not instead of, antiviral treatment and monitoring.

evidence.quote: Chronic hepatitis C is now curable in the large majority of people with a short course of direct-acting antivirals -- a very different picture from the older, harder-to-treat disease many still associate it with.
evidence.recovery: Curative in the large majority with an 8-12 week course of direct-acting antivirals, regardless of fibrosis stage
evidence.seekCareIf: Signs of decompensated cirrhosis (jaundice, confusion, abdominal swelling, GI bleeding) need urgent assessment.
evidence.source: CDC/ACIP recommendations for Hepatitis A vaccination in chronic liver disease, MMWR 2020

conventional.remedy: Complete the full direct-acting antiviral course once started
conventional.note: Cure rates exceed 95% in most groups with a completed course -- stopping early risks treatment failure and resistance.

conventional.remedy: Avoid alcohol
conventional.note: Alcohol accelerates fibrosis progression on top of active viral infection.

conventional.remedy: Hepatitis A vaccination, if not already immune
conventional.note: [Guideline] The CDC/ACIP specifically recommends Hepatitis A vaccination for people with chronic liver disease, including chronic hepatitis B and C -- a second liver infection on top of existing chronic disease can be far more serious.

conventional.remedy: Fibrosis staging before and monitoring after treatment
conventional.note: Confirms treatment response and identifies the minority who still need cirrhosis surveillance even after the virus is cleared.

ayurveda.remedy: Milk thistle / silymarin -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Cochrane systematic review] A Cochrane review of milk thistle in alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C liver disease found NO significant effect on mortality, complications, or liver histology, despite widespread traditional and commercial use. May be used alongside, but should not be relied on instead of, guideline-directed treatment.

yoga.remedy: General stress-management practice -- evidence gap for hepatitis C specifically, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No condition-specific trial evidence exists. A general low-risk supportive practice alongside, not instead of, antiviral treatment.

evidence.quote: Losing 7-10% of body weight is the single most effective intervention for NAFLD -- a prospective biopsy-paired study found this reversed the inflammatory changes of NASH in the large majority who achieved it.
evidence.recovery: Reversible in many people with sustained weight loss and management of associated conditions; can progress to fibrosis/cirrhosis if untreated, especially with ongoing metabolic risk factors
evidence.seekCareIf: Signs of advancing liver disease (jaundice, abdominal swelling, confusion) need urgent assessment -- rare, but change the management path significantly.
evidence.source: Vilar-Gomez E et al., Weight Loss Through Lifestyle Modification Significantly Reduces Features of Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis, Gastroenterology 2015

conventional.remedy: Weight loss of 7-10% of body weight through diet and physical activity
conventional.note: [High-quality prospective cohort with paired liver biopsies] The single most effective intervention -- this study found NASH resolution in 90% and fibrosis regression in 45% of those who achieved >=10% weight loss; 7-10% loss gave significant but less consistent benefit.

conventional.remedy: Regular coffee consumption (2-3 cups/day, if otherwise tolerated)
conventional.note: [Multiple meta-analyses of observational studies] A consistent, dose-dependent association between coffee intake and lower risk of liver fibrosis progression and hepatocellular carcinoma has been shown across several independent meta-analyses -- not RCT-proven causation, but a reasonable, low-risk habit to continue or adopt.

conventional.remedy: Manage associated diabetes, dyslipidaemia and hypertension
conventional.note: These conditions commonly coexist with and drive NAFLD progression -- see this app's entries for each for condition-specific dietary guidance.

conventional.remedy: Avoid unnecessary alcohol
conventional.note: Even moderate alcohol intake can accelerate fatty liver progression on top of a metabolic cause.

ayurveda.remedy: Turmeric (curcumin) -- preliminary evidence, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Small single RCT] One placebo-controlled trial (~80 patients) found curcumin supplementation reduced ultrasound-graded liver fat and liver enzymes compared with placebo -- a genuine but preliminary finding, not yet confirmed by larger trials or adopted into major guidelines.

ayurveda.remedy: Milk thistle / silymarin -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Cochrane systematic review] A Cochrane review of milk thistle in alcoholic and/or hepatitis B or C liver disease found NO significant effect on mortality, complications, or liver histology, despite widespread traditional and commercial use. May be used alongside, but should not be relied on instead of, guideline-directed treatment.

yoga.remedy: Regular physical activity as part of the weight-loss programme
yoga.note: Physical activity supports the weight loss shown above to be effective, even though no NAFLD-specific yoga trial exists as such -- any sustainable, enjoyable form of regular activity is reasonable; see Yoga4U for general practices.

evidence.quote: Smoking causes roughly half of all bladder cancer cases -- the single most important modifiable risk factor, both before and after diagnosis.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage and grade at diagnosis -- non-muscle-invasive disease has a good outlook with surveillance; muscle-invasive disease needs more intensive treatment
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent urology assessment already -- if not yet under specialist care, seek that without delay rather than trying self-care first.
evidence.source: Freedman ND et al., Association between smoking and risk of bladder cancer among men and women, JAMA 2011

conventional.remedy: Stop smoking completely
conventional.note: [Large prospective cohort] Smoking causes an estimated ~50% of bladder cancer cases. One retrospective single-centre study found better recurrence-free survival in those who quit at diagnosis (70% vs 45% at 3 years) -- promising but not yet confirmed by a randomised trial.

conventional.remedy: Do not delay the 2-week-wait-equivalent referral pathway
conventional.note: Early diagnosis substantially changes treatment options -- this is the single most important 'self-care' step for painless visible blood in the urine.

conventional.remedy: Nutrition support through surgery/intravesical therapy/chemotherapy
conventional.note: [Guideline] Standard supportive oncology nutrition care improves treatment tolerance -- ask for a dietitian referral if appetite or weight is affected.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy treats bladder cancer itself
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Given how much early treatment changes outcomes, do not delay or substitute urgent specialist assessment for alternative remedies. General wellbeing practices may support quality of life alongside treatment.

yoga.remedy: Regular yoga practice for quality of life during treatment
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, general cancer evidence] Improves quality of life, fatigue and psychological wellbeing in cancer patients broadly -- supportive care during treatment, not a cancer treatment itself.

evidence.quote: Pelvic floor muscle training is genuinely effective for stress incontinence -- women who do it are over eight times more likely to report a cure than women who don't, according to a Cochrane review of 31 trials.
evidence.recovery: Often significantly improves with pelvic floor training and/or weight loss within a few months of consistent practice; some need medication or surgery for lasting relief
evidence.seekCareIf: Back pain, saddle numbness or leg weakness alongside new incontinence need urgent assessment for cauda equina syndrome -- this is a neurological emergency, not routine incontinence.
evidence.source: Dumoulin C et al., Pelvic floor muscle training versus no treatment for urinary incontinence in women, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018

conventional.remedy: Pelvic floor muscle training (Kegel exercises), done consistently
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, strong evidence for stress incontinence] Women with stress incontinence were over 8 times more likely to report a cure than untreated women (31 trials, 1,817 women). Evidence for urge incontinence alone is much thinner -- ask a physiotherapist for correct technique, since doing it wrong reduces the benefit.

conventional.remedy: Weight loss if overweight or obese
conventional.note: [Randomised controlled trial -- the PRIDE trial] A structured weight-loss programme (about 8% body weight lost) reduced incontinence episodes by 47%, compared with 28% in the control group -- benefit was specific to stress-type leakage.

conventional.remedy: Bladder training (scheduled voiding, gradually increasing intervals) for urge symptoms
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, weak/tentative evidence] Point estimates favoured bladder training but the evidence base is old and underpowered -- Cochrane's own conclusion was that 'definitive research has yet to be conducted.' Reasonable to try, but don't expect guaranteed benefit.

ayurveda.remedy: No specific Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for incontinence
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] General strengthening and dietary practices may support overall pelvic health alongside, not instead of, pelvic floor training.

yoga.remedy: Yoga postures that engage the pelvic floor (e.g. Mula Bandha-focused practice) -- evidence gap, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No incontinence-specific yoga trial was identified. Pelvic floor muscle training itself (see Conventional) has the actual trial evidence -- yoga may be a pleasant way to build general core/pelvic awareness alongside it, not a substitute.

evidence.recovery: Usually improves within 1-2 weeks with appropriate antibiotics
evidence.seekCareIf: Sudden severe onset, especially in a younger patient, must be treated as testicular torsion until proven otherwise -- go to an emergency department, do not wait to see if it settles.
evidence.source: Commonly practised supportive care, not independently cited

conventional.remedy: Complete the full prescribed antibiotic course
conventional.note: Standard treatment -- searched specifically for RCT evidence on scrotal support/NSAIDs/conservative measures alongside antibiotics and found none; these remain standard, sensible supportive care rather than independently trial-proven.

conventional.remedy: Scrotal support and elevation, plus regular analgesia
conventional.note: Commonly recommended supportive measures for comfort while antibiotics take effect.

conventional.remedy: Abstain from sex until treated, and arrange partner testing/treatment if a sexually transmitted cause is likely
conventional.note: Prevents reinfection and onward transmission when chlamydia/gonorrhoea is the likely cause.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for epididymo-orchitis
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] This is a bacterial/STI-driven infection needing antibiotic treatment -- do not delay or substitute this with alternative remedies.

evidence.quote: Structured lifestyle change -- diet, exercise and weight loss -- meaningfully improved erectile function in a randomised trial of obese men, and this has since been supported by a systematic review of similar trials.
evidence.recovery: Often improves with lifestyle change and/or PDE5 inhibitor treatment; underlying cardiovascular/diabetes risk should be assessed, especially with new ED at a younger age
evidence.seekCareIf: New ED in a younger man, especially with other cardiovascular risk factors, deserves cardiovascular risk assessment, not just symptomatic treatment.
evidence.source: Esposito K et al., Effect of lifestyle changes on erectile dysfunction in obese men, JAMA 2004

conventional.remedy: Structured diet, exercise and weight-loss programme
conventional.note: [Randomised controlled trial, supported by a later systematic review] A 2-year RCT in obese men found significantly improved erectile function scores with lifestyle change vs no change; a later review of 7 RCTs (478 men) confirmed a meaningful average improvement with exercise programmes.

conventional.remedy: Stop smoking, limit alcohol, review medications with a doctor
conventional.note: Standard reversible-cause review -- smoking, heavy alcohol and several common medications (antihypertensives, antidepressants) can all contribute to ED.

conventional.remedy: Cardiovascular and diabetes risk assessment
conventional.note: New ED, especially in a younger man, can be an early marker of undiagnosed vascular disease or diabetes -- worth checking, not just treating the symptom.

ayurveda.remedy: Panax ginseng -- real but weak evidence, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Cochrane review, low-certainty evidence] A Cochrane review of 9 trials (587 men) found only a trivial effect on erectile function scores, with low-certainty evidence overall -- a real review exists, but the honest conclusion is that ginseng is not a convincingly effective treatment on current evidence.

yoga.remedy: Yoga for erectile dysfunction -- evidence gap, stated honestly (a commonly mis-cited claim)
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No proper comparative trial of yoga for ED exists. The one study sometimes cited for this was an uncontrolled pilot in a general yoga-camp population (not men diagnosed with ED, and with no exercise/walking comparison group) -- it does not show yoga is effective for ED, and is not presented here as evidence for that claim. The lifestyle-change evidence above (diet, exercise, weight loss) is the genuinely trial-backed option.

evidence.recovery: Many infant hydroceles resolve by age 1-2 without treatment; adult hydroceles usually need surgery if persistent, large or symptomatic
evidence.seekCareIf: A hydrocele that becomes painful, enlarges rapidly, or no longer transilluminates should be assessed promptly to exclude an underlying testicular tumour or other cause.
evidence.source: Commonly practised supportive care, not independently cited

conventional.remedy: Watchful waiting in infants
conventional.note: Many resolve on their own by age 1-2 without any treatment needed.

conventional.remedy: Supportive underwear for comfort with a large hydrocele
conventional.note: Simple comfort measure while awaiting review or surgery -- searched specifically for RCT evidence on conservative management of hydrocele and found none; this remains a common-sense comfort measure rather than a trial-proven treatment.

conventional.remedy: Surgical repair (hydrocelectomy) if persistent, large or symptomatic
conventional.note: The definitive treatment once a hydrocele doesn't resolve on its own or is causing symptoms.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for hydrocele
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] This is a structural fluid collection -- resolution or surgical repair are the evidence-based paths, not herbal treatment.

evidence.quote: Standard topical antifungals clear tinea reliably; tea tree oil, though widely promoted, has actually performed no better than placebo for fungal cure in the randomised trials that have tested it.
evidence.recovery: Usually clears within 2-4 weeks of consistent topical antifungal treatment; longer for scalp/nail involvement
evidence.seekCareIf: Widespread, atypical, or treatment-resistant tinea should prompt a check for undiagnosed diabetes or immunosuppression.
evidence.source: Tong MM et al., Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of tea tree oil for tinea pedis, Australas J Dermatol 1992

conventional.remedy: Topical antifungal (terbinafine/clotrimazole) applied as directed for the full course
conventional.note: First-line, reliable treatment -- stopping early because the rash looks better is the most common reason for recurrence.

conventional.remedy: Keep the area clean and dry; avoid tight synthetic clothing
conventional.note: Reduces the warm, moist conditions dermatophyte fungi need to thrive -- particularly relevant in India's humid climate.

conventional.remedy: Treat close contacts and avoid sharing towels/clothing
conventional.note: Tinea spreads by direct and fomite contact -- treating only the visible case risks reinfection.

ayurveda.remedy: Tea tree oil -- real trials, but honestly disappointing results
ayurveda.note: [Randomised controlled trials] Three RCTs tested tea tree oil for tinea; none showed it clearing the fungal infection better than placebo, though symptom comfort was sometimes similar to weak comparators. Not a substitute for standard topical antifungals.

ayurveda.remedy: Neem (Azadirachta indica) -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap] Despite long traditional use, no human clinical trial evidence was found for neem in this condition -- only preclinical/in vitro data. May be used traditionally alongside, not instead of, standard treatment.

evidence.quote: Permethrin cream and oral ivermectin work about equally well for scabies when dosed correctly -- but treating every household member at the same time, regardless of symptoms, is what actually determines whether treatment succeeds.
evidence.recovery: Itching can continue for 2-4 weeks after successful treatment as the skin reaction settles -- this doesn't mean treatment has failed
evidence.seekCareIf: Widespread crusted (Norwegian) scabies in an immunosuppressed or elderly patient needs prompt, more aggressive treatment.
evidence.source: Rosumeck S et al., Ivermectin and permethrin for treating scabies, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018

conventional.remedy: Permethrin 5% cream applied to the whole body as directed
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Roughly as effective as oral ivermectin with adequate dosing, and may act faster after a single application.

conventional.remedy: Treat ALL household/close contacts at the same time, regardless of symptoms
conventional.note: The single most important step -- missing even one untreated contact is the main cause of reinfection.

conventional.remedy: Wash bedding and clothing in hot water on the day of treatment
conventional.note: Mites do not survive long off the body, but this reduces reinfection risk from recently-used fabric.

ayurveda.remedy: Tea tree oil -- promising but unproven, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Preclinical evidence + an unresolved registered trial] Laboratory studies show it kills mites, and a proper trial comparing it with permethrin is registered but not yet reporting results -- promising, but not yet proven effective, and not a substitute for permethrin/ivermectin today.

ayurveda.remedy: Neem (Azadirachta indica) -- evidence gap, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap] Despite long traditional use, no human clinical trial evidence was found for neem in this condition -- only preclinical/in vitro data. May be used traditionally alongside, not instead of, standard treatment.

evidence.quote: Avoiding the trigger is the real treatment for contact dermatitis -- barrier creams and moisturisers give a modest, genuine protective effect on top of that, according to a Cochrane review, but they're not a substitute for identifying and avoiding what's causing it.
evidence.recovery: Usually settles within 1-3 weeks once the trigger is avoided and a flare is treated
evidence.seekCareIf: Rapidly spreading rash with facial/airway swelling suggests a severe allergic reaction, not simple contact dermatitis -- this needs emergency care.
evidence.source: Bauer A et al., Interventions for preventing occupational irritant hand dermatitis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018

conventional.remedy: Identify and avoid the trigger
conventional.note: The actual treatment -- common India-relevant triggers include kumkum/bindi adhesives, mehendi (henna) additives, footwear dyes, and occupational exposures (agriculture, construction), alongside jewellery, cosmetics and plants.

conventional.remedy: Barrier creams and/or moisturisers where re-exposure is hard to avoid entirely (e.g. occupational)
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] A modest but genuine protective effect -- low-certainty evidence, so this supports, and does not replace, avoiding the trigger where possible.

conventional.remedy: Emollients and a topical corticosteroid for the flare; oral antihistamine for itch
conventional.note: Standard treatment for the active flare once the trigger is identified.

ayurveda.remedy: Turmeric (curcumin) -- real evidence in other skin contexts, extrapolated here
ayurveda.note: [Randomised controlled trials, different conditions] RCTs support topical curcumin for wound healing (diabetic foot ulcers) and for psoriasis/radiodermatitis, but no trial has tested it specifically for contact dermatitis -- a reasonable extrapolation, not direct evidence.

evidence.quote: Warm compresses to help a small boil localise and drain are standard, guideline-recommended advice -- though, honestly, no randomised trial has specifically tested them; the recommendation rests on clinical consensus, not RCT evidence.
evidence.recovery: Small boils often drain and settle within a week or two with warm compresses; larger ones usually need incision and drainage
evidence.seekCareIf: Facial boils, fever, or spreading redness need urgent assessment rather than home drainage -- facial boils carry a risk of spread to the veins behind the eye.
evidence.source: Stevens DL et al., Practice Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Management of Skin and Soft Tissue Infections, IDSA, Clin Infect Dis 2014

conventional.remedy: Warm compresses several times a day for a small boil
conventional.note: [Guideline-level expert consensus, not RCT-tested] Standard advice to help the boil localise and drain naturally -- no randomised trial has specifically tested this, but it's the recommended first step in major treatment guidelines.

conventional.remedy: Do not squeeze or attempt to drain a large or facial boil yourself
conventional.note: Risks spreading the infection -- larger or fluctuant boils need clinical incision and drainage.

conventional.remedy: Check fasting glucose if boils are recurrent
conventional.note: Recurrent furunculosis is a recognised clue to undiagnosed diabetes -- worth screening for, not just treating each boil in isolation.

ayurveda.remedy: Turmeric (curcumin) -- real wound-healing evidence, extrapolated here
ayurveda.note: [Randomised controlled trial, different context] An RCT found topical turmeric improved diabetic foot ulcer healing -- no trial has tested it specifically for boils, so this is a reasonable extrapolation from related wound-healing evidence, not direct proof.

evidence.recovery: The patch usually fades over 1-2 weeks once the causative drug is stopped, sometimes leaving temporary darker skin behind
evidence.seekCareIf: Widespread blistering or skin sloughing with mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals) suggests Stevens-Johnson syndrome/TEN -- a medical emergency needing immediate hospital assessment, not home care.
evidence.source: Commonly practised supportive care, not independently cited

conventional.remedy: Stop and permanently avoid the causative drug
conventional.note: [Evidence gap for anything beyond this, stated honestly] This is the actual treatment -- no self-care measure beyond identifying and avoiding the drug has trial evidence. Common culprits are NSAIDs, sulfonamides and antimalarials, often taken over-the-counter without prescription.

conventional.remedy: Document the drug allergy clearly and tell every future prescriber/pharmacist
conventional.note: Prevents accidental re-exposure -- the reaction recurs at the exact same site every time the drug is taken again.

conventional.remedy: Topical corticosteroid for the lesion, if advised by a doctor
conventional.note: Standard symptomatic treatment for the individual patch -- not a substitute for identifying and avoiding the causative drug.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for fixed drug eruption
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] This is a drug-reaction diagnosis -- identifying and avoiding the causative drug is the only evidence-based path.

evidence.quote: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I) is recommended ahead of medication as the first treatment to try -- a major guideline made this a strong recommendation based on a meta-analysis of 20 randomised trials.
evidence.recovery: CBT-I typically shows benefit within 4-8 weeks of structured sessions; sleep hygiene advice alone is a much weaker, slower fix
evidence.seekCareIf: Excessive daytime sleepiness with loud snoring or witnessed pauses in breathing should prompt consideration of obstructive sleep apnoea instead.
evidence.source: Qaseem A et al., Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians, Ann Intern Med 2016

conventional.remedy: CBT for insomnia (CBT-I), ideally with a trained therapist
conventional.note: [Guideline, strong recommendation + meta-analysis of 20 RCTs] Recommended as the first treatment to try, ahead of medication -- more durable than sleeping tablets, which are a bridge, not a long-term solution.

conventional.remedy: Sleep hygiene measures (consistent bedtime, limiting caffeine/screens before bed)
conventional.note: [Evidence gap for the combined package as standalone treatment, stated honestly] Individual components have some supporting evidence, but a review found the standard sleep-hygiene advice package, on its own, has not been shown to be an effective treatment -- useful as a foundation alongside CBT-I, not a substitute for it.

ayurveda.remedy: Ashwagandha -- real evidence for stress/anxiety, not insomnia specifically, stated honestly
ayurveda.note: [Randomised controlled trial, different indication] A trial found ashwagandha reduced stress-scale scores and cortisol -- genuine evidence exists, but for stress/anxiety, not tested specifically for insomnia. Not presented here as an insomnia treatment without that direct evidence.

yoga.note: [Randomised controlled trials] Two real trials found mindfulness meditation improved sleep, with one showing it beat standard sleep hygiene education directly.

yoga.remedy: Yoga specifically -- weaker evidence than mindfulness, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Uncontrolled pilot study only] The evidence for yoga specifically (as opposed to seated mindfulness meditation) is a small pilot with no comparison group -- promising but far less established than mindfulness meditation above.

evidence.quote: Omega-3 fatty acids have real trial evidence for the depressive phase of bipolar disorder specifically -- but not for mania -- and should be seen as a minor adjunct alongside mood-stabiliser medication, not a replacement for it.
evidence.recovery: Highly variable and episode-dependent -- medication (mood stabilisers) is the primary evidence-based treatment; self-care measures are adjuncts, not substitutes
evidence.seekCareIf: Mania with psychotic features, or significant risk to self/others during an episode, needs urgent psychiatric assessment -- this is not something to manage with self-care alone.
evidence.source: Sarris J et al., Omega-3 for bipolar disorder: meta-analyses of use in mania and bipolar depression, J Clin Psychiatry 2011

conventional.remedy: Keep mood-stabiliser medication consistent -- never stop or adjust without medical advice
conventional.note: The primary evidence-based treatment; self-care supports but never replaces this.

conventional.remedy: Regular sleep-wake routine
conventional.note: Sleep disruption is a well-recognised trigger for mood episodes in clinical experience -- a stable routine is standard supportive advice.

conventional.remedy: Exercise -- evidence gap for mood stability specifically, stated honestly
conventional.note: [Randomised controlled trial] A dedicated small trial found exercise improved general functioning but showed no significant difference in mood symptoms between groups -- reasonable for general health, but not yet proven to stabilise mood on its own.

ayurveda.remedy: Omega-3 fatty acids, as an adjunct during depressive episodes specifically
ayurveda.note: [Meta-analysis] Found a significant effect for bipolar depression but explicitly not for mania -- a minor adjunct alongside, never instead of, mood-stabiliser medication.

yoga.remedy: General stress-reduction practice -- evidence gap for bipolar disorder specifically, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Evidence gap] No bipolar-specific yoga trial was identified. May support general wellbeing alongside, not instead of, medication and psychiatric follow-up.

evidence.quote: Motivational interviewing has a real, Cochrane-reviewed effect on alcohol use -- though honestly, that benefit tends to fade at longer follow-up, so it works best as part of ongoing structured support, not a one-off conversation.
evidence.recovery: Highly variable -- depends on severity of dependence and engagement with structured support; withdrawal itself typically settles within a week with appropriate medical supervision
evidence.seekCareIf: Hallucinations, seizures, confusion or marked agitation during withdrawal need urgent, monitored medical detoxification -- this is not something to manage alone at home.
evidence.source: Smedslund G et al., Motivational interviewing for substance abuse, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011

conventional.remedy: Motivational interviewing / structured counselling
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, 59 trials] A real, moderate short-term effect on reducing alcohol use compared with no treatment -- though the benefit fades at longer follow-up compared with other treatment-as-usual approaches, so ongoing engagement matters more than a single conversation.

conventional.remedy: Thiamine (vitamin B1) supplementation if dependent or malnourished
conventional.note: [Standard of care, though the Cochrane review itself found thin RCT-level dosing evidence] Universally recommended to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy before or alongside glucose -- an honest note that the ideal dose/route hasn't been nailed down by strong trials, but the practice itself is standard and not optional.

conventional.remedy: Do not attempt to self-detox from heavy, long-standing drinking
conventional.note: Withdrawal can be medically dangerous (seizures, delirium tremens) -- medically supervised detoxification is safer than stopping abruptly alone.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for alcohol use disorder
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Structured counselling and, where needed, medically supervised detoxification are the evidence-based paths.

evidence.quote: Exposure and response prevention (a specific form of CBT) outperforms both SSRIs and older medications for OCD in a large network meta-analysis of over 50 trials -- it's genuinely the first-line treatment, not just one option among several.
evidence.recovery: Often improves significantly with a full course of ERP (typically 12-20 sessions); many need an SSRI alongside, often at higher doses than used for depression
evidence.seekCareIf: Obsessions involving harm to others, plus a plan or intent, need urgent psychiatric risk assessment -- this is not 'just OCD' and shouldn't be managed with self-care alone.
evidence.source: Skapinakis P et al., Pharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions for management of obsessive-compulsive disorder in adults: a systematic review and network meta-analysis, Lancet Psychiatry 2016

conventional.remedy: Exposure and response prevention (ERP) with a trained therapist
conventional.note: [Network meta-analysis, 54 trials] Outperformed SSRIs and clomipramine -- genuinely first-line, not just an alternative to medication.

conventional.remedy: SSRIs, often at higher doses than used for depression
conventional.note: An effective adjunct or alternative when ERP alone isn't enough or isn't accessible -- discuss dosing specifically for OCD with a psychiatrist.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for OCD
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] ERP and, where needed, SSRIs are the evidence-based paths.

yoga.remedy: Kundalini yoga meditation, as an add-on -- thin evidence, stated honestly
yoga.note: [Small randomised controlled trial, add-on only] One trial in treatment-refractory OCD found greater improvement with Kundalini yoga meditation added to usual care versus a relaxation-response comparator -- a real but small, preliminary finding, not compared head-to-head with ERP or medication, and not a substitute for either.

evidence.quote: Family-based therapy for adolescents with anorexia wasn't better than individual therapy right at the end of treatment, but a randomised trial found it led to significantly more people in full remission a year later -- the real benefit shows up in durability, not an immediate difference.
evidence.recovery: Highly variable and often prolonged -- multidisciplinary care (medical, dietetic, psychological) gives the best outcomes; family-based therapy shows its advantage over the following year, not immediately
evidence.seekCareIf: Bradycardia, hypotension, electrolyte disturbance, or a very low BMI need urgent medical stabilisation alongside psychiatric care -- these can be physically life-threatening and are not a self-care situation.
evidence.source: Lock J et al., Randomized clinical trial comparing family-based treatment with adolescent-focused individual therapy for adolescents with anorexia nervosa, Arch Gen Psychiatry 2010

conventional.remedy: Multidisciplinary care (medical, dietetic, psychological) -- do not try to manage this alone
