conventional.note: This is a condition that can be physically life-threatening -- self-care is not a substitute for professional multidisciplinary treatment.

conventional.remedy: Family-based therapy, specifically for adolescents
conventional.note: [Randomised controlled trial] Not superior to individual therapy immediately, but significantly more likely to produce full remission at 6-12 month follow-up -- the benefit is in durability, not an immediate difference.

conventional.remedy: Regular medical monitoring (weight/BMI, ECG, electrolytes) especially if purging
conventional.note: Catches physically dangerous complications (bradycardia, electrolyte disturbance) early -- essential alongside, not instead of, psychological treatment.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy has trial evidence for eating disorders
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Given the physical risks involved, do not delay or substitute urgent medical and psychological care with alternative remedies.

yoga.remedy: Exercise and yoga -- an important caution, not a recommendation
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly with a clinical caution] No trial evidence supports yoga or exercise as a treatment here, and both can become part of compensatory or compulsive behaviour patterns in eating disorders -- any physical activity should only be introduced under the guidance of the treating team, not as self-directed self-care.

evidence.source: National Eye Institute (NEI)
evidence.quote: The only way to treat a cataract is with surgery to remove it -- there is no medicine, eye drop, exercise, or diet that will make a cataract go away once it has formed.
evidence.recovery: Vision does not improve on its own; cataract surgery is same-day and highly effective when the cataract meaningfully affects daily life.
evidence.seekCareIf: Sudden vision loss, eye pain, or a rapid change over days -- these are NOT typical of cataract and need urgent assessment for another cause.

conventional.remedy: Cataract surgery (lens replacement) when vision affects daily life
conventional.note: NEI / AAO consensus: surgery is the only effective treatment once a cataract has formed. No supplement or medical therapy reverses or slows an established cataract.

conventional.remedy: UV-blocking sunglasses (wraparound, blocking <400nm)
conventional.note: [Case-control study] High-altitude mountain guides with heavy unprotected UV exposure had significantly more cataract and cataract surgery than controls; wearing UV-blocking eyewear was independently protective (OR 0.50-0.53). No RCT exists (ethically impossible to randomise decades of sun exposure), but this is well-supported preventive advice, not a proven cure.

conventional.remedy: Updated glasses prescription while awaiting/deciding on surgery
conventional.note: NEI: a stronger glasses prescription, brighter reading light, or anti-glare lenses can temporarily improve function in early cataract, though they do not treat the cataract itself.

ayurveda.remedy: Triphala eye-care preparations (Netra Tarpana/Netra Basti) -- adjunctive only
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Ayurveda ophthalmology (Netra Chikitsa) traditionally uses Triphala-based preparations for general eye nourishment; no controlled trial demonstrates reversal or slowing of an established cataract (Linga Nasha of Timira). Should not delay surgical referral once vision is significantly affected.

ayurveda.remedy: General Ayurveda dietary/lifestyle measures for eye health (Ahara-Vihara for Netra Roga)
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Classical texts describe general dietary and lifestyle measures for eye health; no evidence base specific to reversing lens opacity was found in the peer-reviewed literature.

evidence.source: JAMA (He et al., Guangzhou outdoor-time cluster RCT)
evidence.quote: Adding 40 minutes of daily outdoor time at school reduced the 3-year incidence of myopia from 39.5% to 30.4% compared with schools without the intervention.
evidence.recovery: Refractive error itself does not resolve without correction; glasses/contacts/refractive surgery correct vision immediately, and outdoor time can slow -- not reverse -- progression in children.
evidence.seekCareIf: Sudden, painful, or rapidly progressive vision change, or vision loss not corrected by glasses -- these need assessment for a different underlying cause.

conventional.remedy: Corrective glasses or contact lenses
conventional.note: Standard first-line correction for any refractive error; immediately effective and does not need clinical-trial justification here as the correction itself is the diagnostic test.

conventional.remedy: 40+ minutes/day outdoor time for children (myopia prevention/slowing)
conventional.note: [Genuine cluster-RCT] 12 schools, 1,903 grade-1 children: an extra 40 min/day outdoor class time cut 3-year myopia incidence from 39.5% to 30.4% (absolute difference -9.1%, 95% CI -14.1 to -4.1%, P<.001). This followed an earlier large observational study (Sydney Myopia Study) that first flagged the association. One of the few genuinely RCT-proven preventive measures in this entire dataset.

conventional.remedy: Regular eye check-ups to update prescription
conventional.note: AAO/NEI: refractive error can change over time, especially in growing children -- periodic re-checks keep correction accurate.

ayurveda.remedy: General Ayurveda supportive eye-care measures (Netra Raksha)
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Traditional supportive eye-care practices are described for general ocular health; no controlled trial demonstrates correction or reversal of refractive error itself, which is a structural/optical mismatch, not a disease process.

yoga.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: "eye exercises" to cure or reverse refractive error
yoga.note: [Systematic review/meta-analysis, explicitly negative] 11 studies, 921 participants: visual acuity did not improve versus control after eye-exercise programmes, and refractive error showed no difference from control. A separate cohort of ~20,000 rural Chinese schoolchildren also found no effect of eye exercises on vision change. The authors explicitly recommend retiring decades-old eye-exercise policies. Included here ONLY to state plainly that this common belief is not supported -- glasses/contacts and outdoor time (above) are the evidence-based options.

[Systematic review, mixed evidence] Scoping review of yoga for eye health: some studies show reduced eye strain/improved visual comfort -- evidence is for general eye strain/ocular function, not this specific condition, and trials were small.

evidence.source: DCCT Research Group, NEJM 1993
evidence.quote: Intensive glycaemic therapy reduced the risk of new retinopathy by 76% and slowed progression of existing retinopathy by 54%, compared with conventional therapy.
evidence.recovery: Existing damage is not reversed by control measures alone -- the goal is to prevent further progression and vision loss; laser/injection treatment addresses damage that has already occurred.
evidence.seekCareIf: Any sudden vision loss, new floaters, flashes of light, or a curtain/shadow across vision -- these need same-day ophthalmology assessment (possible retinal haemorrhage or detachment).

conventional.remedy: Tight blood-glucose control (HbA1c target as advised by your doctor)
conventional.note: [Landmark RCT] DCCT: 1,441 type 1 diabetics, 6.5-yr follow-up -- intensive therapy cut new-retinopathy risk by 76% (95% CI 62-85%) and slowed progression of existing retinopathy by 54% (95% CI 39-66%). Among the strongest evidence in all of diabetes medicine. Benefit persists years later even after the groups' HbA1c levels converge ("metabolic memory").

conventional.remedy: Blood-pressure control to standard targets (not ultra-aggressive)
conventional.note: [RCT, UKPDS 38] Tight BP control (<150/85 vs <180/105) cut 2-step retinopathy deterioration by 34% and vision loss by 47%. IMPORTANT nuance: a later, larger trial (ACCORD-Eye) found pushing BP even lower (<120mmHg) did NOT add further retinopathy benefit over standard targets -- so "control to your doctor's target" is supported, but "as low as possible" is not.

conventional.remedy: Fenofibrate (prescription lipid medication) -- ask your doctor
conventional.note: [Two large RCTs: FIELD n=9,795, ACCORD-Eye n=2,856] Fenofibrate reduced need for laser treatment (3.4% vs 4.9%, HR 0.69) and slowed 2-step progression in those with existing retinopathy (14.6% to 3.1% in a sub-analysis). Notably, the benefit did NOT correlate with cholesterol levels -- the mechanism is still unclear. This is a prescription decision to discuss with your physician, not a supplement.

conventional.remedy: Annual (or doctor-advised interval) dilated eye screening
conventional.note: American Diabetes Association position statement: regular screening catches sight-threatening changes before symptoms appear, since retinopathy is often asymptomatic in its early, most treatable stage.

ayurveda.remedy: General Madhumeha (diabetes) dietary discipline as supportive care
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Classical Ayurveda frames Timira/Netra Roga arising from Madhumeha as needing control of the root Dosha imbalance; no controlled trial isolates an Ayurveda-specific effect on retinopathy itself, separate from general glycaemic control (see conventional measures above, which are the evidence-based lever).

evidence.source: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (hordeolum)
evidence.quote: We did not find any evidence for or against the effectiveness of non-surgical interventions for the treatment of hordeolum.
evidence.recovery: Most styes drain and settle within 1-2 weeks; chalazia can take longer (weeks to a couple of months) and occasionally need in-clinic drainage.
evidence.seekCareIf: Spreading redness/swelling beyond the eyelid, fever, reduced eye movement, or drowsiness -- these suggest a spreading infection (orbital cellulitis) needing urgent care, not a simple stye.

conventional.remedy: Warm compress, 10-15 minutes, several times a day
conventional.note: [Honest evidence gap] Standard first-line advice in every clinical guideline and textbook -- but three successive Cochrane reviews (2010/2013/2017) each explicitly found ZERO randomised trials testing warm compresses (or any non-surgical hordeolum treatment) against no treatment. It is biologically plausible (softens the blocked gland's contents and promotes drainage) and essentially risk-free, but it is guideline-consensus, not RCT-proven -- the same evidence gap found for furunculosis in a related entry.

conventional.remedy: Do not squeeze or attempt to pop the lump
conventional.note: Standard clinical advice: squeezing can spread infection deeper into the eyelid tissue or push it toward the eye.

conventional.remedy: Lid hygiene (gentle cleaning of the eyelid margin)
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, 34 RCTs, 2,169 participants -- weak-to-moderate] Lid hygiene may give symptomatic relief for related eyelid-gland conditions (blepharitis), but the same review states there is no strong evidence for curing the underlying gland blockage/inflammation -- framed here as reasonable, low-risk supportive care, not a proven cure or guaranteed preventive.

conventional.remedy: In-clinic incision and drainage, or steroid injection, for a persistent chalazion
conventional.note: AAO: reserved for lumps that do not resolve after several weeks of warm compresses.

ayurveda.remedy: Triphala eye irrigation / general Netra Chikitsa supportive measures
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Triphala-based preparations have direct clinical-trial support for acute conjunctivitis (Abhisyanda) specifically, not for a discrete eyelid-gland lump (closer to classical Anjananamika) -- included as a general supportive measure only, not as trial-proven for this specific condition.

evidence.source: DREAM Study Research Group, NEJM 2018
evidence.quote: Among patients with moderate-to-severe dry eye disease, daily supplementation with 3g of fish-oil-derived omega-3 fatty acids for 12 months did not provide greater symptom or sign relief than placebo.
evidence.recovery: Chronic, relapsing-remitting condition -- the goal is ongoing symptom management rather than a one-time cure.
evidence.seekCareIf: Eye pain, light sensitivity, or reduced vision alongside dryness -- these need assessment to rule out corneal damage or another cause.

conventional.remedy: Artificial tears / lubricant eye drops, used regularly
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, 43 RCTs, 3,497 participants] Universally recommended first-line therapy and biologically sound, but the review found low-certainty evidence overall -- mostly due to trial-design heterogeneity and 18 additional unpublished registered trials with no available results (a publication-bias signal), not because tears don't work. Frame as standard first-line and low-risk, not as formally 'proven superior to placebo' in head-to-head trials.

conventional.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: omega-3 fish-oil supplements reliably relieve dry eye
conventional.note: [Largest, best-designed RCT] DREAM study, NIH-funded, 535 patients with moderate-to-severe dry eye, 3g/day omega-3 vs olive-oil placebo for 12 months: NO significant difference in symptom score (-13.9 vs -12.5 points, 95% CI -5.0 to 1.1, P=.21) or any objective sign (tear break-up time, corneal staining, Schirmer test). A broader Cochrane review found the wider evidence base 'uncertain and inconsistent.' Included here specifically to correct the common belief that omega-3 supplements are a proven dry-eye remedy.

conventional.remedy: 20-20-20 rule during screen use (every 20 min, look 20 feet away for 20 sec)
conventional.note: [Mechanistically sound, consensus-recommended -- honest evidence gap] Reduced blink rate and sustained near-focus during screen use is a well-documented mechanism for tear-film instability, and this is universal clinical/ergonomic advice, but no dedicated randomised trial of the specific 20-20-20 protocol against a control arm was found. Low-risk and reasonable to follow.

conventional.remedy: Room humidification / avoiding direct air drafts (fans, AC, car vents)
conventional.note: [Observational/occupational epidemiology, honest evidence gap] Reviews of office/occupational eye symptoms support that relative humidity above ~40% benefits the tear film, and low humidity plus reduced blink rate is a specific risk factor -- but no dedicated RCT of home/office humidifiers for dry-eye outcomes was found. Reasonable, low-risk environmental modification.

ayurveda.remedy: Netra Tarpana / Ghrita-based eye treatments -- adjunctive only
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Classical Ayurveda ophthalmology describes ghee-based Netra Tarpana for dryness-type eye conditions (Shushkakshipaka has some conceptual overlap); no controlled trial specific to modern-diagnosed dry eye disease was found in the peer-reviewed literature.

evidence.source: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews (Offringa 2021)
evidence.quote: Antipyretic agents did not reduce the recurrence of febrile seizures.
evidence.recovery: The seizure itself typically resolves within a few minutes with full recovery within an hour; most children outgrow the tendency by age 5-6 and it does not cause brain damage.
evidence.seekCareIf: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, focal features (affecting only one side), or incomplete recovery within an hour -- call emergency services. Any FIRST seizure should still be seen urgently to exclude meningitis or another cause.

conventional.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: giving paracetamol/ibuprofen during a fever to prevent another febrile seizure
conventional.note: [Cochrane review + RCT, explicitly negative] A 2021 Cochrane review found antipyretics did not reduce febrile-seizure recurrence. A separate placebo-controlled RCT of 231 children followed for 2 years reached the same conclusion. This is one of the most common and understandable parental beliefs, and it is not supported -- antipyretics can be given for the child's comfort during a fever, but not as seizure prevention.

conventional.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: tepid sponging/cool baths to bring the fever down faster
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, explicitly negative] Found tepid sponging was less effective than antipyretic medication at reducing fever, and caused more discomfort (shivering) in children. Not recommended as a fever-control measure.

conventional.remedy: During the seizure: lay the child on their side, do not restrain them or put anything in their mouth, time the episode
conventional.note: Standard first-aid guidance -- protects the airway and gives an accurate duration to report, which is the single most useful piece of information for the treating clinician.

conventional.remedy: Reassurance: a first simple febrile seizure carries only a modest epilepsy-risk increase
conventional.note: [Epidemiological review] About 1-2% of children with a simple febrile seizure later develop epilepsy, compared with roughly 0.5% of children who never had one -- a real but small increase, not the dramatic risk many parents fear. Complex febrile seizures (focal, prolonged, or recurring within 24 hours) carry a higher risk (6-8%) and need closer follow-up.

ayurveda.remedy: General Bala Roga (paediatric) supportive care for fever
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Classical Ayurveda paediatrics (Kaumarabhritya) describes general fever-management measures in children; no controlled trial addresses febrile seizure specifically, and reassurance/safety-netting (left column) is the evidence-based priority here.

yoga.remedy: General relaxation / comfort measures for the child
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No dedicated paediatric trial for this specific condition was found; included only as a general comfort/relaxation practice suitable for a distressed child or worried parent.

evidence.source: American Academy of Pediatrics Clinical Practice Guideline (Ralston 2014)
evidence.quote: Clinicians should not administer... bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, or antibiotics to infants and children with a diagnosis of bronchiolitis in any setting.
evidence.recovery: Symptoms typically peak around day 3-5 and resolve over 1-2 weeks; the cough can linger for several weeks after the infant is otherwise well.
evidence.seekCareIf: Apnoea (pauses in breathing), grunting, marked chest recession, nasal flaring, or a low oxygen reading -- seek urgent hospital assessment. Poor feeding (less than half normal intake) is also a key marker of severity in an infant.

conventional.remedy: Supportive care: small frequent feeds, minimal handling, upright positioning
conventional.note: AAP guideline: mainstay of management -- there is no medicine that treats the virus itself, so comfort and hydration are what genuinely help.

conventional.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: bronchodilators (e.g. salbutamol) reliably help bronchiolitis
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, 30 trials, 1,992 infants, explicitly negative] Bronchodilators did not improve oxygen levels, did not reduce hospitalisation, and did not shorten illness duration -- despite being commonly reached for because bronchiolitis can sound like asthma. Not recommended for routine use.

conventional.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: steroids (oral or inhaled) speed up recovery
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, explicitly negative] Found no improvement in length of hospital stay, clinical severity score, or admission/readmission rates from systemic or inhaled corticosteroids, in hospital or in the emergency department.

conventional.remedy: Nasal saline drops with gentle bulb suction before feeds
conventional.note: [Honest evidence gap] Widely recommended and low-risk, but the evidence for meaningful benefit is genuinely thin -- a 2023 RCT comparing enhanced vs minimal suctioning after emergency-department discharge found no difference in return visits or feeding/sleeping outcomes. Reasonable comfort measure, not a proven treatment.

conventional.remedy: Nebulised hypertonic (3%) saline -- only in a clinical/hospital setting
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, low-to-very-low certainty] May modestly reduce length of hospital stay (~9.6 hours) and improve severity scores, but the certainty of evidence is low due to inconsistency across trials. Not a home remedy -- requires nebulisation equipment and monitoring.

conventional.remedy: SAFETY: do NOT give honey to an infant under 12 months for cough
conventional.note: [Established safety evidence] Honey can contain Clostridium botulinum spores, which a baby's immature gut cannot yet neutralise, risking infant botulism. This is a genuine safety point, not just general caution -- honey is a common home cough remedy in Indian households and is unsafe before 12 months regardless of source or preparation.

evidence.quote: Acyclovir therapy, initiated within 24 hours of the onset of rash, reduced the duration of symptomatic illness by about 24 hours in otherwise healthy children.
evidence.recovery: New spots usually stop appearing within 5-7 days; the illness is no longer contagious once all lesions have crusted over, usually 1-2 weeks from onset.

conventional.remedy: Calamine lotion and oral antihistamines for itch

conventional.remedy: Keep nails short and cool, loose clothing to reduce scratching

conventional.remedy: Aciclovir is NOT routinely recommended for otherwise-healthy children

conventional.remedy: SAFETY: avoid aspirin/salicylate-containing medicines in a child with chickenpox

conventional.remedy: For the future: varicella vaccination

evidence.quote: There is no specific treatment for hand, foot, and mouth disease. Symptoms usually go away in 7 to 10 days.

conventional.remedy: Paracetamol or ibuprofen for fever and mouth-pain discomfort

conventional.remedy: No evidence-based treatment beyond supportive care

conventional.remedy: Know the rare red flags: lethargy, myoclonic jerks, unsteadiness

evidence.source: American Heart Association Scientific Statement (McCrindle 2017)
evidence.quote: Kawasaki disease is an acute vasculitis of childhood that leads to coronary artery aneurysms in approximately 25% of untreated cases.
evidence.recovery: With timely IVIG treatment, most children recover fully; the entire point of urgent treatment is to prevent the coronary-artery damage that untreated disease can cause.
evidence.seekCareIf: This condition IS the red flag. Persistent high fever for 5+ days in a young child, plus any of: rash, red eyes, red/cracked lips or strawberry tongue, swollen hands/feet, or neck gland swelling -- needs same-day paediatric assessment, not a wait-and-see approach.

conventional.remedy: There is genuinely no home-remedy or self-care angle here -- this is worth saying plainly
conventional.note: [Honest framing, not a hedge] Unlike most conditions in this app, Kawasaki disease has no meaningful lifestyle, dietary, or supportive self-care role. It is entirely a time-critical hospital-treatment diagnosis. Presenting a self-care section for this condition would risk delaying the one thing that actually matters: getting the child seen urgently.

conventional.remedy: IVIG (intravenous immunoglobulin) plus high-dose aspirin, given within the first 10 days
conventional.note: [Landmark RCT] The original placebo-controlled trial found coronary-artery abnormalities in 23% of children on aspirin alone vs 8% with IVIG added, at 2 weeks -- roughly a 3-fold reduction. A later trial confirmed a single large IVIG dose is more effective than the same total dose split over 4 days.

conventional.remedy: Treatment works best within 10 days of fever onset -- earlier is better still
conventional.note: [Guideline + trial evidence] The 10-day window is when treatment most reliably prevents coronary damage; treatment given even later still has value (calming inflammation) but is less effective at preventing aneurysms specifically, which is why urgent same-day assessment for prolonged unexplained fever matters so much.

conventional.remedy: Follow-up echocardiograms and paediatric cardiology review after the acute illness
conventional.note: AHA guideline: standard practice to monitor coronary arteries even after successful treatment, since some change can still develop or evolve over the following weeks.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurveda correlate offered for this condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Kawasaki disease is a modern-recognised, time-critical vasculitis with no established classical correlate and no meaningful adjunct role for supportive therapies during the acute, urgent phase. Inventing a plausible-sounding traditional remedy here would be actively misleading for a not-to-miss emergency-adjacent diagnosis.

yoga.remedy: For the parent, while awaiting urgent assessment: a brief grounding/breathing practice
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Not a treatment for Kawasaki disease itself -- included only as a general stress-relief practice for an understandably frightened parent, with the same eye-health/general-relaxation review as its closest available source. Does not substitute for, or delay, urgent medical assessment.

evidence.source: Suissa et al., NEJM 2000 (landmark cohort study)
evidence.quote: Regular use of inhaled corticosteroids was associated with a reduced rate of death from asthma, with a further decrease for each additional canister dispensed.
evidence.recovery: Not curable, but very well controllable -- most people on appropriate treatment live symptom-free, normal lives with normal activity levels.
evidence.seekCareIf: Increasing reliever-inhaler use, night-time symptoms becoming more frequent, or a fall in peak flow -- these signal poor control and rising exacerbation risk, and need a treatment review before a full flare-up happens.

conventional.remedy: MYTH TO AVOID: steroid inhalers are dangerous for long-term daily use and best avoided
conventional.note: [Landmark cohort study, explicitly positive] A large Canadian cohort found regular inhaled-corticosteroid use REDUCED the rate of death from asthma, with a further reduction for each additional canister used over the prior year. Fear of long-term steroid inhaler use is a genuine and understandable barrier to adherence, but the evidence points the opposite way to the common fear -- daily preventer use is what keeps asthma controlled and safe.

conventional.remedy: Take the prescribed inhaled corticosteroid (preventer) daily, even when feeling well
conventional.note: Standard GINA/BTS guidance: control comes from regular daily use, not from using the reliever inhaler more often when symptoms appear.

conventional.remedy: Reduce exposure to outdoor and indoor air pollution where practical
conventional.note: [Indian population-level evidence] Studies specifically from India (Bangalore time-series data; national survey data) found both outdoor particulate matter/NO2 and indoor air pollution are real, measurable drivers of asthma exacerbations and poorer control -- a genuinely India-relevant counselling point beyond generic trigger-avoidance advice.

conventional.remedy: Use a written asthma action plan and track peak flow if advised
conventional.note: Standard guideline advice -- helps recognise early loss of control before it becomes an emergency.

evidence.source: Anthonisen et al., JAMA 1994 (Lung Health Study)
evidence.quote: Participants in the smoking-intervention groups showed significantly smaller declines in FEV1 than the control group, with sustained quitters showing the largest benefit.
evidence.recovery: Not reversible, but progression can be genuinely slowed -- the single biggest lever is removing the causative smoke exposure, whether tobacco or biomass cooking fuel.
evidence.seekCareIf: Worsening breathlessness, increased sputum volume/colour change, or fever despite treatment -- these suggest an exacerbation or an alternative diagnosis needing reassessment, not just 'more of the same.'

conventional.remedy: Stop smoking -- and stop biomass/occupational smoke exposure specifically
conventional.note: [Landmark RCT, 5,887 participants] The defining trial found smoking cessation significantly slowed the rate of FEV1 decline, with sustained quitters benefiting most -- this remains the single most effective intervention. In Indian women with COPD who have never smoked, biomass cooking-fuel smoke (wood, dung, crop residue) is a documented cause of the same lung-function decline and needs the same explicit counselling, not just a 'smoker' assumption.

conventional.remedy: Improve kitchen ventilation or switch to cleaner cooking fuel (LPG) where possible
conventional.note: [Indian cohort study] Pre-menopausal Indian women exposed to biomass smoke showed measurable lung-function decrement and COPD development even without any smoking history -- a genuinely different at-risk group than the Western 'smoker' stereotype.

conventional.remedy: Pulmonary rehabilitation (structured exercise + education programme)
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Found consistent, clinically meaningful improvements in quality of life and exercise capacity -- one of the best-evidenced non-drug interventions in COPD, though access in India is often limited outside larger centres.

conventional.remedy: Annual influenza vaccination and pneumococcal vaccination
conventional.note: Standard guideline advice -- reduces the risk of infection-triggered exacerbations.

evidence.source: Shaw et al., Respirology 2019 (tuberculous pleural effusion review)
evidence.quote: Pleural tuberculosis accounts for a substantial proportion of pleural effusions in high-TB-burden settings.
evidence.recovery: Recovery depends entirely on treating the underlying cause -- heart failure, infection, TB, or malignancy -- rather than on managing the fluid itself as a standalone problem.
evidence.seekCareIf: A large effusion causing significant breathlessness, or one that is rapidly reaccumulating or bloodstained, needs urgent drainage and work-up rather than a wait-and-see approach.

evidence.quote: Exercise programmes, whether home-based or supervised, improved movement and physical function compared with no exercise, with supervised group exercise showing greater benefit than home exercise alone.

conventional.remedy: Regular movement and exercise -- the opposite instinct to most back pain
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Both home-based and supervised exercise improved spinal mobility and physical function; supervised group physiotherapy showed the greatest benefit. conventional.remedy: NSAIDs, taken regularly rather than only when pain flares

conventional.note: Standard physiotherapy advice to help maintain spinal extension and reduce the stooped posture that can develop over years -- practical, low-risk, and widely taught alongside formal exercise programmes.

conventional.remedy: Do not smoke

conventional.remedy: Mention new joint pain to whoever manages your psoriasis, don't assume it's unrelated

conventional.remedy: Continue standard psoriasis skin treatment alongside joint treatment

conventional.note: Standard monitoring practice -- lupus nephritis can develop with few symptoms early on, which is why routine urinalysis matters even between flares.

evidence.source: Prospective Indian hospital study, Tropical Doctor 2002
evidence.quote: Rheumatic heart disease was the most frequent underlying heart lesion in this Indian cohort of infective endocarditis patients.
evidence.recovery: Recovery depends entirely on prompt IV antibiotics (and surgery if needed) -- weeks of treatment, not a home-managed illness.
evidence.seekCareIf: This condition IS the reason for same-day admission if suspected -- embolic phenomena (stroke, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler's nodes), a new regurgitant murmur, or persistent fever despite antibiotics all need urgent reassessment.

conventional.remedy: This is a hospital-treatment condition -- there is no meaningful home-care substitute
conventional.note: [Honest framing] Weeks of IV antibiotics, guided by blood cultures taken before treatment starts, is the only evidence-based path -- delaying this for home remedies risks permanent valve damage or embolic stroke.

conventional.remedy: If you have known valve disease, a prosthetic valve, or a history of rheumatic fever, mention it proactively to any doctor treating a fever
conventional.note: [Indian cohort data] Rheumatic heart disease was the leading underlying predisposing lesion in this Indian endocarditis cohort -- a genuinely different risk profile than the injecting-drug-use/prosthetic-valve picture emphasised in most Western resources, and worth raising explicitly rather than waiting to be asked.

conventional.remedy: Dental antibiotic prophylaxis, if your cardiologist has specifically prescribed it for your condition
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, honest thin evidence] A 2022 Cochrane review found essentially no controlled-trial evidence proving dental antibiotic prophylaxis prevents endocarditis, despite being long-recommended for high-risk patients. conventional.remedy: Good general dental hygiene
conventional.note: Standard advice for anyone at elevated endocarditis risk -- reduces the bacteraemia that dental procedures (and poor oral health generally) can cause, independent of the prophylaxis-antibiotic question above.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurveda correlate offered for this condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Infective endocarditis is a life-threatening infection of a heart valve with no established classical correlate and no meaningful adjunct role during the acute, urgent phase. Inventing a plausible-sounding traditional remedy here would be actively misleading for a not-to-miss emergency-adjacent diagnosis.

evidence.source: Indian schoolchildren RHD screening study, Echocardiography 2021
evidence.quote: Systematic echocardiographic screening reveals a substantially higher prevalence of rheumatic heart disease than clinical (stethoscope-only) screening in Indian schoolchildren.
evidence.recovery: Mild disease can be monitored for years without symptoms; once severe or symptomatic, valve repair or replacement is the definitive treatment -- there is no medication that reverses valve damage.
evidence.seekCareIf: Syncope (especially with suspected aortic stenosis), signs of heart failure (worsening breathlessness, ankle swelling), or a new murmur with fever (possible endocarditis) all need prompt assessment.

conventional.remedy: Regular follow-up echocardiograms even while asymptomatic
conventional.note: Mild valve disease is often silent for years -- monitoring tracks progression so treatment starts at the right threshold, not too early or too late.

conventional.remedy: If you had rheumatic fever as a child, or grew up in a lower-resource setting in India, mention this explicitly at any cardiac assessment
conventional.note: [Indian screening study] Systematic echocardiographic screening found substantially more rheumatic heart disease in Indian schoolchildren than clinical examination alone detected -- rheumatic mitral stenosis remains a genuinely common cause here, distinct from the age-related degenerative aortic stenosis picture most Western resources default to.

conventional.remedy: Continue prescribed antibiotic prophylaxis if you have confirmed rheumatic heart disease
conventional.note: Standard secondary-prevention advice for confirmed rheumatic heart disease specifically -- distinct from the endocarditis dental-prophylaxis question, this is about preventing further rheumatic damage from recurrent streptococcal infection.

conventional.remedy: Pace exertion to your symptoms, and report new or worsening breathlessness promptly
conventional.note: Standard advice -- exertional symptoms are usually the first sign that a previously mild valve lesion has become significant enough to need intervention.

ayurveda.remedy: General Hridroga (heart disease) supportive dietary measures
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Classical texts describe general dietary guidance for heart conditions; no controlled trial specific to structural valve disease was found. Regular echocardiographic monitoring (left column) is the evidence-based priority for tracking when intervention becomes necessary.

evidence.source: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay
evidence.quote: Nonrandomised studies strongly suggest permanent pacing improves survival in patients with third-degree AV block, particularly if syncope has occurred.
evidence.recovery: A reversible cause (drugs, electrolytes, hypothyroidism) resolves once corrected; an irreversible conduction problem is definitively treated with a pacemaker, after which most people return to normal activity.
evidence.seekCareIf: Syncope with a slow pulse, Stokes-Adams attacks (sudden loss of consciousness without warning), or a known complete heart block on ECG all need urgent pacing assessment -- not routine follow-up.

conventional.remedy: Review all your medications with a doctor, don't stop or adjust them yourself
conventional.note: Beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, and digoxin are common reversible causes of bradycardia -- adjusting the dose or switching medication is often enough, but this needs medical review, not self-adjustment (stopping a beta-blocker abruptly can itself cause harm).

conventional.remedy: Mention any recent ivermectin use, verapamil overdose, or possible organophosphate/pesticide exposure
conventional.note: Regionally relevant reversible causes of bradycardia in India, alongside the standard drug review -- worth raising proactively since these aren't always the first things asked about.

conventional.remedy: A permanent pacemaker, if recommended for symptomatic or irreversible bradycardia
conventional.note: [Guideline, based on consistent non-randomised evidence] Pacing improves survival in complete heart block, particularly when syncope has occurred -- one of the more robust survival benefits from a single intervention in cardiology, even though the evidence comes from observational rather than randomised comparisons (a placebo-pacemaker RCT is not ethically feasible once the survival signal is this strong).

conventional.remedy: Avoid driving or operating machinery until assessed, if you have had a genuine blackout
conventional.note: Standard safety advice following any syncopal episode of unclear cause, pending medical assessment and, where relevant, local driving-license guidance.

ayurveda.remedy: General Hridroga (heart disease) and Rasavaha Srotas (circulation channel) supportive measures
ayurveda.note: [Review, honest evidence gap] Classical texts describe general circulatory-health guidance; no controlled trial specific to conduction-system disease (a distinct electrical, not circulatory-flow, problem) was found. Reversible-cause review and pacing assessment (left column) remain the evidence-based priorities.

evidence.source: Gupta P et al., Acta Parasitologica 2022 (systematic review)
evidence.quote: Prevalence of amoebiasis ranged from 3-23% in the asymptomatic population and 0.64-11% in symptomatic patients across 12 Indian states and 4 union territories.
evidence.recovery: Symptoms usually settle within days of starting treatment, but a second luminal-clearing drug is needed afterwards to prevent relapse.
evidence.seekCareIf: Fever with right-upper-quadrant pain (possible liver abscess), heavy ongoing blood loss, or symptoms not settling within a few days of starting treatment.

conventional.remedy: Metronidazole or tinidazole (tissue-active phase)
conventional.note: [Standard guideline therapy] Clears invasive trophozoites from the bowel wall and any liver abscess -- the first step in a two-drug course.

conventional.remedy: A luminal agent afterwards (e.g. paromomycin), even once symptoms have resolved
conventional.note: [Standard guideline therapy] Nitroimidazoles do not reliably clear intraluminal cysts -- skipping this second drug is a common cause of relapse.

conventional.remedy: Oral rehydration solution and adequate fluids
conventional.note: General supportive measure for any diarrhoeal illness -- replaces fluid and electrolyte losses while the specific treatment takes effect.

conventional.remedy: Safe drinking water and food hygiene to prevent reinfection
conventional.note: Faeco-oral transmission via contaminated water is the usual route -- boiling/filtering water and hand hygiene reduce both the initial infection and household spread.

ayurveda.remedy: Kutaja (Holarrhena antidysenterica) bark
ayurveda.note: [Small, uncontrolled human study] A 1986 open-label study of 40 Entamoeba histolytica cyst passers found a 70% "good response" (reduced loose stools, cramps, mucus) with Kutaja bark over 15 days. This is genuine human clinical data, but small, old, and not placebo-controlled -- not equivalent to a modern RCT, and not a substitute for the two-drug conventional course above.

yoga.remedy: Gentle Pawanmuktasana once acute symptoms have settled
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to amoebiasis recovery -- included only as a gentle, generally-used digestive-comfort practice for once the acute phase has passed, not during active bloody diarrhoea. Evidence link is a general digestive-health yoga RCT, not amoebiasis-specific.

evidence.source: Taylor-Robinson DC et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015
evidence.quote: Treating children known to be infected with a single dose of deworming drugs may increase weight gain over the following one to six months (low-quality evidence).
evidence.recovery: Usually clears within days of treatment; a repeat dose or whole-household treatment is sometimes needed, especially for pinworm.
evidence.seekCareIf: Severe colicky pain with vomiting and no bowel motions (possible obstruction from a heavy roundworm burden) -- rare, but needs urgent assessment, especially in a child.

conventional.remedy: Albendazole or mebendazole, as directed
conventional.note: [Meta-analysis] A 2024 meta-analysis found albendazole more effective against hookworm (~93%) than mebendazole (~77%), while both work well against roundworm (>95% egg reduction) -- the right drug can genuinely depend on which worm is most likely.

conventional.remedy: Treat the whole household together for pinworm
conventional.note: Pinworm eggs spread easily between household members via hands and shared surfaces -- treating only the symptomatic person often leads to reinfection.

conventional.remedy: Iron replacement if anaemic
conventional.note: Hookworm is a genuine, easily-missed cause of iron-deficiency anaemia -- treating the worm alone does not replace already-depleted iron stores.

conventional.remedy: Footwear outdoors and hand hygiene, especially before eating
conventional.note: Hookworm is acquired through bare skin contact with contaminated soil; handwashing reduces faeco-oral transmission of roundworm and pinworm.

ayurveda.remedy: Vidanga (Embelia ribes)
ayurveda.note: [In-vitro/animal pharmacology only] Classical Krimighna (anthelmintic) herb described in Charaka and Sushruta Samhita. Its active compound embelin shows anthelmintic activity in laboratory and animal studies -- but no human RCT was located, so this is pharmacological plausibility, not clinical proof, and does not replace albendazole/mebendazole.

yoga.remedy: General Pawanmuktasana practice for digestive comfort
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to helminthiasis -- included only as a generally-used gentle digestive-comfort practice, not a treatment for the infestation itself. Evidence link is a general digestive-health yoga RCT, not helminthiasis-specific.
yoga.video: Pawanmuktasana Series 1, 2, 3 -- Bihar School of Yoga

evidence.source: de la Iglesia-Garcia D et al., Gut 2017 (systematic review and meta-analysis)
evidence.quote: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy improved the coefficient of fat absorption and reduced faecal fat excretion compared with placebo, without significant adverse events.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, often lifelong condition managed rather than cured -- enzyme replacement, diet and treating complications aim to control symptoms and malabsorption.
evidence.seekCareIf: New-onset diabetes together with unexplained weight loss (also raises the question of pancreatic cancer, not just disease progression), severe pain, or jaundice.

conventional.remedy: Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) with meals
conventional.note: [Systematic review/meta-analysis] Improves fat absorption and reduces steatorrhoea and abdominal pain compared with placebo -- the best-evidenced single intervention for exocrine insufficiency.

conventional.remedy: Antioxidant supplementation, if your doctor suggests it
conventional.note: [Genuinely mixed evidence] A landmark 2009 double-blind RCT (n=127) found antioxidants significantly reduced painful days per month. A later 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis, though, questioned whether antioxidant therapy actually relieves pain overall -- the evidence base is real but does not point in one clear direction, and this is not a substitute for enzyme replacement or alcohol cessation.

conventional.remedy: Alcohol cessation, if alcohol is a contributing factor
conventional.note: Standard advice where alcohol is relevant -- but idiopathic and tropical calcific pancreatitis (a recognised pattern in parts of South India) occur without an alcohol history, so this is not always the driver and should not be assumed.

conventional.remedy: Smaller, more frequent, lower-fat meals
conventional.note: General dietary measure to reduce the digestive load on a gland with reduced exocrine capacity, alongside enzyme replacement rather than instead of it.

ayurveda.remedy: Ayurvedic management under specialist supervision, alongside conventional care
ayurveda.note: [Single case report only -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] One published Cureus case report describes an Ayurvedic protocol alongside standard care in one patient with hereditary/chronic pancreatitis. This is one patient's experience, not a controlled trial -- it does not establish that this approach works in general, and should never replace enzyme replacement, diabetes monitoring, or the standard workup for a new symptom.

yoga.remedy: Diaphragmatic breathing / gentle Pawanmuktasana between flares
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to chronic pancreatitis -- included only as a generally-used gentle relaxation/digestive-comfort practice for the periods between painful flares, never during an acute flare. Evidence link is a general digestive-health yoga RCT, not pancreatitis-specific.
yoga.video: Pawanmuktasana Series 1, 2, 3 -- Bihar School of Yoga

evidence.source: Gogoi MP et al., Lancet Regional Health Southeast Asia 2025 (ICiCLe multicentre India study, n=2695)
evidence.quote: Overall survival rates of children with ALL in high-income countries approach 90%, while outcomes in India on comparable protocols were substantially lower, driven largely by access to risk-stratified treatment and standardised testing.
evidence.recovery: Recovery depends entirely on prompt, correctly risk-stratified chemotherapy -- not a home-managed illness.
evidence.seekCareIf: This condition IS the reason for same-day haematology referral if suspected -- a pancytopenia pattern (anaemia + low platelets + abnormal white count together), unexplained bruising/bleeding, or bone pain in a child all warrant urgent same-day assessment.

conventional.remedy: This is a hospital-treatment condition -- there is no meaningful home-care substitute
conventional.note: [Honest framing] Combination chemotherapy per subtype and risk stratification is the only evidence-based path -- delaying this for home remedies risks disease progression.

conventional.remedy: Ask specifically about access to a centre offering risk-stratified treatment protocols
conventional.note: [Indian cohort data] The largest driver of the India-vs-high-income-country survival gap in this cohort was access to risk-stratified treatment and standardised genetic/MRD testing, not the disease biology itself -- worth actively seeking out a specialist centre rather than the nearest available one where possible.

conventional.remedy: Infection-precaution awareness during and after chemotherapy
conventional.note: [Guideline] Standard practice during periods of neutropenia includes prompt reporting of fever, avoiding raw/undercooked food and crowded sick-contact settings, and good hand hygiene -- reduces serious infection risk while immunity is suppressed.

conventional.remedy: Gentle, supervised physical activity between treatment cycles, once cleared by the treating team
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] A review of exercise programmes during and after childhood cancer treatment found benefit for fatigue and physical deconditioning -- an adjunct to recovery, not a cancer treatment itself, and only once medically cleared (e.g. platelet count checked before anything vigorous).

ayurveda.remedy: Ayurvedic quality-of-life support alongside chemotherapy, only with your oncologist's knowledge
ayurveda.note: [Human study, general cancer population -- not condition-specific] A 2014 study found combinations of Ayurvedic drugs alongside chemotherapy improved quality-of-life scores and reduced drug toxicity in cancer patients generally. This was not a leukaemia- or lymphoma-specific trial, so treat it as supportive evidence, not proof for this exact condition. Only start alongside chemotherapy with your oncologist's knowledge -- some herbo-mineral formulations can interact with chemotherapy drugs, and this is never a substitute for or reason to delay chemotherapy itself.

yoga.remedy: Calm breathing practice for the anxious wait between tests and treatment cycles
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Not a treatment for the underlying disease -- included only as a general stress-relief practice for the anxiety that naturally comes with a cancer workup, with the same general-relaxation evidence as its closest available source.
yoga.video: 1 Minute Meditation for Quick Stress Relief -- brief grounding practice

evidence.source: The impact of tuberculosis misdiagnosis in Hodgkin lymphoma patients, Indian J Med Res 2025
evidence.quote: More than 10 per cent of the participants in this Indian cohort received empirical anti-tubercular therapy before their diagnosis of Hodgkin lymphoma, leading to a longer duration of symptoms, a higher stage of disease at diagnosis, and lower serum albumin.
evidence.recovery: Recovery depends on chemotherapy +/- radiotherapy per subtype and stage -- not a home-managed illness.
evidence.seekCareIf: A node over 2cm, hard, fixed, or persisting beyond 4-6 weeks without an obvious infective cause needs biopsy. If a course of anti-TB treatment has been tried without response, that itself is a reason to push for biopsy rather than extending or repeating the anti-TB course.

conventional.remedy: If persistent lymphadenopathy has been treated empirically for TB without a clear response, push for a lymph node biopsy
conventional.note: [Indian cohort data] Over 10% of Hodgkin lymphoma patients in this Indian cohort had empirical anti-TB therapy first, which measurably worsened their disease stage and outcomes by the time lymphoma was correctly diagnosed -- appropriate as a first differential given how common TB is in India, but persistence without response should prompt biopsy, not a longer or repeated anti-TB course.

conventional.remedy: Insist on an excision biopsy, not just a fine-needle aspirate, if lymphoma is suspected
conventional.note: A fine-needle aspirate alone frequently cannot diagnose or subtype lymphoma reliably -- worth being explicit about this with the treating team to avoid a diagnostic dead end.

conventional.remedy: Supervised exercise during and after treatment
conventional.note: [Systematic review/meta-analysis, lymphoma-specific] A review of exercise interventions in lymphoma survivors found improved quality of life and reduced cancer-related fatigue -- an adjunct to recovery, not a treatment for the lymphoma itself.

ayurveda.remedy: Ayurvedic quality-of-life support alongside chemotherapy, only with your oncologist's knowledge
ayurveda.note: [Human study, general cancer population -- not condition-specific] A 2014 study found combinations of Ayurvedic drugs alongside chemotherapy improved quality-of-life scores and reduced drug toxicity in cancer patients generally. This was not a leukaemia- or lymphoma-specific trial, so treat it as supportive evidence, not proof for this exact condition. Only start alongside chemotherapy with your oncologist's knowledge -- some herbo-mineral formulations can interact with chemotherapy drugs, and this is never a substitute for or reason to delay chemotherapy itself.

yoga.note: [Human study, lymphoma-specific] A home-based yoga programme designed specifically for lymphoma patients on chemotherapy showed feasibility and promise for wellbeing during treatment -- start only once cleared by the treating team, and stop or scale back on days you feel unwell.

evidence.source: Naik S et al., British Journal of Nutrition 2018
evidence.quote: Vitamin B12 deficiency is highly prevalent among vegetarian Indians, largely independent of any underlying gastrointestinal disease.
evidence.recovery: Fatigue and anaemia typically improve within weeks of starting replacement; established neurological damage may only partially recover, which is why prompt treatment matters.
evidence.seekCareIf: Numbness, tingling, or gait unsteadiness alongside anaemia -- these need prompt B12 replacement, as subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord can become irreversible if delayed.

conventional.remedy: Vitamin B12 replacement (IM injection or high-dose oral, per your doctor's assessment)
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, honest low-quality evidence] Very-low-quality evidence suggests high-dose oral B12 (1000-2000mcg) may be about as effective as intramuscular injections for correcting deficiency -- genuinely uncertain evidence, not a confident claim that oral is equivalent, so this remains a discussion with your doctor rather than a self-directed choice, especially if pernicious anaemia or malabsorption is suspected.

conventional.remedy: Identify and treat the underlying cause
conventional.note: Dietary deficiency (common in vegetarians), pernicious anaemia, and malabsorption all need different long-term management -- lifelong replacement is usually needed for pernicious anaemia/malabsorption but not for a purely dietary cause once diet is corrected.

conventional.remedy: Vegetarians: include fortified foods, dairy and eggs (if eaten), or a regular B12 supplement
conventional.note: No plant food reliably supplies B12 -- this is a genuine, common, and easily prevented deficiency in India's large vegetarian population, not something diet alone can fix without fortified sources or supplementation.

ayurveda.remedy: No specific Ayurveda correlate for B12/folate deficiency
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] B12 deficiency is a purely biochemical, modern-nutrition concept with no classical correlate. Classical guidance on balanced Ahara (diet) is genuine and worth following generally, but it does not substitute for B12 replacement once a deficiency is confirmed, especially given that no plant source reliably supplies B12.

yoga.remedy: Gentle, gradually-progressed practice while fatigue is present
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to B12/folate-deficiency fatigue -- included only as a generally-used gentle practice for fatigue, and only once any gait unsteadiness or numbness has been assessed, since balance-dependent poses may be unsafe until neurological symptoms are evaluated.

evidence.source: Misdiagnosis-Driven Dental Extractions in Patients with Trigeminal Neuralgia, J Multidiscip Healthc 2025
evidence.quote: A substantial proportion of trigeminal neuralgia patients presenting with tooth-like pain underwent irreversible dental treatment, including unnecessary tooth extraction, before the correct diagnosis was made.
evidence.recovery: Carbamazepine often gives dramatic relief within days once started; attacks can also remit spontaneously for periods even without treatment.
evidence.seekCareIf: Sensory loss on the face, symptoms on both sides, or onset under 40 -- these should prompt MRI to exclude a structural cause rather than assuming classical trigeminal neuralgia.

conventional.remedy: Carbamazepine, as prescribed
conventional.note: [Meta-analysis] Carbamazepine significantly reduces pain intensity and frequency and remains first-line for classical trigeminal neuralgia -- effective for many, though not everyone responds and side effects need monitoring.

conventional.remedy: Before agreeing to any dental extraction or root canal for facial pain, ask specifically whether trigeminal neuralgia has been considered
conventional.note: [Indian cohort data] A large proportion of trigeminal neuralgia patients in this study had irreversible dental treatment, including extraction, before the correct diagnosis -- worth raising explicitly rather than assuming a dentist has already ruled this out.

conventional.remedy: Identify and avoid your specific trigger, where possible (light touch, cold wind, chewing on that side)
conventional.note: Trigger-zone avoidance does not treat the underlying nerve problem, but can reduce the frequency of provoked attacks day-to-day while medication takes effect.

ayurveda.remedy: Ayurvedic protocol (Anantavata) alongside conventional management, only with your neurologist's knowledge
ayurveda.note: [Single case report only] A single published case report describes an Ayurvedic protocol used in the acute management of Type 1 trigeminal neuralgia. This is one patient's experience, not a controlled trial -- it does not establish that this approach works in general, and should never replace or delay carbamazepine or MRI when indicated.

yoga.remedy: Calm breathing practice for the stress of unpredictable attacks
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Not a treatment for the nerve pain itself -- included only as a general stress-relief practice for the anxiety that comes with unpredictable, severe pain episodes.
yoga.video: 1 Minute Meditation for Quick Stress Relief -- brief grounding practice

evidence.source: Update on Medical Treatments for Essential Tremor, MDS Evidence-Based Medicine Review, Movement Disorders 2026
evidence.quote: Propranolol and primidone remain the most commonly used first-line therapies for essential tremor, typically reducing tremor amplitude by around half, though a substantial proportion of patients do not respond.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, usually slowly progressive condition managed rather than cured -- medication controls symptoms in those who respond, and it is generally not dangerous or life-shortening.
evidence.seekCareIf: A tremor present at rest, new slowness of movement, or rigidity -- these point to Parkinson's disease rather than essential tremor and need a different assessment.

conventional.remedy: Propranolol or primidone, as prescribed, if the tremor is functionally troublesome
conventional.note: [Current evidence-based review] Both remain first-line and reduce tremor amplitude by roughly half in responders, though the review notes a substantial proportion of patients do not respond and side effects are relatively common -- an honest, not overstated, picture of the evidence.

conventional.remedy: Thyroid function testing if not already done
conventional.note: Hyperthyroidism can cause or worsen a fine tremor -- worth excluding as a contributing or alternative cause before assuming essential tremor is the whole picture.

conventional.remedy: Avoid caffeine and other stimulants if they noticeably worsen your tremor
conventional.note: A simple, low-risk self-observation -- not curative, but stimulants can transiently worsen action tremor in some people.

ayurveda.remedy: No specific Ayurveda correlate identified for essential tremor
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A specific search for a PubMed-indexed Ayurveda study on essential tremor found none. Kampavata, the classical correlate often cited for tremor, is specifically mapped to PARKINSON'S disease (a materially different, progressive condition already modelled elsewhere in this app) -- reusing that literature here would conflate two distinct conditions rather than offer genuine evidence.

yoga.remedy: General relaxation practice, since stress and anxiety can transiently worsen action tremor
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to essential tremor -- included only as a generally-used gentle relaxation practice, since stress is a well-known transient aggravating factor for action tremor generally.
yoga.video: Pawanmuktasana Series 1, 2, 3 -- Bihar School of Yoga

evidence.source: Guillain-Barre syndrome: association with Campylobacter jejuni and Mycoplasma pneumoniae infections in India, Natl Med J India 2006
evidence.quote: Evidence of recent Campylobacter jejuni infection was found significantly more often in Indian GBS patients than in matched controls, supporting it as a key antecedent trigger in this population.
evidence.recovery: Recovery depends entirely on prompt IVIG or plasma exchange plus monitored supportive care -- weeks to months of recovery and physiotherapy, not a home-managed illness in the acute phase.
evidence.seekCareIf: This condition IS the reason for urgent same-day assessment if suspected -- any breathlessness, difficulty swallowing, or rapidly progressing weakness needs emergency admission for monitoring.

conventional.remedy: This is a hospital-treatment condition in the acute phase -- there is no meaningful home-care substitute
conventional.note: [Honest framing] IVIG or plasma exchange in a monitored setting is the only evidence-based path in the acute phase -- delaying this for home remedies risks respiratory failure.

conventional.remedy: If you have had diarrhoea or a respiratory illness in the last 1-3 weeks and now have new limb weakness, say so explicitly and urgently
conventional.note: [Indian cohort data] Recent Campylobacter jejuni infection was significantly more common in Indian GBS patients than controls -- this specific history is a genuine red flag worth stating explicitly, not just mentioning in passing.

conventional.remedy: Physiotherapy during the recovery phase, once the acute phase has stabilised
conventional.note: [Guideline] Standard part of the recovery pathway once medically stable -- supports regaining strength and function over the following weeks to months.

ayurveda.remedy: Adjunct Ayurveda and Yoga during the RECOVERY phase only, alongside ongoing physiotherapy and with your neurologist's knowledge
ayurveda.note: [Single case report only -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] One published case study describes adjunct Ayurveda and Yoga added after physiotherapy alone had plateaued, with reported further improvement in sensation and strength. This is one patient's experience, not a controlled trial, and was used only in recovery -- never during the acute, urgent phase, and never as a substitute for IVIG/plasma exchange or physiotherapy.

yoga.remedy: Adjunct yoga therapy during the recovery phase, from the same case study
yoga.note: [Single case report only] The same case study included yoga alongside Ayurveda and physiotherapy during recovery, with reported further functional gains after physiotherapy alone had plateaued. One patient's experience -- promising, but not proof it works in general, and only appropriate once medically stable and guided by the treating team.

evidence.source: Chong LY et al., Saline irrigation for chronic rhinosinusitis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016
evidence.quote: Saline irrigation is beneficial for the symptoms of chronic rhinosinusitis, whether used alone or as an adjunct to other treatment, though it is generally less effective than an intranasal corticosteroid.
evidence.recovery: A long-term condition managed rather than quickly cured -- saline irrigation and intranasal steroid together are often very effective, but flares and relapses are common.
evidence.seekCareIf: Unilateral symptoms with blood-stained discharge, or any visual or neurological symptom -- these should prompt imaging to exclude a structural or malignant cause rather than assuming simple chronic sinusitis.

conventional.remedy: Large-volume (150ml) saline nasal irrigation, daily
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Genuinely beneficial as a stand-alone treatment or add-on -- though generally less effective than an intranasal steroid on its own, so best used alongside one rather than instead of one.

conventional.remedy: Intranasal corticosteroid spray, as directed
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] First-line and generally more effective than saline alone for controlling chronic symptoms.

conventional.remedy: Where practical, reduce exposure to air pollution, dust and known allergens
conventional.note: [Systematic review -- not India-specific, mechanism is general] Air pollutants (NO2, SO2, particulate matter) impair mucociliary clearance and increase airway reactivity, worsening chronic rhinosinusitis -- the underlying studies are mostly from East Asia, not India specifically, but the mechanism is general and directly relevant given the high ambient pollution and allergen load in many Indian cities.

ayurveda.remedy: Pradhamana Nasya with Trikatu and Triphala Churna, under practitioner supervision
ayurveda.note: [Randomised clinical study] A 2010 trial found marked improvement in 81.82% of chronic sinusitis (Dushta Pratishyaya) patients receiving this Nasya protocol, compared with 10% on oral medication alone -- a genuinely stronger evidence tier than the single case reports used elsewhere in this project, though still one trial, not yet confirmed at scale, and administered by a trained practitioner rather than self-applied.

yoga.remedy: Jala Neti (nasal cleansing) and gentle pranayama, once acute inflammation has settled
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No controlled trial evidence specific to chronic rhinosinusitis was found for this practice on its own -- included as a commonly-practised complement to saline irrigation, not a substitute for the evidence-based saline/steroid regimen above.
