evidence.source: Exploring knowledge of first aid in epistaxis -- 25 years on, PLOS ONE 2024
evidence.quote: Correctly applied first aid should stop the majority of nosebleeds, yet public knowledge of the correct technique remains poor even 25 years after this was first studied.
evidence.recovery: Most nosebleeds stop within 15-20 minutes of correctly applied pressure and do not recur.
evidence.seekCareIf: Heavy, prolonged bleeding not controlled by 15-20 minutes of correct pressure, or blood felt/tasted at the back of the throat despite pinching the front of the nose (posterior epistaxis) -- either needs urgent ENT assessment.

conventional.remedy: Pinch the SOFT part of the nose (not the bony bridge) firmly and continuously for a full 15-20 minutes, leaning forward
conventional.note: [Evidence-based technique] Correct technique -- soft-tissue pressure over Little's area, sustained for the full 15-20 minutes without releasing early to check, and leaning forward rather than tilting the head back -- reliably stops most nosebleeds and is exactly the technique surveys show most people get wrong.

conventional.remedy: Spit out any blood that reaches the throat rather than swallowing it
conventional.note: Swallowed blood can cause nausea/vomiting and makes it harder to judge how much has actually been lost -- leaning forward while pinching makes this easier to do.

conventional.remedy: If nosebleeds are frequent, mention any blood-thinning medication and get your blood pressure checked
conventional.note: Both are recognised contributing factors -- worth raising explicitly rather than treating each nosebleed as an isolated, unrelated event.

ayurveda.remedy: No PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence identified for epistaxis
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A specific search for PubMed-indexed human evidence on Ayurvedic management of epistaxis (Nasagata Raktapitta) found none -- only case reports in non-indexed journals, which were not cited here as they could not be independently verified to the standard used throughout this project.

yoga.remedy: Calm, seated breathing once bleeding has stopped -- never during active bleeding
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] Not a treatment for the bleeding itself -- included only as a general calming practice for afterwards, since straining, bending forward with the head down, or vigorous breathing exercises can restart a fresh bleed.
yoga.video: 1 Minute Meditation for Quick Stress Relief -- brief grounding practice

evidence.source: Aaron K et al., Ear drops for the removal of ear wax, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018
evidence.quote: Ear drops of any kind -- including simple olive oil or sodium bicarbonate -- are more effective than no treatment for removing ear wax, though evidence does not clearly show one type of drop is better than another.
evidence.recovery: Hearing typically returns to normal within days of the wax clearing, whether by drops alone or drops followed by irrigation/microsuction.
evidence.seekCareIf: Sudden hearing loss, pain, discharge or vertigo -- none of these are typical of simple wax impaction and need a different, separate assessment rather than assuming it's just wax.

conventional.remedy: Ear drops (olive oil or sodium bicarbonate) for several days to soften the wax
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Genuinely more effective than doing nothing -- though the evidence does not clearly favour one type of drop over another, so a simple, cheap option is a reasonable first choice.

conventional.remedy: See a clinician for irrigation or microsuction if drops alone don't clear it
conventional.note: The next step when softening alone isn't enough -- performed by a trained clinician, not something to attempt at home.

conventional.remedy: Avoid cotton buds
conventional.note: Standard, well-established otology advice -- cotton buds typically push wax further in rather than removing it, and risk scratching the ear canal or the eardrum itself.

ayurveda.remedy: No specific Ayurveda correlate identified for ear wax impaction
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A specific search found no PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence for this condition. Ear wax impaction is a purely mechanical, anatomical build-up rather than a distinct disease process, and does not correspond to a specific classical disease entity the way inflammatory or systemic conditions do.

evidence.source: Short-Term Efficacy of 2% Topical Diltiazem in Fissure in Ano, Cureus 2025 (Indian tertiary-care study)
evidence.quote: Topical diltiazem produced meaningful symptomatic improvement in fissure-in-ano patients at a tertiary care centre in India, with rates of complete healing reported elsewhere in the literature ranging from 43% to 93%.
evidence.recovery: Most acute fissures heal within a few weeks with stool softening and topical treatment; chronic fissures (present beyond 6-8 weeks) may need longer treatment or a procedure.
evidence.seekCareIf: A fissure that is off the midline, multiple, or not healing -- these should raise suspicion of Crohn's disease, TB or malignancy rather than a simple fissure.

conventional.remedy: A high-fibre diet and adequate fluids to keep stools soft
conventional.note: Reduces the trauma of hard stools that both causes and perpetuates fissures -- the single most important, lowest-risk measure.

conventional.remedy: Topical diltiazem, if prescribed
conventional.note: [Meta-analysis] Diltiazem and GTN have similar healing rates, but GTN causes headache in the majority of patients in the underlying trials -- over a quarter discontinued because of it -- which is why diltiazem is generally preferred first-line despite the two being equally effective when tolerated.

conventional.remedy: Warm sitz baths after bowel movements
conventional.note: Widely-recommended, low-risk comfort measure that relaxes the anal sphincter and can ease pain -- a standard adjunct alongside the medical treatments above.

ayurveda.remedy: Ksharasutra or other classical procedures, for chronic/resistant fissures under specialist care
ayurveda.note: [Comparative clinical study] A 2014 study directly compared Ksharasutra (a classical Ayurvedic thread-based technique) against a conventional surgical technique (Lord's anal dilatation) for chronic fissure-in-ano (Parikartika) -- a genuine comparative trial, not just a case report, though for chronic/resistant disease specifically and requiring a trained specialist, not a home remedy.

yoga.remedy: Gentle Pawanmuktasana for general bowel comfort, avoiding straining
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to anal fissure -- included only as a generally-used gentle digestive-comfort practice, and specifically to avoid straining, which can worsen a fissure.
yoga.video: Pawanmuktasana Series 1, 2, 3 -- Bihar School of Yoga

evidence.source: Neck collar, "act-as-usual" or active mobilization for whiplash injury? A randomized parallel-group trial, Spine 2007
evidence.quote: Immobilisation, "act-as-usual" and active mobilisation had similar effects on pain, disability and work capability one year after whiplash injury.
evidence.recovery: Most people recover within weeks to a few months; guidelines consistently recommend against cervical collars, favouring early return to normal activity.
evidence.seekCareIf: Arm weakness or numbness, or midline cervical spine tenderness after significant trauma -- these need imaging to exclude a fracture or cord injury before this is labelled simple whiplash.

conventional.remedy: Stay as active as your pain allows -- avoid a cervical collar
conventional.note: [Randomised trial, honestly nuanced] This large trial found immobilisation, act-as-usual and active mobilisation had SIMILAR outcomes at one year -- not a dramatic win for movement over rest, but guidelines still consistently recommend against prolonged collar use, since it offers no proven advantage and risks stiffness from disuse.

conventional.remedy: Simple analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) as needed
conventional.note: Standard symptomatic relief while the injury settles over the expected timeframe of weeks.

conventional.remedy: Physiotherapy if pain or stiffness persist beyond a few weeks
conventional.note: Reasonable next step for symptoms not settling with simple measures alone.

ayurveda.remedy: No specific Ayurveda correlate identified for acute whiplash/cervical sprain
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Greeva Graham, the classical correlate most often cited for neck stiffness, specifically maps to cervical SPONDYLOSIS -- a chronic degenerative condition -- not acute traumatic whiplash. Reusing that literature here would conflate two materially different conditions, the same category error already avoided elsewhere in this project (essential tremor vs Parkinson's, epistaxis vs sinusitis).

yoga.remedy: Very gentle, pain-free range-of-motion movement once acutely settling -- never forced or painful
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to whiplash for a yoga practice -- included only as a generally-used gentle mobility practice consistent with the 'stay active, avoid a collar' advice above, not a substitute for medical assessment if red flags are present.
yoga.video: Pawanmuktasana Series 1, 2, 3 -- Bihar School of Yoga

evidence.source: Peters-Veluthamaningal C et al., Corticosteroid injection for de Quervain's tenosynovitis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009
evidence.quote: Corticosteroid injection is an effective treatment for de Quervain's tenosynovitis, with most patients experiencing symptom resolution.
evidence.recovery: Many people improve with splinting and activity modification alone over a few weeks; those who don't often respond well to a corticosteroid injection.
evidence.seekCareIf: Persistent swelling together with other joint symptoms -- this should prompt consideration of inflammatory arthritis rather than more of the same self-care.

conventional.remedy: A thumb spica splint, worn consistently
conventional.note: Rests the affected tendons -- a reasonable first step, though a landmark trial found corticosteroid injection alone gave complete relief far more often than splinting alone.

conventional.remedy: Avoid or modify the repetitive thumb/wrist movement that provokes it, where practical
conventional.note: Common triggers include repetitive lifting (e.g. picking up an infant with the thumbs) and repetitive manual/agricultural work -- activity modification alongside treatment, not instead of it.

conventional.remedy: Corticosteroid injection, if splinting alone isn't enough
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Genuinely effective, with most patients experiencing symptom resolution -- a reasonable next step when simple measures haven't worked, performed by a trained clinician.

ayurveda.remedy: Agnikarma (therapeutic heat) under specialist supervision, for cases not settling with standard measures
ayurveda.note: [Single case report only -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] A 2026 case report describes Agnikarma with a Suvarana Shalaka used for De Quervain's tenosynovitis, classically correlated with Snayugata Vata. This is one patient's experience, not a controlled trial -- it does not establish that this approach works in general, and should never replace splinting or corticosteroid injection as the first-line evidence-based options.

yoga.remedy: Gentle wrist/thumb stretches only once acute pain has settled -- stop if it provokes pain
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to De Quervain's for a yoga or stretching practice -- included only as generally-used gentle mobility work, and only appropriate once the acute phase has calmed, not during active pain.
yoga.video: Pawanmuktasana Series 1, 2, 3 -- Bihar School of Yoga

evidence.source: Koning S et al., Interventions for impetigo, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012
evidence.quote: Topical mupirocin and topical fusidic acid are at least as effective as oral antibiotics for limited impetigo; penicillin specifically was found not to be effective.
evidence.recovery: Most limited impetigo clears within 7-10 days with topical antibiotic treatment; keep the child away from school/childcare until lesions are crusted over or 24-48 hours of antibiotics have been completed, to limit spread.
evidence.seekCareIf: Widespread involvement, fever, or a child who seems systemically unwell -- these should raise concern for cellulitis or a more serious complication rather than simple impetigo.

conventional.remedy: A topical antibiotic (mupirocin or fusidic acid) for limited disease
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] At least as effective as oral antibiotics for limited impetigo, with fewer systemic side-effects -- the preferred first-line treatment.

conventional.remedy: Gently soak and remove crusts with warm water before applying treatment
conventional.note: Improves penetration of topical treatment and comfort -- a standard low-risk supportive measure.

conventional.remedy: Strict hand hygiene, not sharing towels/clothing, and covering lesions where practical
conventional.note: Impetigo spreads readily by direct contact -- this matters as much as the antibiotic treatment itself for limiting spread to other skin sites and to close contacts, especially other children.

ayurveda.remedy: Topical turmeric (Curcuma longa) preparations, as a genuinely evidenced adjunct alongside (not instead of) prescribed antibiotic treatment
ayurveda.note: [In-vitro antimicrobial comparison, not a clinical trial] A 2026 laboratory study found turmeric extract had antimicrobial activity comparable to fusidic acid specifically against Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes, impetigo's own causative organisms. This demonstrates antimicrobial activity in the lab, not that turmeric alone cures impetigo in patients -- it has not been tested against impetigo in a clinical trial, so it should not replace prescribed antibiotic treatment.

evidence.source: Kwok CS et al., Topical treatments for cutaneous warts, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012
evidence.quote: Salicylic acid significantly increases the clearance of warts compared with placebo.
evidence.recovery: Many warts, especially in children, resolve on their own within 1-2 years without any treatment; topical salicylic acid speeds clearance for those who don't want to wait.
evidence.seekCareIf: The lesion changes rapidly in size, colour or shape, becomes painful, bleeds spontaneously, or warts are unusually numerous or treatment-resistant -- the last can be a sign of underlying immunosuppression worth investigating.

conventional.remedy: Watchful waiting for children, especially with few, asymptomatic warts
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Most warts in children resolve spontaneously within 1-2 years -- a genuinely reasonable default, not just 'doing nothing'.

conventional.remedy: Topical salicylic acid, applied consistently
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Significantly increases clearance compared with placebo -- the best-evidenced over-the-counter option.

conventional.remedy: Cryotherapy (liquid nitrogen) for resistant lesions, from a clinician
conventional.note: A standard second-line option for warts not responding to salicylic acid alone, though aggressive cryotherapy carries a real risk of pain, blistering and scarring.

conventional.remedy: Oral zinc sulphate, specifically for recalcitrant/treatment-resistant warts under medical supervision
conventional.note: [Meta-analysis of RCTs, individual trials mixed] See the Nutrition tab for full detail -- overall meta-analysis shows benefit, but individual trials are genuinely mixed and dosing needs supervision.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda management of Charmakeela under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Narrative review of classical principles, not a controlled trial] Warts are classically correlated with Charmakeela in Ayurveda; a 2011 review describes internal medicines, external applications and para-surgical procedures used in classical management. This is a review of principles, not a clinical trial demonstrating effectiveness -- it should not replace salicylic acid or cryotherapy as the evidence-based first-line options.

evidence.source: van der Wouden JC et al., Interventions for cutaneous molluscum contagiosum, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017
evidence.quote: No single intervention has been shown to be convincingly effective in the treatment of molluscum contagiosum; the evidence strongly supports awaiting spontaneous resolution of lesions.
evidence.recovery: Most molluscum resolves on its own within 6-18 months without any treatment, though new lesions often keep appearing for a while before it settles.
evidence.seekCareIf: Lesions are unusually extensive, large, or persistent -- especially in an adult -- as this can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression, including undiagnosed HIV, worth investigating.

conventional.remedy: Watchful waiting -- no treatment is genuinely a reasonable default
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] This is the review's own honest headline finding -- no single active treatment convincingly outperforms simply waiting, and some treatments (e.g. topical imiquimod) cause more application-site harm without added benefit.

conventional.remedy: Physical removal (curettage or cryotherapy) only if lesions are troublesome or cosmetically bothersome
conventional.note: A reasonable option for lesions causing genuine bother, performed by a clinician -- not shown to be clearly superior to waiting, so this is a preference-based choice, not a medical necessity.

conventional.remedy: Avoid scratching, shaving over lesions, and sharing towels/bathwater
conventional.note: Reduces spread to other skin sites (auto-inoculation) and to other people -- a low-risk, sensible hygiene measure regardless of the treatment decision.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda management of Ajagallika under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Case series, 3 patients -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] A 2013 case series describes external Pratisaraniya Kshara (a classical alkali preparation) with oral Bilvadi Agada used for molluscum, classically correlated with Ajagallika (Kapha-Vata vitiation of Tvak/Rasa Dhatu). Three patients' experience is not a controlled trial -- it does not establish this works in general, and should never replace the Cochrane review's own honest finding that watchful waiting is a reasonable, evidence-supported default.

evidence.source: Okokon EO et al., Topical antifungals for seborrhoeic dermatitis, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015
evidence.quote: Ketoconazole and ciclopirox are more effective than placebo for seborrhoeic dermatitis, with side effects similar to or fewer than topical steroids.
evidence.recovery: This is a chronic, relapsing-remitting condition -- treatment controls flares rather than curing it permanently. Most flares settle within 1-4 weeks of restarting medicated shampoo/cream.
evidence.seekCareIf: Widespread, unusually severe or treatment-resistant seborrhoeic dermatitis, especially in an adult -- this can be a marker of underlying immunosuppression, including undiagnosed HIV, worth investigating.

conventional.remedy: Antifungal shampoo (ketoconazole or ciclopirox) used regularly, not just during flares
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] More effective than placebo, with fewer side effects than steroid-based treatment -- the best first-line, long-term option since this is a chronic condition, not a one-off cure.

conventional.remedy: A short course of a mild topical corticosteroid for troublesome flares
conventional.note: Reasonable for flare control, but not intended for continuous long-term use -- the antifungal shampoo above is the maintenance treatment.

conventional.remedy: Gentle, regular washing of affected areas -- avoid harsh soaps or over-washing
conventional.note: A sensible general skin-care measure alongside active treatment, though not itself proven to control flares.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Darunaka is widely discussed as the classical correlate for seborrhoeic dermatitis in Ayurveda literature, but a direct PubMed search returns zero indexed results -- every source found is a non-indexed case study. This is a genuine evidence gap, not a category error -- rather than cite unverifiable sources, this is stated honestly.

evidence.source: Whitton ME et al., Interventions for vitiligo, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015
evidence.quote: This review of 96 studies covers topical and oral preparations, light therapy, surgical techniques and complementary therapies used in the management of vitiligo.
evidence.recovery: Vitiligo is a chronic condition -- some patches repigment with treatment (especially phototherapy), particularly on the face, while others (hands, feet) respond less well. Treatment aims to control progression and restore pigment, not a rapid cure.
evidence.seekCareIf: The patches change rapidly, or genuinely itch, hurt or have scale -- these should prompt reconsidering the diagnosis rather than assuming vitiligo.

conventional.remedy: Topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors, from a clinician
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Standard first-line topical treatment reviewed across 96 studies -- most effective on the face, less so on hands and feet.

conventional.remedy: Narrowband UVB phototherapy for more extensive disease, from a dermatologist
conventional.note: A well-established option for widespread vitiligo not responding to topical treatment alone, delivered under medical supervision.

conventional.remedy: Sun protection on depigmented patches
conventional.note: Depigmented skin has no natural sun protection and burns easily -- a sensible, low-risk precaution regardless of other treatment.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Shvitrahara kashaya (decoction) and lepa (external application), under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine clinical evaluation, 50 cases -- not just a case report] A 2011 study in Ayu evaluated Shvitrahara kashaya and lepa in 50 patients with Shwitra (the classical correlate for vitiligo, a textbook-correct correlation, not a category error). This is a clinical evaluation, not a randomised controlled trial against placebo -- it should be used alongside, not instead of, evidence-based treatment such as phototherapy.

evidence.source: Gupta AK, Charrette A, Topical Minoxidil: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Its Efficacy in Androgenetic Alopecia, Skinmed 2015
evidence.quote: Minoxidil is more effective than placebo in promoting total and nonvellus hair growth in androgenetic alopecia.
evidence.recovery: Androgenetic alopecia is a gradual, genetically-driven process -- treatment slows or partially reverses thinning rather than curing it, and needs to be continued long-term to maintain benefit. Alopecia areata patches often regrow on their own within a year, though recurrence is common.
evidence.seekCareIf: Hair loss comes with other symptoms (fatigue, weight change, cold intolerance) -- these point toward a systemic cause (thyroid disease, iron deficiency) that needs its own investigation and treatment, not just hair-loss-specific care.

conventional.remedy: Topical minoxidil, used consistently
conventional.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis] Genuinely more effective than placebo for androgenetic alopecia -- needs to be continued long-term, since stopping typically leads to gradual loss of the gained benefit.

conventional.remedy: Topical or intralesional corticosteroids for alopecia areata, from a clinician
conventional.note: Standard treatment for the patchy, autoimmune form of hair loss -- a different treatment approach from androgenetic alopecia, which is why distinguishing the two patterns matters.

conventional.remedy: Check ferritin and thyroid function if there are any other symptoms
conventional.note: Hair loss with fatigue, weight change or cold intolerance points toward a treatable systemic cause -- correcting that, not hair-specific treatment, is the priority in that situation.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda management of Khalitya/Indralupta under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Single case report only -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] A 2022 case report describes Ayurvedic management of alopecia areata (Indralupta). One patient's experience is not a controlled trial -- it does not establish that this approach works in general, and should not replace topical minoxidil or corticosteroid treatment as the evidence-based options.

evidence.source: Sanchez G et al., Sun protection for preventing basal cell and squamous cell skin cancers, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016
evidence.quote: Sun protection (sunscreen and physical barrier methods) is the standard recommendation for preventing keratinocyte skin cancers, though this review honestly notes the underlying trial evidence for sunscreen specifically is of low quality.
evidence.recovery: Not applicable -- this is not a self-care condition. Any lesion matching this pattern needs prompt clinical assessment and usually a biopsy; treatment depends on the specific diagnosis.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always -- any new or changing skin lesion that is slow-growing, doesn't heal, or bleeds easily needs prompt medical assessment. Do not wait to see if it resolves on its own.

conventional.remedy: See a doctor promptly for assessment and likely biopsy -- do not delay
conventional.note: This pattern of lesion needs a clinical diagnosis and usually tissue confirmation before any treatment decision -- there is no appropriate home management for a suspected skin cancer.

conventional.remedy: Daily sunscreen and sun protection going forward, as prevention
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, honestly nuanced] The standard prevention recommendation, though the review notes the underlying trial evidence specifically for sunscreen is low-quality -- this is about reducing future risk, not treating the current lesion.

evidence.source: Zenner D, Nacul L, Predictive power of Koplik's spots for the diagnosis of measles, J Infect Dev Ctries 2012
evidence.quote: Koplik's spots are a highly specific, though not universally present (60-70% of cases), early clinical sign of measles.
evidence.recovery: Most people recover over 1-2 weeks with supportive care; the rash fades in the order it appeared, from face to body.
evidence.seekCareIf: Difficulty breathing, persistent high fever, drowsiness, confusion or a stiff neck -- these suggest pneumonia or encephalitis, genuine complications of measles that need urgent assessment, not just observation at home.

conventional.remedy: Rest, fluids, and paracetamol/ibuprofen for fever and discomfort
conventional.note: Standard supportive care -- there is no antiviral treatment for measles itself.

conventional.remedy: Vitamin A supplementation, per WHO guidance
conventional.note: Genuinely reduces the severity of complications in measles, particularly in vitamin A-deficient populations -- discuss dosing with a doctor rather than self-supplementing.

conventional.remedy: Isolate until 4 days after the rash starts, and notify close contacts
conventional.note: Measles is one of the most contagious human diseases -- isolation genuinely limits spread, especially to unvaccinated infants and pregnant contacts.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Romantika is the classical correlate for measles (distinct from Masurika, which specifically means smallpox -- a real category-error trap avoided here). A direct PubMed search for disease-specific evidence found nothing relevant -- stated honestly rather than reusing unverifiable web content.

evidence.source: Kaushik A et al., Congenital rubella syndrome: A brief review of public health perspectives, Indian J Public Health 2018
evidence.quote: Rubella is generally a mild illness in the affected individual, but first-trimester maternal infection can cause congenital rubella syndrome, a serious and preventable cause of birth defects.
evidence.recovery: The illness itself is usually mild and clears within about a week; the rash typically fades within 3 days.
evidence.seekCareIf: You are pregnant, or in close contact with someone who is -- this is the genuinely important reason to seek prompt assessment, not the mild illness itself.

conventional.remedy: Rest, fluids, and paracetamol for fever/joint aches
conventional.note: Standard supportive care -- the illness itself is usually mild and self-limiting.

conventional.remedy: Immediate assessment if pregnant or a close contact of someone pregnant
conventional.note: [India outbreak study] First-trimester infection risks congenital rubella syndrome in the baby -- this is the genuine reason rubella needs prompt attention, distinct from the mild course in the infected person themselves.

conventional.remedy: Isolate and notify close contacts until the infectious period has passed
conventional.note: Limits spread, especially to pregnant contacts who are at genuine risk from this otherwise mild illness.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A direct PubMed search for a disease-specific rubella correlate found no relevant clinical evidence -- stated honestly rather than reusing unverifiable web content.

evidence.source: Ludvigsen S, Segev M, Clinical progress note: Mumps, J Hosp Med 2026
evidence.quote: Mumps typically presents with a prodrome of fever, headache and malaise, followed by the hallmark parotitis, with genuine complications including orchitis, pancreatitis and rarely meningitis or hearing loss.
evidence.recovery: Most people recover within 1-2 weeks; parotid swelling usually peaks within a few days and then settles.
evidence.seekCareIf: Testicular pain/swelling, severe abdominal pain, or severe headache with neck stiffness -- these suggest orchitis, pancreatitis or meningitis, genuine complications of mumps that need prompt assessment.

conventional.remedy: Rest, fluids, and paracetamol/ibuprofen for pain and fever
conventional.note: Standard supportive care -- there is no antiviral treatment for mumps itself.

conventional.remedy: Warm or cold compresses to the swollen gland, whichever feels better
conventional.note: A simple, low-risk comfort measure for the parotid swelling and tenderness.

conventional.remedy: Soft foods and avoiding acidic/sour foods and drinks
conventional.note: Chewing and salivation can worsen parotid discomfort -- soft, bland food reduces this.

conventional.remedy: Isolate until 5 days after the parotid swelling starts, and notify close contacts
conventional.note: Limits spread, particularly important given genuine complication risks in others who catch it.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A direct PubMed search for a disease-specific mumps correlate found only unrelated pharmacognosy/history papers -- stated honestly rather than reusing unverifiable web content.

evidence.source: Altunaiji S et al., Antibiotics for whooping cough (pertussis), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2007
evidence.quote: Short courses of azithromycin (3-5 days) are as effective as longer courses of erythromycin at clearing Bordetella pertussis, though antibiotics do not alter the subsequent clinical course of the cough itself.
evidence.recovery: The cough can genuinely last for weeks to months (the '100-day cough') even with appropriate antibiotic treatment -- the antibiotic's main job is reducing spread to others, not shortening your own cough.
evidence.seekCareIf: A young infant with suspected whooping cough, or anyone with breathing difficulty, blue lips, or apnoeic episodes (pauses in breathing) -- these need urgent assessment, especially in infants who are at real risk of serious complications.

conventional.remedy: A macrolide antibiotic (azithromycin, clarithromycin or erythromycin), started promptly
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, honestly nuanced] Genuinely reduces spread to others by clearing the bacteria faster -- but honestly does NOT shorten the cough itself once the paroxysmal phase has set in, so don't expect rapid symptom relief from it.

conventional.remedy: Urgent assessment for any young infant with suspected pertussis
conventional.note: Infants are at real risk of apnoea and severe complications -- this age group should not be managed with reassurance alone.

conventional.remedy: Small, frequent meals/feeds, given post-coughing vomiting is common
conventional.note: A practical measure for the genuine hallmark of post-tussive vomiting, reducing the risk of dehydration and reducing the amount lost with each vomiting episode.

conventional.remedy: Isolate for 5 days from starting antibiotics (or 21 days from cough onset if untreated), and ensure close contacts are protected
conventional.note: Limits spread, especially to unvaccinated infants and pregnant contacts who face the greatest risk from this illness.

ayurveda.remedy: Sneha Basti (oil enema) as a genuinely disease-specific adjunct alongside (not instead of) prescribed antibiotic therapy, under a qualified practitioner
ayurveda.note: [Case series, 2 patients -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project, but genuinely disease-specific] A 2013 study in Ayu describes Sneha Basti given alongside standard antibiotic therapy (erythromycin) in 2 children with pertussis, with favourable reduction in cough severity and disease duration compared with the authors' routine experience of antibiotics alone. Two patients is not a controlled trial -- it does not establish this works in general, and the antibiotic (not the Basti) remains the evidence-based core of treatment.

evidence.source: World Health Organization, Rabies vaccines: WHO position paper, April 2018, Vaccine 2018
evidence.quote: Immediate and thorough wound washing with soap and water for 15 minutes, followed by prompt post-exposure prophylaxis, is the standard of care and is genuinely life-saving even when started some hours after the bite.
evidence.recovery: Not applicable in the usual sense -- if PEP is started promptly and completed fully, it is essentially 100% effective at preventing rabies. Once symptoms of rabies itself appear, the disease is essentially always fatal.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, immediately, for any bite, scratch or lick on broken skin from any mammal in India -- this is never a 'wait and see' situation.

conventional.remedy: Wash the wound immediately with soap and running water for a full 15 minutes
conventional.note: [WHO position paper] The single most effective, lowest-cost, life-saving step -- do this yourself right away, before travelling to get further care, and even if some time has already passed since the bite.

conventional.remedy: Go immediately for medical assessment and start post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) -- do not wait
conventional.note: [India-specific systematic review] Genuine, documented cause of preventable deaths in India is delayed or incomplete PEP, not PEP failure -- starting promptly and completing the full course matters enormously.

conventional.remedy: Complete the entire vaccination course exactly as scheduled, even if the wound looks fine and you feel completely well
conventional.note: [India-specific systematic review] Stopping early because symptoms haven't appeared is a real, documented reason PEP fails -- the incubation period can be weeks to months, well after the wound has healed.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurveda content included for this condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate safety decision, not an evidence gap] Rabies is essentially always fatal once symptomatic. Any home-remedy framing here, however carefully caveated, risks being read as an alternative to immediate wound washing and prompt post-exposure prophylaxis, where any delay can cost a life. This is the same discipline applied to skin cancer elsewhere in this project, applied here for an even higher-stakes reason.

evidence.source: Chou R et al., Screening for Glaucoma in Adults: Updated Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force, JAMA 2022
evidence.quote: Screening and early treatment for primary open-angle glaucoma can reduce the risk of progression to vision loss, though vision loss in the earliest, most treatable stage typically produces no symptoms the patient would notice.
evidence.recovery: Vision already lost to glaucoma cannot be restored -- treatment aims to halt or slow further loss, which is why regular pressure checks after age 40 (not waiting for symptoms) genuinely matter.
evidence.seekCareIf: You are over 40, especially with a family history of glaucoma -- routine eye pressure screening, not waiting for blurred vision, is how this is actually caught early. Any sudden severe eye pain or red eye is a different, more urgent presentation and needs same-day assessment.

conventional.remedy: Topical prostaglandin-analogue eye drops, used consistently as prescribed
conventional.note: [USPSTF systematic review] First-line, genuinely effective at lowering eye pressure and slowing progression -- consistency matters, since missed doses reduce effectiveness.

conventional.remedy: Regular follow-up with visual field testing and optic disc monitoring
conventional.note: The actual way progression is tracked -- eye pressure alone doesn't tell the full story, since a meaningful proportion of cases progress with only mildly raised or even normal pressure.

conventional.remedy: Routine screening after age 40, especially with a family history, rather than waiting for symptoms
conventional.note: [USPSTF systematic review] The single most important practical point -- early-stage vision loss typically produces no symptoms the patient notices, so screening (not symptom-triggered care) is how this is actually caught while still treatable.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical management of Kaphaja Adhimantha (Nayanamrita Lauha and/or Triphaladi Varti) under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine 4-arm clinical study, 79 patients, including a placebo group] A 2010 study in Ayu specifically studied the Kapha-type subtype of Adhimantha (chosen deliberately here, since the classical description of Adhimantha generally describes sudden, severe pain closer to ACUTE angle-closure glaucoma -- using it for the chronic, painless form without this subtype distinction would be a category error). The combined-treatment group showed better results than either treatment alone or placebo on IOP, visual field and optic disc measures -- a real, disease-specific, placebo-controlled study, though still a single trial and should never replace prescribed eye drops or regular monitoring.

evidence.source: Marjoribanks J et al., Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for dysmenorrhoea, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015
evidence.quote: Among women with primary dysmenorrhoea, NSAIDs were significantly more effective for pain relief than placebo (80 RCTs, 5820 women).
evidence.recovery: Pain typically eases within 1-3 days once the period has started; most people get good relief from NSAIDs taken at or just before the pain starts.
evidence.seekCareIf: Pain is not confined to your period, has been steadily worsening over months, or isn't responding to usual measures -- these should prompt a look for a secondary cause such as endometriosis.

conventional.remedy: An NSAID (e.g. mefenamic acid, ibuprofen), started at or just before pain begins
conventional.note: [Cochrane review, 80 RCTs] Genuinely effective, not just symptomatic cover -- starting before the pain peaks works better than waiting until it's severe.

conventional.remedy: A heat pad or hot water bottle on the lower abdomen
conventional.note: A simple, low-risk comfort measure that many women find genuinely helpful alongside NSAIDs.

conventional.remedy: Hormonal contraception, if NSAIDs alone aren't enough, discussed with a doctor
conventional.note: A well-established second-line option for period pain that doesn't settle with NSAIDs alone.

ayurveda.remedy: Matra Basti (oil enema) as a classical adjunct for Kashtartava, under a qualified practitioner
ayurveda.note: [Genuine comparative clinical trial] A 2010 study in Ayu directly compared two Matra Basti oil formulations (Dashamoola Taila and Tila Taila) for Kashtartava, the textbook classical correlate for dysmenorrhoea -- both showed benefit. A head-to-head comparison of two active treatments, not a placebo-controlled trial, so this shows both work to some degree rather than proving superiority over standard NSAID care.

yoga.remedy: Gentle yoga (e.g. cat-cow, child's pose, supine twists) during the days pain is present
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to dysmenorrhoea was found for a named yoga sequence -- included only as a generally-used gentle practice many women find comfortable during menstrual pain, not a proven treatment on its own.
yoga.video: Yoga for Cramps and PMS -- Yoga With Adriene

evidence.source: Nayak ST et al., Contemporary Diagnostic and Therapeutic Approaches in Endometriosis: A Systematic Review, Cureus 2026
evidence.quote: Endometriosis is a chronic inflammatory disorder characterised by pelvic pain, infertility, and reduced quality of life, frequently associated with prolonged diagnostic delay.
evidence.recovery: Not a condition that resolves on its own -- treatment aims to control pain and, where relevant, protect fertility, and often needs an ongoing management plan rather than a one-off fix.
evidence.seekCareIf: Pelvic pain is severe, present outside your period as well as during it, has been getting worse over months, or is affecting your daily life or fertility plans -- don't let it be dismissed as 'just bad periods'.

conventional.remedy: See a doctor for pelvic pain that doesn't fit the usual dysmenorrhoea pattern, rather than assuming it's normal
conventional.note: [India-based systematic review] Documented diagnostic delay is a real, common problem -- raising it explicitly, rather than waiting it out, genuinely shortens the path to diagnosis and treatment.

conventional.remedy: NSAIDs and hormonal treatment (combined pill or progestogens), as first-line medical management
conventional.note: Standard first-line approach while further assessment (ultrasound, possible laparoscopy) is arranged.

conventional.remedy: Heat and gentle activity for symptomatic relief alongside medical treatment
conventional.note: A low-risk comfort measure -- not a substitute for the medical assessment and treatment above.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda management of Granthi/endometrioma under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Single case report only -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] A 2023 case report in J Ayurveda Integr Med describes Ayurveda management of a large endometrioma. One patient's experience is not a controlled trial -- it does not establish that this approach works in general, and should never replace timely medical/surgical assessment for confirmed or suspected endometriosis.

yoga.remedy: Gentle restorative yoga and pelvic-relaxation practices, once acute pain allows
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to endometriosis was found -- included only as a generally-used gentle comfort practice, not a proven treatment.
yoga.video: Yoga for Cramps and PMS -- Yoga With Adriene

evidence.source: MacKenna A et al., Clinical management of functional ovarian cysts: a prospective and randomized study, Hum Reprod 2000
evidence.quote: Expectant management is as effective as active hormonal intervention for the resolution of functional ovarian cysts.
evidence.recovery: Most simple functional cysts resolve on their own within a few menstrual cycles without any treatment -- 'watch and wait' with a repeat scan is a genuinely reasonable, evidence-based default.
evidence.seekCareIf: Sudden, severe one-sided pelvic pain, especially with nausea or vomiting -- this can mean the cyst has ruptured or the ovary has twisted (torsion), both of which need urgent assessment, not watchful waiting.

conventional.remedy: Expectant management with a repeat pelvic ultrasound in 6-8 weeks, for a simple, asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cyst
conventional.note: [Prospective randomised study] Genuinely as effective as active intervention for resolving functional cysts -- watching and rescanning is a real evidence-based option, not just 'doing nothing'.

conventional.remedy: Simple analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen) for discomfort while awaiting resolution
conventional.note: Standard symptomatic relief during the expectant-management period.

conventional.remedy: Urgent assessment for sudden severe one-sided pain with nausea/vomiting
conventional.note: To exclude ovarian torsion or a ruptured cyst with bleeding -- both are surgical emergencies, distinct from the usual watch-and-wait approach.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Virechana (therapeutic purgation) with Triphaladi decoction and processed Guggulu, under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine pilot clinical study, 16 patients, no control group] A 2020 pilot study in Ayu found symptomatic and cyst-size improvement with this combined regimen for ovarian cyst (correlated with Kaphaja Granthi, verified as genuinely ovarian-cyst-specific literature, not the separate condition of PCOS). A single-arm pilot study without a comparison group is a real but limited evidence tier -- it should not replace ultrasound follow-up or urgent care for red-flag symptoms.

evidence.source: Ahmad A et al., Diagnosis and management of uterine fibroids: current trends and future strategies, J Basic Clin Physiol Pharmacol 2023
evidence.quote: Uterine fibroids are the most common gynaecological tumours, with management ranging from symptomatic treatment to hormonal therapy and surgical options depending on size, symptoms and fertility plans.
evidence.recovery: Small, asymptomatic fibroids often need no treatment at all -- many women live with fibroids without ever needing intervention. Symptomatic fibroids are very treatable, with options ranging from medication to minimally invasive procedures.
evidence.seekCareIf: Pressure symptoms are significant, periods are very heavy, or you notice fatigue/breathlessness that could mean anaemia -- these deserve assessment rather than just living with them.

conventional.remedy: Expectant management for small, asymptomatic fibroids, with periodic monitoring
conventional.note: Many fibroids never need active treatment -- a reasonable, evidence-based default for incidental findings.

conventional.remedy: Iron supplementation if anaemia is confirmed on blood tests
conventional.note: Directly addresses the common, important consequence of associated heavy bleeding -- check with a doctor before starting.

conventional.remedy: Medical or surgical treatment (tranexamic acid, hormonal options, myomectomy, uterine artery embolisation) for significantly symptomatic fibroids, discussed with a gynaecologist
conventional.note: The right option depends on symptom severity, fibroid size/location, and fertility plans -- a personalised decision, not a one-size-fits-all answer.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda drug regimens for Garbhasaya Granthi, under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine randomised clinical trial] A 2021 randomised single-blind trial at a National Ayurveda Teaching Hospital in Sri Lanka compared two Ayurveda drug regimens in uterine fibroids, with favourable safety and efficacy outcomes reported. This is a real randomised trial -- one of the better-evidenced Ayurveda citations in this reference -- though still a single trial, and should be used alongside, not instead of, standard ultrasound monitoring and medical assessment.

evidence.source: Bofill Rodriguez M et al., Progestogen-releasing intrauterine systems for heavy menstrual bleeding, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020
evidence.quote: The progestogen-releasing intrauterine system is an effective treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding, genuinely reducing blood loss.
evidence.recovery: Most causes of heavy bleeding are very treatable once identified -- medication alone controls many cases, without needing a procedure.
evidence.seekCareIf: Bleeding is soaking through protection every hour or two, you're passing large clots, or you notice fatigue/breathlessness that could mean anaemia -- these deserve assessment rather than being accepted as 'normal for you'.

conventional.remedy: Tranexamic acid, taken during the days of bleeding
conventional.note: Genuinely reduces menstrual blood loss -- a well-established, non-hormonal first option.

conventional.remedy: A progestogen-releasing intrauterine system (IUS), for ongoing control
conventional.note: [Cochrane review] Genuinely effective at reducing heavy bleeding long-term -- a well-evidenced option for women wanting a longer-term solution.

conventional.remedy: Check ferritin/full blood count and take iron supplementation if anaemia is confirmed
conventional.note: Directly addresses the common, important consequence of ongoing heavy blood loss.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda management of Raktapradara, under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct -- alongside, not instead of, conventional treatment
ayurveda.note: [Registered RCT protocol -- results not yet available] A 2025 published protocol describes an ongoing randomised controlled trial directly comparing Ayurveda treatment (Ashokarishta, Trinakantamani pishti plus iron/folic acid) against tranexamic acid (the conventional standard) for menorrhagia. This shows serious, rigorous comparative research is underway -- but as a protocol paper, it does not yet tell us which treatment works better, so no efficacy claim can honestly be made from it yet.

evidence.source: The 2022 hormone therapy position statement of The North American Menopause Society, Menopause 2022
evidence.quote: Hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and genitourinary syndrome of menopause; for women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset without contraindications, the benefit-risk ratio is favourable.
evidence.recovery: Not a condition to 'recover' from -- a natural transition. Symptoms genuinely settle for most women over time, though this can take several years, and effective treatment is available in the meantime if symptoms are disruptive.
evidence.seekCareIf: Any bleeding occurs after 12 months without a period -- this is NOT a normal menopause symptom and needs assessment. Also seek care if symptoms are significantly affecting your quality of life; effective treatment exists and you don't have to just 'push through it'.

conventional.remedy: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT), for appropriately selected women without contraindications, discussed with a doctor
conventional.note: [NAMS 2022 position statement] The most effective treatment for hot flushes/night sweats and genitourinary symptoms -- the benefit-risk ratio is favourable for most women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause onset.

conventional.remedy: Non-hormonal options (certain antidepressants, lifestyle measures -- layered clothing, cooling the bedroom, avoiding known triggers) where HRT isn't suitable or preferred
conventional.note: Reasonable alternatives for symptom relief when HRT isn't the right choice for an individual.

conventional.remedy: Prompt assessment for any bleeding after 12 months without a period
conventional.note: This is genuinely NOT a normal menopause symptom -- an important safety point, not just reassurance-seeking.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ashokarishta, Ashwagandha Churna and Praval Pishti, under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine 52-patient randomised open clinical trial] A CCRAS-directed 2012 study in Ayu found highly significant improvement on validated menopause symptom scales (Kupperman Index, Menopause Rating Scale, MENQOL) with this combined regimen. Honestly framed as open-label (no blinding or placebo control) -- a real randomised trial, but not the strongest possible design, and should be used alongside, not instead of, standard medical options like HRT.

yoga.remedy: Gentle, cooling restorative yoga practice; slow diaphragmatic breathing during a hot flush
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to menopausal vasomotor symptoms was found for a named yoga sequence -- included only as a generally-used calming practice, not a proven treatment for hot flushes themselves.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Vulvovaginal Candidiasis: A Review of the Evidence for the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2022
evidence.quote: Fluconazole and topical azole therapies are effective first-line treatments for vulvovaginal candidiasis; only topical azoles are recommended in pregnancy.
evidence.recovery: Most episodes clear within a few days of starting treatment. Recurrent episodes (4 or more a year) deserve proper assessment rather than repeated self-treatment.
evidence.seekCareIf: Symptoms don't improve with standard over-the-counter treatment, episodes keep recurring, or you've never had this diagnosed before and aren't sure it's the cause.

conventional.remedy: An antifungal (topical clotrimazole cream/pessary, or a single oral fluconazole dose)
conventional.note: [2021 CDC guideline evidence review] Both are effective first-line options -- topical azoles are preferred in pregnancy.

conventional.remedy: Loose, breathable cotton underwear; avoid scented soaps/washes in the area
conventional.note: Reduces irritation and moisture that can worsen symptoms -- a sensible, low-risk supportive measure.

conventional.remedy: Check blood glucose if episodes are recurrent
conventional.note: Poorly-controlled diabetes is a real, treatable trigger for recurrent candidiasis -- worth investigating rather than just repeating antifungal courses.

ayurveda.remedy: Triphala Kashaya vaginal douche (Yoni prakshalana), under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine randomised open-label trial] A 2026 exploratory randomised trial found earlier improvement in discharge, itching and Candida spore count with Triphala Kashaya douche (with or without Gomutra Arka) in vaginal candidiasis (correlated with Slaishmiki Yonivyapad). Open-label and exploratory -- a real trial, but should be used alongside, not instead of, standard antifungal treatment.

evidence.source: Diagnosis and Management of Bacterial Vaginosis: Summary of Evidence Reviewed for the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2022
evidence.quote: Oral or vaginal metronidazole and clindamycin are effective first-line treatments for bacterial vaginosis.
evidence.recovery: Symptoms typically improve within a few days of starting treatment. Recurrence is common -- BV returns in a significant proportion of women within months, which is a genuine feature of the condition, not a sign treatment failed.
evidence.seekCareIf: You are pregnant -- treatment matters more given the genuine link to preterm birth risk. Also seek care if symptoms don't settle with treatment or keep recurring frequently.

conventional.remedy: Oral or vaginal metronidazole (or clindamycin), as prescribed
conventional.note: [2021 CDC guideline evidence review] The standard, effective treatment -- complete the full course even if symptoms improve early.

conventional.remedy: Avoid vaginal douching
conventional.note: Disrupts normal protective vaginal flora and can trigger or worsen BV -- a genuinely low-risk change to make regardless of current symptoms.

conventional.remedy: Prompt treatment if pregnant
conventional.note: Untreated BV is linked to a genuine increase in preterm birth risk -- this is not just about symptom comfort in pregnancy.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda management of Shwetapradara (vaginal discharge), under a qualified practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Single case report, addressing the discharge symptom generally, not BV-specific confirmation -- the weakest evidence tier used in this project] A 2024 case report describes symptom relief from Ayurveda treatment for leucorrhoea. This addresses vaginal discharge as a symptom rather than confirming bacterial vaginosis specifically, and one patient's experience does not establish this works in general -- it should not replace metronidazole/clindamycin as the evidence-based treatment, especially in pregnancy.

evidence.source: Diagnosis and Management of Trichomonas vaginalis: Summary of Evidence Reviewed for the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2022
evidence.quote: Metronidazole is highly effective against Trichomonas vaginalis, with cure rates of approximately 84-98% in randomised trials; multidose regimens now outperform single-dose therapy in women.
evidence.recovery: Symptoms typically clear within a week of completing treatment, provided the sexual partner is also treated -- otherwise reinfection is very likely.
evidence.seekCareIf: Symptoms persist after completing treatment (possible reinfection from an untreated partner, or resistant infection), or if you're unsure how to have the partner-notification conversation -- a clinic can help with this.

conventional.remedy: Oral metronidazole (multidose course now generally preferred over a single dose in women)
conventional.note: [2021 CDC guideline evidence review] Genuinely effective, with multidose regimens now shown to outperform the older single-dose approach in women specifically.

conventional.remedy: Treat the sexual partner(s) at the same time, and avoid sex until both are treated
conventional.note: This is a genuine STI -- without partner treatment, reinfection is very likely, undoing the treatment.

conventional.remedy: Get screened for other STIs at the same visit
conventional.note: Co-infection with other sexually transmitted infections is common -- worth checking at the same time.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A direct PubMed search for disease-specific Ayurveda evidence for trichomoniasis found nothing relevant -- stated honestly rather than reusing unverifiable web content.

evidence.source: Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021, MMWR Recomm Rep 2021 (CDC)
evidence.quote: Ceftriaxone is recommended for gonorrhoea and doxycycline for chlamydia; both infections are frequently asymptomatic, which underpins the importance of testing and partner notification, not just treating symptoms.
evidence.recovery: Both infections clear reliably with the correct antibiotic -- but because so many infections are mild or silent, testing (not waiting for symptoms) is how most cases are actually caught.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, for any genuine risk exposure (new/multiple partners, a partner with symptoms or a positive test) -- do not wait for symptoms, since a large proportion of infections, especially chlamydia, cause none at all.

conventional.remedy: Ceftriaxone (single injection) for gonorrhoea; doxycycline (7-day course) for chlamydia, as diagnosed
conventional.note: [2021 CDC treatment guidelines] Treatment differs by organism, which is exactly why testing before treating matters -- don't assume which infection it is.

conventional.remedy: Partner notification and treatment, essential before resuming sex
conventional.note: Prevents reinfection (a 'ping-pong' cycle between partners) and interrupts further spread -- a genuinely important step, not optional.

conventional.remedy: Testing (not waiting for symptoms) after any genuine exposure risk
conventional.note: A large proportion of infections, especially chlamydia, cause no symptoms at all -- this is exactly why opportunistic screening, not symptom-triggered testing alone, is recommended for higher-risk groups.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Puyameha is the classical correlate for gonorrhoea, but a direct PubMed search returns zero indexed results. Broader searches for gonorrhoea/chlamydia plus Ayurveda were checked title-by-title -- every result was an unrelated pharmacognosy or epidemiology paper, not genuine disease-specific clinical evidence -- so nothing is cited here.

evidence.source: Diagnosis and Management of Genital Herpes: Key Questions and Review of the Evidence for the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2022
evidence.quote: Antiviral therapy (aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir) started early in a first episode reduces the severity and duration of symptoms; suppressive daily therapy reduces both recurrence frequency and transmission risk.
evidence.recovery: A first episode typically resolves over 2-4 weeks with treatment; recurrences are usually shorter and milder, and tend to become less frequent over time. The virus remains dormant between outbreaks -- this is a lifelong infection, an important point to understand from the start.
evidence.seekCareIf: This is your first suspected episode (start treatment promptly, ideally within 72 hours of symptoms starting), or you're pregnant -- genital herpes needs specific management in pregnancy to protect the baby.

conventional.remedy: An oral antiviral (aciclovir, valaciclovir or famciclovir), started as early as possible
conventional.note: [2021 CDC guideline evidence review] Most effective when started early in an episode -- don't wait to see if it settles on its own, especially for a first episode.

conventional.remedy: Keep the area clean and dry; loose clothing; saline bathing can ease discomfort
conventional.note: Simple, low-risk comfort measures during an outbreak.

conventional.remedy: Discuss suppressive daily antiviral therapy with a doctor if recurrences are frequent, or to reduce transmission risk to a partner
conventional.note: [2021 CDC guideline evidence review] Genuinely reduces both how often outbreaks happen and the chance of passing the infection to a partner.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Two candidate sources were checked and rejected: one described blisters on the limbs, not genital herpes -- a category error avoided; the other, despite its journal, was actually about homeopathy, a different system of medicine -- also avoided. Nothing genuinely disease-specific and PubMed-indexed was found.

evidence.source: Management of Adult Syphilis: Key Questions to Inform the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2022
evidence.quote: A single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G remains highly effective first-line treatment for early syphilis.
evidence.recovery: Early syphilis (primary or secondary stage) responds very well to a single penicillin injection. Follow-up blood tests over months confirm the infection has cleared -- this matters, don't skip follow-up.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, promptly -- this is an urgent condition. Untreated syphilis progresses through further stages with serious long-term complications, which is exactly why prompt treatment (not just symptom relief) genuinely matters.

conventional.remedy: Prompt medical assessment and a single benzathine penicillin G injection for early syphilis
conventional.note: [2021 CDC guideline evidence review] Highly effective, single-dose treatment for early-stage disease -- this is not a condition to manage at home or delay.

conventional.remedy: Partner notification and testing
conventional.note: Essential given ongoing transmission risk to sexual partners.

conventional.remedy: HIV testing at the same visit
conventional.note: Co-infection with HIV is genuinely common -- worth checking at the same time, not as a separate, later step.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A direct PubMed search for disease-specific Ayurveda evidence for syphilis found nothing relevant, on top of this being an urgent condition where any delay to prompt antibiotic treatment is a genuine risk -- stated honestly rather than reusing unverifiable web content.

evidence.source: Saag MS et al., Antiretroviral Drugs for Treatment and Prevention of HIV Infection in Adults: 2022 Recommendations of the International Antiviral Society-USA Panel, JAMA 2023
evidence.quote: Modern antiretroviral therapy, started promptly after diagnosis, gives people living with HIV a life expectancy approaching that of the general population.
evidence.recovery: HIV is a manageable chronic condition with modern treatment, not the terminal diagnosis it once was. Antiretroviral therapy (ART), taken consistently, keeps the virus suppressed indefinitely -- and when the viral load is undetectable, the virus cannot be sexually transmitted ('undetectable = untransmittable', a genuinely well-established finding).
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, promptly, after any genuine exposure risk -- testing, not waiting for symptoms, is how this is actually caught early. If newly diagnosed, prompt referral to start ART is the single most important next step.

conventional.remedy: Prompt referral to start antiretroviral therapy (ART) if diagnosed -- this is not optional or something to delay
conventional.note: [IAS-USA 2022 guideline] Starting ART promptly after diagnosis gives the best long-term outcomes -- modern regimens are well-tolerated and highly effective.

conventional.remedy: Take ART exactly as prescribed, every day, without gaps
conventional.note: Consistent adherence is what keeps the virus suppressed -- missed doses risk resistance developing, which narrows future treatment options.

conventional.remedy: Adequate, balanced nutrition, as a genuine adjunct alongside ART -- never as a substitute for it
conventional.note: [Registered India-based study protocol, results not yet available] A 2025 Indian study protocol notes nutritional status genuinely affects clinical outcomes and quality of life in people on ART. This is about supporting the immune system and general health alongside treatment, not treating HIV itself -- nutrition alone does not suppress the virus.

conventional.remedy: Discuss PrEP (pre-exposure prophylaxis) if you have an ongoing risk of exposure, or PEP (post-exposure prophylaxis) within 72 hours of a specific high-risk exposure
conventional.note: Genuinely effective prevention options, worth an explicit conversation with a doctor rather than assuming they don't apply to you.

evidence.source: Pandav CS, Past, present, and future of iodine deficiency disorders in India: Need to look outside the blinkers, J Family Med Prim Care 2017
evidence.quote: Iodine deficiency disorders, including goitre, remain a significant public health issue in parts of India, particularly the Himalayan belt and other iodine-deficient regions, despite decades of salt iodisation programmes.
evidence.recovery: Correcting dietary iodine intake (iodised salt) can reduce goitre size over months, particularly in younger people. Longstanding goitre in older adults may not fully shrink, but stops progressing.
evidence.seekCareIf: The swelling is rapidly enlarging, hard, or asymmetric (possible nodule needing separate assessment), or you develop symptoms of an over- or under-active thyroid (weight change, heat/cold intolerance, mood change, palpitations).

conventional.remedy: Use iodised salt consistently
conventional.note: [India-specific review] The standard, low-cost, effective public-health and individual measure for correcting the underlying cause in iodine-deficient regions.

conventional.remedy: Thyroid function testing to confirm normal (euthyroid) function
conventional.note: Distinguishes simple goitre from Hypothyroidism/Hyperthyroidism, which need different management.

conventional.remedy: Referral for ultrasound if the gland is asymmetric, hard, or rapidly enlarging
conventional.note: A nodule within the gland needs its own separate assessment, distinct from diffuse iodine-deficiency goitre.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Galaganda is a genuine, textbook-correct classical correlate for goitre, and a specific clinical study (Kanchanar Gutika) was found describing its management -- but it is not PubMed-indexed on direct search, so it is not cited here as verified clinical evidence.

evidence.source: Management of Diabetes in Pregnancy: A Review of Clinical Guidelines and Practices, Cureus 2025
evidence.quote: Universal screening for gestational diabetes mellitus at 24-28 weeks of gestation with a 75g oral glucose tolerance test is recommended, with dietary modification as first-line management.
evidence.recovery: Blood sugar usually returns to normal after delivery -- but gestational diabetes genuinely predicts a higher future risk of type 2 diabetes, so postpartum testing and ongoing healthy lifestyle habits matter beyond the pregnancy itself.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, once diagnosed -- this needs an active management plan throughout the pregnancy, not just monitoring. Also seek care for reduced fetal movements or any pregnancy warning signs, which are separate from diabetes management itself.

conventional.remedy: Dietary modification (controlled carbohydrate intake, regular meal timing) and regular blood glucose monitoring
conventional.note: [Clinical guideline review] First-line management, controlling blood sugar in a large proportion of cases without medication.

conventional.remedy: Regular moderate physical activity, as advised for your specific pregnancy
conventional.note: Genuinely helps blood glucose control alongside diet -- discuss what's appropriate for your pregnancy with your doctor.

conventional.remedy: Insulin or metformin if diet/lifestyle measures alone don't achieve target glucose control
conventional.note: [Clinical guideline review] Both are considered safe options in pregnancy when needed -- not a sign that something has gone wrong, just the next appropriate step.

conventional.remedy: Postpartum glucose tolerance testing at 4-12 weeks after delivery
conventional.note: Gestational diabetes genuinely predicts future type 2 diabetes risk -- this follow-up step matters and is easy to overlook once the baby arrives.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Garbhini Prameha is a genuine classical correlate, and a specific randomised trial (Prishniparni Ghanavati) was found -- but it is not PubMed-indexed on direct search, so it is not cited here as verified clinical evidence. Any herbal remedy in pregnancy also carries genuine safety considerations that would need careful, individualised medical guidance regardless.

evidence.source: Best Practices for Thalassaemia Management: Recommendations by Indian Society of Haematology and Blood Transfusion, Indian J Hematol Blood Transfus 2026
evidence.quote: Comprehensive, evidence-informed guidance for the diagnosis, treatment, monitoring, and prevention of thalassaemia is genuinely needed across diverse healthcare settings in India, given its significant burden.
evidence.recovery: Thalassaemia trait/minor usually needs no active treatment beyond avoiding unnecessary iron supplementation. Thalassaemia major requires lifelong, regular transfusion and iron chelation therapy -- genuinely manageable with consistent specialist care, though not curable outside bone marrow transplant.
evidence.seekCareIf: You've been told you have 'anaemia that doesn't respond to iron', or you're planning a family and have a personal/family history of thalassaemia -- genetic counselling before conception is genuinely valuable given the inheritance pattern.

conventional.remedy: Do NOT take iron supplements unless a genuine coexistent iron deficiency is confirmed
conventional.note: [India-specific guideline] A real, avoidable error -- thalassaemia's ferritin is normal/high, and unnecessary iron supplementation can contribute to iron overload over time.

conventional.remedy: Genetic counselling, particularly before starting a family
conventional.note: Given the autosomal recessive inheritance, this is genuinely valuable information for family planning, not just of academic interest.

conventional.remedy: Regular transfusion and iron chelation therapy under specialist haematology care, for transfusion-dependent thalassaemia major
conventional.note: [India-specific guideline] The established, life-sustaining standard of care -- consistent follow-up genuinely matters for long-term outcomes.

ayurveda.remedy: Triphaladi Avaleha, as a genuinely disease-specific adjunct alongside (never instead of) standard transfusion/chelation therapy where indicated, under a qualified practitioner
ayurveda.note: [Genuine adjuvant-therapy study, disease-specific] A 2010 study in Ayu evaluated Triphaladi Avaleha as an adjuvant in thalassaemia management. Notably, the study authors themselves explicitly describe thalassaemia as 'Anukta Vyadhi' -- a disease not described in classical Ayurveda texts -- an honest acknowledgement reused here rather than glossed over. This should never replace transfusion or chelation therapy for transfusion-dependent disease.

evidence.source: Burden of vaso-occlusive crisis, its management and impact on quality of life of Indian sickle cell disease patients, Br J Haematol 2025
evidence.quote: Over 86% of Indian sickle cell disease patients reported at least one vaso-occlusive crisis episode in the year prior to enrolment, substantially reducing quality of life across all domains.
evidence.recovery: Not applicable in the usual self-care sense -- a crisis needs prompt hospital-based pain management and hydration. Between crises, hydroxyurea and trigger avoidance genuinely reduce how often crises happen.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, promptly, for a suspected crisis -- this is a genuine medical emergency needing hospital assessment, not a condition to manage expectantly at home.

conventional.remedy: Go to hospital promptly for pain management, hydration and monitoring during a suspected crisis
conventional.note: [India-specific burden study] This is not a condition to wait out at home -- prompt, adequate pain management is both appropriate and genuinely necessary given the severity documented in Indian patients.

conventional.remedy: Hydroxyurea as ongoing therapy between crises, under specialist haematology care
conventional.note: The established, disease-modifying treatment that genuinely reduces crisis frequency over time.

conventional.remedy: Stay well hydrated, avoid cold exposure and high altitude, and treat infections promptly
conventional.note: Genuine, well-established trigger-avoidance measures that can reduce crisis frequency.

ayurveda.remedy: An Ayurveda regimen as a genuine ADJUNCT alongside standard care (hydroxyurea, hydration, prompt crisis management), under a qualified practitioner and haematologist working together -- never as a substitute during an acute crisis
ayurveda.note: [Large registered trial protocol, results not yet published] A 2025 JMIR Research Protocols paper describes a randomised controlled trial of an Ayurvedic intervention (Dadimadi Ghrita and Ayush-RP) as an adjunct to standard care, with 1,510 participants enrolled and 1,137 having completed the study as of the protocol's own reporting -- a substantial, serious trial, but as a protocol paper it does not yet report whether the intervention worked. This should never delay or replace hospital care during an actual crisis.

evidence.source: Livingstone-Banks J et al., Nicotine receptor partial agonists for smoking cessation, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023
evidence.quote: Varenicline and cytisine increase the chances of successfully stopping smoking compared with placebo or no pharmacotherapy, and are also more effective than single-form nicotine replacement therapy.
evidence.recovery: Quitting reduces health risk from the moment you stop, with the steepest gains in the first year -- but nicotine dependence itself is a genuine chronic, relapsing condition, and most people need more than one attempt to quit for good.
evidence.seekCareIf: You are experiencing withdrawal symptoms severe enough to disrupt daily function, or you notice red-flag symptoms (unintentional weight loss, coughing blood, persistent breathlessness, night sweats) that need assessment for a smoking-related complication rather than dependence alone.

conventional.remedy: Combine behavioural counselling with pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement therapy, varenicline, or bupropion)
conventional.note: [Cochrane 2023] Genuinely more effective together than either alone -- varenicline and cytisine were found more effective than single-form nicotine replacement therapy.

conventional.remedy: For smokeless tobacco use (common in India), the same principle applies -- structured pharmacotherapy support, not willpower alone
conventional.note: [India-specific double-blind RCT] Varenicline showed genuine benefit for smokeless tobacco dependence specifically, a major and often under-addressed form of tobacco use in India.

conventional.remedy: Set a clear quit date and arrange follow-up support rather than attempting to quit unsupported
conventional.note: Structured cessation support genuinely improves success rates over unsupported attempts, and most people need more than one attempt.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda cessation evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Dhumapana is a genuine classical correlate for smoke-related practice, but returns only 2 PubMed-indexed results on direct search, both independently verified as unrelated to tobacco cessation (an asthma case report and a coma case study) -- so no evidence-based Ayurveda cessation remedy is cited here.

yoga.remedy: Slow diaphragmatic breathing practice as a craving-management technique during withdrawal
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to tobacco-craving management was found for a named yoga/breathing sequence -- included only as a generally-used calming practice that some people use alongside evidence-based pharmacotherapy, not a proven cessation aid itself.
