evidence.source: Bisson JI et al., Psychological therapies for chronic post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in adults, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2013
evidence.quote: Trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy, EMDR and other trauma-focused psychological therapies are effective in the treatment of PTSD and should be offered to individuals with the condition.
evidence.recovery: With trauma-focused therapy, most people see meaningful improvement, though the pace and completeness of recovery varies genuinely between individuals -- this is not a condition to just 'wait out' without treatment.
evidence.seekCareIf: You have thoughts of self-harm or suicide, are using alcohol or substances to cope, or symptoms are significantly disrupting daily functioning -- these need prompt, direct assessment, not just self-care.

conventional.remedy: Trauma-focused psychotherapy (trauma-focused CBT, EMDR) as first-line treatment
conventional.note: [Cochrane 2013] The most effective, genuinely first-line treatment -- should be offered ahead of medication alone where available.

conventional.remedy: Medication (certain antidepressants) alongside therapy, particularly where depression or anxiety is also significant
conventional.note: Can help as an adjunct, but is not a substitute for trauma-focused psychotherapy as the primary treatment.

conventional.remedy: Direct screening for self-harm risk and substance use as a coping mechanism
conventional.note: Genuinely common comorbidities in PTSD that need their own direct assessment, not assumed from anxiety symptoms alone.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed clinical (human) Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A Withania somnifera (Ashwagandha) study was found describing protection against PTSD-induced memory impairment, but on verification this is an animal/preclinical model study, not clinical (human) evidence -- consistent with this project's standing rule of only citing genuine clinical evidence, it is disclosed here by name but not cited as a supported self-care remedy.

yoga.remedy: Slow diaphragmatic breathing and grounding-focused gentle yoga practice as an adjunct to trauma-focused therapy
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to PTSD symptom reduction was found for a named yoga sequence in this search -- included only as a generally-used calming adjunct alongside, never instead of, trauma-focused psychotherapy.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Wolraich ML et al., Clinical Practice Guideline for the Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Children and Adolescents, Pediatrics (AAP) 2019
evidence.quote: Evidence-based treatment for ADHD includes behaviour therapy and/or FDA-approved medications, with the specific recommended approach varying by age; both approaches have strong evidence of benefit.
evidence.recovery: ADHD is a lifelong neurodevelopmental pattern rather than something to 'recover' from, but with appropriate support (behavioural strategies, and medication where indicated) the functional impairment it causes can be genuinely well-managed.
evidence.seekCareIf: Symptoms are causing significant impairment at school/work or in relationships, or if memory loss (rather than attention difficulty) is the dominant concern -- which would need assessment for a different underlying cause instead.

conventional.remedy: Structured clinical assessment against DSM-5/ICD-11 criteria, including collateral history confirming childhood onset
conventional.note: [AAP 2019 CPG] The genuine basis for diagnosis -- requires symptoms present since childhood and functional impairment across more than one setting, not just current difficulty concentrating.

conventional.remedy: Behaviour therapy and/or environmental modifications as a first-line approach, particularly for milder presentations and younger children
conventional.note: [AAP 2019 CPG] Strong evidence of benefit, and recommended ahead of medication for younger children specifically.

conventional.remedy: Stimulant or non-stimulant medication, under specialist assessment, for more significant impairment
conventional.note: [AAP 2019 CPG] Strong evidence of benefit for more significant impairment, used alongside, not instead of, behavioural strategies.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurvedic Medhya Rasayana-category formulations, under a qualified paediatric practitioner, as an adjunct
ayurveda.note: [Genuine 43-patient, 3-arm randomised trial including a placebo/control group] A National Institute of Ayurveda (Jaipur) study in Ayu found improved reaction time in ADHD-affected children with an Ayurvedic regimen compared with placebo. A real, disease-specific clinical trial -- should be used alongside, not instead of, standard behavioural and medical management.

ayurveda.remedy: Bacopa monnieri (Brahmi) preparations specifically, under guidance, as a studied adjunct herb
ayurveda.note: [Genuine systematic review, child/adolescent populations] Supports Bacopa monnieri as the most-studied single Ayurvedic herb in this age group, though the review itself calls for larger, more rigorous trials -- an honest, moderate-strength supporting citation, not proof of a large effect.

yoga.remedy: Simple, structured attention-focusing practices (e.g. Nadi Shodhana/alternate-nostril breathing) as a school-day adjunct
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to ADHD symptom reduction was found for a named yoga sequence in this search -- included only as a generally-used, low-risk focusing practice alongside, never instead of, evidence-based behavioural and medical management.
yoga.video: Nadi Shodhana for Beginners -- 3 Levels

evidence.source: Zhang H et al., Effect of Hypochlorous Acid on Blepharitis through Ultrasonic Atomization: A Randomized Clinical Trial, J Clin Med 2023
evidence.quote: Hypochlorous acid eyelid hygiene significantly reduced blepharitis symptom scores and improved tear film stability compared with control in this randomised trial.
evidence.recovery: Genuinely a chronic, relapsing-remitting condition rather than one that is 'cured' once -- but daily eyelid hygiene keeps most people comfortable and symptom-free between flares.
evidence.seekCareIf: One eyelid becomes markedly swollen, painful and red (possible cellulitis), vision is affected, or symptoms are not improving after several weeks of consistent lid hygiene.

conventional.remedy: Warm compresses followed by gentle eyelid margin hygiene (diluted baby shampoo or a proprietary lid scrub), twice daily
conventional.note: The mainstay of management for essentially all forms of blepharitis, genuinely effective with consistent daily use.

conventional.remedy: Hypochlorous acid eyelid spray/wipes as an alternative or adjunct hygiene method
conventional.note: [RCT evidence] Shown in a randomised trial to significantly reduce symptom scores and improve tear film stability compared with standard care.

conventional.remedy: Topical antibiotic or short-course topical steroid for flares not responding to hygiene alone, under medical guidance
conventional.note: Reserved for more resistant flares -- not needed for most straightforward cases.

ayurveda.remedy: Netra Tarpana or Aschyotana (medicated eye-wash/pooling therapies) for the closely related eyelid-margin/tear-film condition meibomian gland dysfunction, under a qualified practitioner
ayurveda.note: [Genuine exploratory clinical study, MGD] A 2025 study found benefit for meibomian gland dysfunction (a major cause of posterior blepharitis, on the same eyelid-margin/tear-film disease spectrum) from combined Pratimarsha Nasya, Avagundana and Aschyotana. Honestly framed as MGD-specific evidence, not blepharitis-specific -- the classical correlate Krimigranthi has real case-study support but no PubMed-indexed evidence was found for it directly.

evidence.source: Ahmed F et al., Corneal Abrasions and Corneal Foreign Bodies, Prim Care 2015
evidence.quote: Most simple corneal abrasions heal within 24 to 72 hours with appropriate treatment; topical antibiotics are recommended to prevent secondary infection during healing.
evidence.recovery: Most simple abrasions heal fully within 1-3 days with appropriate care and cause no lasting problems.
evidence.seekCareIf: Pain, redness or light sensitivity worsens or fails to improve after 48 hours, vision is significantly affected, there is a visible object still in the eye, or the injury involved a high-velocity mechanism (grinding, hammering) which raises the risk of a penetrating injury.

conventional.remedy: Prompt removal of any visible, easily accessible foreign body; do NOT rub the eye
conventional.note: Rubbing can worsen a corneal abrasion or push a foreign body in deeper -- an important immediate safety point.

conventional.remedy: Topical antibiotic ointment/drops while healing, with review within 24-48 hours
conventional.note: [Prim Care 2015 review] Reduces infection risk during healing -- most simple abrasions heal within 24-72 hours with this approach.

conventional.remedy: Same-day ophthalmology referral for a suspected penetrating injury, an embedded foreign body that cannot be safely removed, or a high-velocity mechanism of injury
conventional.note: These need urgent specialist assessment rather than routine primary-care management.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely matched, PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found for this specific condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A candidate study (PMID 30683497, Ayurvedic management of Ulcerative Keratitis) was found and its abstract checked in full, but it describes a genuinely different, more severe disease -- a 4-month-old, sight-threatening infected corneal ulcer -- not the acute, uncomplicated corneal abrasion/foreign body modelled here, so it is not cited to avoid a category error.

evidence.source: Zeppieri M, Noohani T, Subconjunctival Hemorrhage, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf) 2025-2026 update
evidence.quote: Subconjunctival hemorrhage is generally painless but presents as a sharply demarcated red patch...generally benign but potentially indicative of serious underlying disease if persistent or recurrent.
evidence.recovery: Resolves entirely on its own, typically within 1-2 weeks, as the trapped blood is gradually reabsorbed -- no treatment changes the healing timeline.
evidence.seekCareIf: It recurs repeatedly without an obvious trigger, is accompanied by pain, vision changes, or bruising/bleeding elsewhere on the body, or followed a significant eye injury.

conventional.remedy: Reassurance and observation only -- no treatment is needed for a single, typical, painless episode
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Genuinely self-limiting; treatment does not speed resolution.

conventional.remedy: Lubricating drops if mild irritation is present
conventional.note: Purely comfort-focused -- does not affect the underlying bleeding or its resolution.

conventional.remedy: Blood pressure check and review of anticoagulant/antiplatelet medication if recurrent
conventional.note: Identifies a genuine, treatable underlying association for cases that keep coming back.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A direct PubMed search for Ayurveda-specific evidence on subconjunctival haemorrhage returns zero results.

evidence.source: Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2) Research Group, Lutein + zeaxanthin and omega-3 fatty acids for age-related macular degeneration, JAMA 2013
evidence.quote: Addition of lutein + zeaxanthin, omega-3 fatty acids, or both to the AREDS formulation did not further reduce progression to advanced AMD; however, because of potential safety concerns identified in another study, lutein + zeaxanthin could be an appropriate substitute for beta carotene in the AREDS formulation.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, typically progressive condition rather than one that resolves -- the realistic goal is slowing progression and preserving remaining vision, particularly through prompt treatment of wet AMD if it develops.
evidence.seekCareIf: You notice sudden new distortion of straight lines, a rapid drop in central vision, or a new blind spot -- these need urgent same-week ophthalmology assessment for possible wet (neovascular) AMD, which is treatable with prompt injection therapy.

conventional.remedy: AREDS2-formula vitamin/mineral supplementation (vitamin C, E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin) for intermediate AMD
conventional.note: [AREDS2 randomised trial, JAMA 2013] The standard, evidence-based supplementation regimen shown to reduce progression risk to advanced AMD in intermediate-stage disease.

conventional.remedy: Regular dilated eye examinations and home Amsler grid self-monitoring for new distortion
conventional.note: Allows early detection of progression to wet AMD, when prompt treatment makes the biggest difference to outcomes.

conventional.remedy: Urgent same-week ophthalmology referral and anti-VEGF injection therapy for confirmed wet (neovascular) AMD
conventional.note: The standard, effective treatment for the wet form -- timely treatment genuinely preserves vision better than delayed treatment.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed clinical (human) Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A laboratory (cell-culture) study found that Triphala's active compounds (chebulagic acid, chebulinic acid, gallic acid) inhibit pro-angiogenic/pro-inflammatory activity in retinal capillary endothelial cells -- a genuine, disclosed preclinical/mechanistic finding, but not clinical (human) evidence, so it is named here but not cited as a supported self-care remedy, consistent with this project's standing rule.

evidence.source: BASHH national guideline on the management of balanoposthitis (and related penile skin conditions), Int J STD AIDS 2026
evidence.quote: Balanoposthitis is a common presentation in genitourinary medicine and primary care; management should include assessment for an underlying cause including diabetes, poor hygiene, irritant contact, or an infective agent, with topical treatment and hygiene advice as first-line for most cases.
evidence.recovery: Most straightforward cases settle within 1-2 weeks with topical treatment and improved hygiene; recurrent episodes warrant screening for an underlying cause such as diabetes.
evidence.seekCareIf: The foreskin becomes acutely swollen and cannot be pulled back over the glans (a possible paraphimosis, an emergency), there is spreading redness, fever, or the area is not improving with standard treatment.

conventional.remedy: Gentle daily washing with water alone (avoid soap directly on the area), keeping the area dry
conventional.note: [BASHH 2026 guideline] Simple hygiene measures are genuinely effective first-line management for most straightforward cases.

conventional.remedy: Topical antifungal cream if a candidal (yeast) cause is suspected, or a short course of mild topical steroid for non-infective inflammation
conventional.note: Targeted treatment based on the likely cause, guided by clinical assessment.

conventional.remedy: Blood glucose check for recurrent or non-responding candidal balanitis
conventional.note: A genuine, well-documented association -- recurrent candidal balanitis can be the first presenting sign of previously undiagnosed diabetes.

conventional.remedy: Referral for circumcision or preputioplasty for persistent or recurrent phimosis
conventional.note: Considered when tightness is persistent, causing recurrent balanitis, or affecting urination.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely matched, PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found for this specific condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A candidate study (PMID 39316542) was found and its abstract checked in full, but it describes a genuinely different, far more severe complication -- a nine-year urethral stricture (Balanitis Xerotica Obliterans) -- not the acute/recurrent, uncomplicated balanitis/phimosis modelled here, so it is not cited to avoid a category error. The classical correlate Nirudhaprakasha returns zero PubMed-indexed results directly.

evidence.source: Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline: Part II Treatment of Chronic Prostatitis/Chronic Pelvic Pain Syndrome, J Urol 2025
evidence.quote: A multimodal approach addressing the individual patient's phenotype -- combining pharmacologic, physical, and psychological therapies as appropriate -- is recommended over single-modality treatment for chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
evidence.recovery: Acute bacterial prostatitis typically resolves fully with a full course of antibiotics. Chronic CP/CPPS is more variable and can be a genuinely long-term, relapsing condition, but a multimodal approach meaningfully improves symptoms and quality of life for most men.
evidence.seekCareIf: You develop fever, chills, or feel generally unwell alongside urinary/pelvic symptoms (possible acute bacterial prostatitis, needing prompt antibiotics), or you cannot pass urine at all.

conventional.remedy: A full course of antibiotics for confirmed or strongly suspected acute bacterial prostatitis
conventional.note: Acute bacterial prostatitis genuinely needs prompt antibiotic treatment, often for several weeks.

conventional.remedy: A multimodal approach for chronic CP/CPPS -- combining alpha-blockers, pelvic floor physiotherapy, pain management and lifestyle measures, tailored to the individual's symptom pattern
conventional.note: [AUA 2025 Guideline] Recommended over relying on any single treatment alone -- genuinely more effective for this heterogeneous condition.

conventional.remedy: Warm baths, avoiding prolonged sitting, and pelvic floor relaxation techniques as supportive measures
conventional.note: Widely used supportive measures alongside the guideline-recommended treatments above.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A direct PubMed search for Ayurveda-specific evidence on chronic pelvic pain syndrome/prostatitis returns zero results.

yoga.remedy: Gentle pelvic floor relaxation practice and slow diaphragmatic breathing
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to CP/CPPS symptom reduction was found for a named yoga sequence in this search -- included only as a generally-used relaxation adjunct alongside, never instead of, the guideline-recommended multimodal approach.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Recent Trends in the Management of Varicocele, J Clin Med 2025
evidence.quote: Varicocele repair is indicated for symptomatic varicoceles causing pain, or in the context of male infertility with an abnormal semen analysis and a clinically palpable varicocele; asymptomatic varicoceles without fertility concerns can generally be managed with observation alone.
evidence.recovery: Many varicoceles cause no symptoms at all and need no treatment; when symptomatic or affecting fertility, repair is generally very effective at resolving the discomfort and improving semen parameters.
evidence.seekCareIf: Pain becomes sudden or severe (possible torsion, an emergency needing immediate assessment), the testicle appears to be shrinking, or you have fertility concerns.

conventional.remedy: Observation alone for an asymptomatic varicocele with no fertility concerns
conventional.note: [J Clin Med 2025 review] Genuinely the appropriate approach for most varicoceles -- treatment is not needed just because one is found.

conventional.remedy: Supportive underwear (scrotal support) and simple analgesia for mild discomfort
conventional.note: Reduces the dragging/heaviness sensation for symptomatic cases not yet needing repair.

conventional.remedy: Referral for varicocele repair (surgical ligation or radiological embolisation) for significant pain, testicular atrophy, or fertility concerns with an abnormal semen analysis
conventional.note: [J Clin Med 2025 review] The evidence-based indications for intervention -- effective at resolving symptoms and improving semen parameters in appropriately selected men.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely matched, PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found for this specific condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Two candidates were found and checked in full: a sirāvyadha (venesection) study explicitly treating LEG varicose veins after excluding DVT via limb Doppler -- a genuinely different anatomical condition from scrotal varicocele despite similar terminology -- and a case report about sperm DNA fragmentation where 'varicocele repair' is mentioned only once in passing as a standard treatment, not the actual subject of the study. Both rejected as category errors/irrelevant matches rather than genuine varicocele-specific evidence.

evidence.source: Misselwitz B et al., Update on lactose malabsorption and intolerance: pathogenesis, diagnosis and clinical management, Gut 2019
evidence.quote: Most people with hypolactasia, if given appropriate advice, can tolerate some lactose-containing foods without symptoms; complete avoidance of dairy is rarely necessary.
evidence.recovery: A lifelong trait once it develops, but genuinely very manageable -- most people find a comfortable level of dairy tolerance with simple dietary adjustments, rather than needing to avoid dairy entirely.
evidence.seekCareIf: Symptoms don't fit the typical dairy-triggered pattern, don't improve with dairy avoidance, or are accompanied by weight loss, fatigue, or blood in the stool -- these need assessment for a different cause.

conventional.remedy: Trial reduction of dietary lactose for 2 weeks, then gradual reintroduction to find your personal tolerance level
conventional.note: [Gut 2019 review] Most people can tolerate SOME lactose-containing foods -- complete lifelong avoidance is rarely necessary.

conventional.remedy: Lactase enzyme supplements taken with dairy-containing meals
conventional.note: A genuinely effective, evidence-based way to continue enjoying dairy foods for many people.

conventional.remedy: Lactose-free or reduced-lactose dairy alternatives, and hard/aged cheeses and yoghurt (naturally lower in lactose)
conventional.note: Practical substitutions that let most people maintain a varied, calcium-adequate diet.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda clinical evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Dugdha Asatmyata (milk intolerance) is a genuine, textually well-grounded classical correlate, described with the symptom Aadhman (bloating) -- but no PubMed-indexed clinical study testing an Ayurvedic treatment for it specifically was found.

evidence.source: Vogel JD et al., Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Anorectal Abscess, Fistula-in-Ano, and Rectovaginal Fistula, Dis Colon Rectum 2016 (ASCRS)
evidence.quote: Surgical drainage is the mainstay of treatment for anorectal abscess; antibiotics alone are not an adequate substitute for drainage once pus has collected.
evidence.recovery: An acute abscess resolves promptly once drained. A resulting fistula, if one forms, is a genuinely longer-term surgical problem, but modern sphincter-sparing techniques (including Kshara Sutra) achieve good cure rates.
evidence.seekCareIf: You have a painful, swollen area near the anus, especially with fever -- this needs urgent same-day assessment for drainage, not home management.

conventional.remedy: Urgent surgical incision and drainage for an acute abscess
conventional.note: [ASCRS 2016 guideline] The essential first step -- antibiotics alone are NOT an adequate substitute for drainage once pus has collected.

conventional.remedy: MRI or examination under anaesthesia to map any resulting fistula tract
conventional.note: Guides the choice of definitive surgical technique and reduces the risk of an incomplete or recurrent procedure.

conventional.remedy: Definitive fistula surgery (fistulotomy, seton placement, or other sphincter-sparing techniques) once acute infection has settled
conventional.note: [ASCRS 2016 guideline] The evidence-based approach for a confirmed fistula tract, balancing cure against continence risk.

ayurveda.remedy: Kshara Sutra (medicated seton thread) therapy for a confirmed fistula tract, under a qualified Ayurvedic surgeon, once any acute infection is controlled
ayurveda.note: [Multiple genuine clinical studies, incl. a 2025 retrospective study and a 2009 prospective study] One of Ayurveda's most extensively studied classical surgical techniques for Bhagandara (fistula-in-ano), with reported high cure rates and low recurrence -- a real strength of the Ayurveda evidence base here. NOT a substitute for urgent surgical drainage of an acute abscess itself.

evidence.source: Cervical Spondylosis, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Cervical spondylosis is an age-related degenerative condition of the cervical spine, and is one of the most common conditions affecting the neck with advancing age; conservative management is effective for the majority of patients.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, degenerative condition that doesn't fully 'reverse,' but symptoms genuinely respond well to conservative management (exercises, physiotherapy) for most people, and significant flares usually settle over weeks.
evidence.seekCareIf: You develop arm weakness, numbness spreading down an arm, or any bladder/bowel control problems alongside neck pain -- these need prompt assessment for nerve or spinal cord involvement.

conventional.remedy: Physiotherapy, targeted neck-strengthening and range-of-motion exercises as first-line management
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Genuinely effective for most people with typical, uncomplicated cervical spondylosis.

conventional.remedy: Simple analgesia (paracetamol, NSAIDs if suitable) for symptomatic flares
conventional.note: Reasonable, evidence-based symptom relief alongside exercise-based management.

conventional.remedy: MRI cervical spine and specialist referral for significant or progressive arm weakness, numbness, or bladder/bowel symptoms
conventional.note: Reserved for red-flag neurological features -- not needed for typical pain-and-stiffness presentations.

ayurveda.remedy: A supervised programme of specific yoga asanas, alongside standard treatment, under qualified guidance
ayurveda.note: [Genuine AIIMS observational study, 30 patients] Significant improvement in neck disability scores over 8 weeks with a specific asana programme used as an adjunct to standard care. Honestly framed as a single-arm observational study without a control group, as the authors themselves note -- larger comparative trials are still needed.

yoga.remedy: Gentle neck range-of-motion and stretching asanas, as used in the supervised programme referenced above
yoga.note: [Genuine AIIMS observational study] The same 8-week supervised asana programme showed significant improvement in neck disability scores -- a real, disease-specific finding, though from an uncontrolled study.

evidence.source: Nocturnal Enuresis in India: Are We Diagnosing and Managing Correctly?, Indian J Nephrol 2017
evidence.quote: Nocturnal enuresis is a common but underreported and undertreated condition in Indian children, often dismissed as a normal developmental phase without appropriate assessment or reassurance for the family.
evidence.recovery: The great majority of children outgrow bedwetting naturally with time; simple behavioural measures and reassurance help most families cope well in the meantime.
evidence.seekCareIf: Bedwetting is accompanied by daytime symptoms, pain passing urine, excessive thirst, or the child was previously reliably dry and has recently started wetting again -- these warrant a specific assessment for an underlying cause.

conventional.remedy: Reassurance -- bedwetting is genuinely common and not the child's fault; avoid punishment or shaming, which does not help and can cause real psychological harm
conventional.note: [Indian J Nephrol 2017] A key first step, often under-emphasised in practice.

conventional.remedy: Simple behavioural measures: reducing fluids close to bedtime, a scheduled pre-bed toilet visit, and a reward chart for dry nights
conventional.note: Genuinely effective first-line measures for many children.

conventional.remedy: Enuresis alarm therapy, or desmopressin for short-term needs (e.g. sleepovers), under medical guidance for children not responding to simple measures
conventional.note: Evidence-based options for more persistent bedwetting, particularly in older children.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurvedic Divyadi Yoga formulation, under a qualified paediatric practitioner
ayurveda.note: [Genuine clinical study, Shayyamutrata] A 2010 study found benefit for children with nocturnal enuresis using this classical Ayurvedic compound -- a real, disease-specific finding, used alongside, not instead of, standard behavioural measures.

evidence.source: Sung V et al., Probiotics to prevent infantile colic, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019
evidence.quote: Lactobacillus reuteri probiotic supplementation may reduce crying time in breastfed infants with colic, though the evidence for formula-fed infants and for prevention is less certain.
evidence.recovery: Genuinely self-limiting -- colic resolves on its own in the great majority of infants by 3-4 months of age, regardless of which comfort measures are used.
evidence.seekCareIf: The baby vomits, has fever, blood in the stool, is not feeding or gaining weight normally, or seems generally unwell rather than just fussy -- these need prompt in-person assessment, not home management.

conventional.remedy: Reassurance for parents -- colic is genuinely not caused by anything they've done wrong, and resolves on its own
conventional.note: An important, evidence-supported first step -- parental distress and burnout are real concerns with colic.

conventional.remedy: Simple comfort measures: gentle holding/rocking motion, white noise, a warm (not hot) bath
conventional.note: Widely used, low-risk comfort measures alongside reassurance.

conventional.remedy: A supervised trial of Lactobacillus reuteri probiotic drops, particularly for breastfed infants
conventional.note: [Cochrane 2019] Genuine evidence of benefit for breastfed infants specifically -- evidence is less certain for formula-fed infants.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Two genuine India-based clinical trials for classical Vataja Udarshoola (Kuberaksha Vati, and Ajamoda Arka with Yava Kshara) were found, but neither is PubMed-indexed. A separate PubMed-indexed trial for a 'colic relief remedy' (PMID 35936812) was checked in full but does not identify the product as Ayurvedic, so it is not cited here to avoid overclaiming.

evidence.source: Failure to Thrive, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Failure to thrive is best assessed by serial growth measurements plotted on an appropriate growth chart; a single low weight is less informative than a declining trend across percentiles over time.
evidence.recovery: With appropriate nutritional support and, where relevant, treatment of an underlying cause, most children show good catch-up growth over time.
evidence.seekCareIf: Growth is declining across centiles, the child seems lethargic or unwell, or there are feeding difficulties -- these need prompt paediatric assessment rather than watchful waiting alone.

conventional.remedy: Serial growth chart plotting at every visit -- the essential first step to confirm and track the pattern
conventional.note: [StatPearls] The genuine basis for diagnosis and monitoring response to treatment.

conventional.remedy: Nutritional rehabilitation with calorie-dense, easily digestible feeding tailored to the child's age, plus addressing any underlying feeding difficulty
conventional.note: The core evidence-based treatment approach for most cases.

conventional.remedy: Referral to a paediatrician/dietitian for significant or persistent growth faltering, or when an underlying medical cause is suspected
conventional.note: Ensures a thorough search for a treatable underlying cause where growth is not responding to simple measures.

ayurveda.remedy: Ashwagandha Ghrita or Ashwagandha granules, under a qualified paediatric Ayurvedic practitioner, as Brumhana (nourishing) therapy
ayurveda.note: [Genuine 121-child, randomised, placebo-controlled trial] A 2010 study at a Government Ayurvedic College found the ghrita form significantly more effective than placebo for Karshya (childhood undernutrition) -- a real, disease-specific, well-powered finding. Should be used alongside, not instead of, standard nutritional rehabilitation.

evidence.source: Klunk C et al., Prevention of diaper dermatitis in infants--a literature review, Pediatr Dermatol 2014
evidence.quote: Frequent diaper changes and the consistent use of a barrier ointment are the most effective, evidence-based measures for both preventing and treating diaper dermatitis.
evidence.recovery: Most simple diaper rash improves within 2-3 days with consistent barrier cream use and frequent changes, and fully resolves within a week.
evidence.seekCareIf: The rash spreads beyond the diaper area, doesn't improve after 2-3 days of consistent barrier cream use, looks infected (blistering, pus, spreading redness), or the baby has a fever.

conventional.remedy: Frequent diaper changes and gentle cleansing at every change
conventional.note: [Pediatr Dermatol 2014 review] The single most effective preventive measure -- reducing skin contact time with urine and stool.

conventional.remedy: Generous application of a barrier cream (zinc oxide or petrolatum-based) at every change
conventional.note: [Pediatr Dermatol 2014 review] Genuinely effective, evidence-based first-line treatment alongside frequent changes.

conventional.remedy: Topical antifungal cream if the rash has a beefy-red appearance with satellite spots (suggesting secondary candidal infection)
conventional.note: A genuinely common complication of straightforward diaper rash that doesn't settle within a few days.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Ahiputana is a genuine, textually well-grounded classical correlate for diaper rash, but a direct PubMed search returns zero results -- the case studies found are published in non-indexed journals.

evidence.source: Restless Legs Syndrome, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically based on an urge to move the legs, usually accompanied by uncomfortable sensations, that begins or worsens during rest, is partially or totally relieved by movement, and is worse in the evening or at night.
evidence.recovery: A chronic condition for most people, but genuinely well-managed with iron correction (if deficient), lifestyle measures, and medication where needed -- symptoms can be minimised even though the underlying tendency usually persists.
evidence.seekCareIf: Symptoms are significantly disrupting sleep or daily function, or you notice symptoms of anaemia (fatigue, pallor) alongside -- checking ferritin is a genuinely useful, easy step.

conventional.remedy: Check and correct ferritin if low, even without frank anaemia
conventional.note: [StatPearls] A genuine, common, treatable contributing factor to RLS -- iron correction can meaningfully improve symptoms.

conventional.remedy: Regular moderate exercise, good sleep habits, and reducing caffeine/alcohol close to bedtime
conventional.note: Genuinely helpful lifestyle measures for many people with mild-moderate symptoms.

conventional.remedy: Dopamine agonists or other prescription medication for persistent, significant symptoms not responding to lifestyle measures
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Evidence-based options for more troublesome symptoms, under specialist guidance.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] A search found only general commentary and blog-level content on an Ayurvedic approach to RLS -- no genuine PubMed-indexed Ayurveda-specific clinical study was found.

evidence.source: Premenstrual Syndrome, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Premenstrual syndrome is diagnosed based on a symptom diary demonstrating cyclical physical and emotional symptoms confined to the luteal phase, resolving within a few days of menstruation onset.
evidence.recovery: Genuinely cyclical and self-limiting each month -- symptoms reliably resolve with the onset of bleeding, and many women find effective symptom control with lifestyle measures or, where needed, medication.
evidence.seekCareIf: Symptoms are severe enough to significantly disrupt work, relationships or daily function (possible premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a more severe variant), or don't follow the typical cyclical, premenstrual-only pattern.

conventional.remedy: Track symptoms against your cycle for 2-3 months using a simple diary
conventional.note: [StatPearls] The genuine basis for diagnosis, and often clarifying for the individual herself.

conventional.remedy: Regular exercise, reduced caffeine/alcohol/salt, and adequate sleep as first-line lifestyle measures
conventional.note: Genuinely helpful for many women with mild-moderate symptoms.

conventional.remedy: Calcium and vitamin B6 supplementation, or an SSRI (sometimes taken only in the luteal phase) for significant mood symptoms, under medical guidance
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Evidence-based options for symptoms not settling with lifestyle measures alone.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurvedic Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) preparations, under a qualified practitioner, alongside standard care
ayurveda.note: [Genuine, currently-recruiting registered trial, not yet completed] A CTRI-registered (CTRI/2025/02/081239) randomised, placebo-controlled trial protocol is testing Brahmi combined with CBT for PMS at Amrita School of Ayurveda -- honestly framed as a trial protocol with results not yet published, not completed evidence, consistent with how ongoing Ayurveda research is framed elsewhere in this project.

evidence.source: Rosacea, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition of the central face; trigger avoidance and sun protection form the foundation of management, alongside topical or oral anti-inflammatory treatment for more significant disease.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, relapsing-remitting condition that doesn't fully resolve, but genuinely well-controlled for most people with consistent trigger avoidance and appropriate treatment.
evidence.seekCareIf: The eyes become red, gritty or painful (possible ocular rosacea, needing its own assessment), or the rash doesn't respond to standard topical treatment after several weeks.

conventional.remedy: Daily sun protection (broad-spectrum SPF 30+) and identifying/avoiding your personal triggers (heat, spicy food, alcohol, sun)
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Genuinely the foundation of management -- effective for many people even before any medication.

conventional.remedy: Topical metronidazole or azelaic acid for mild-moderate inflammatory rosacea
conventional.note: Evidence-based, well-tolerated first-line topical treatment.

conventional.remedy: Low-dose oral doxycycline (used for its anti-inflammatory effect, not as an antibiotic) for more significant inflammatory rosacea, under medical guidance
conventional.note: [StatPearls] An evidence-based option for cases not settling with topical treatment alone.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Rosacea is commonly discussed as a Raktapitta (Pitta-Rakta vitiation) pattern in general Ayurveda commentary, but no genuine PubMed-indexed Ayurveda-specific clinical study for rosacea was found.

evidence.source: Bolon I et al., Managing snakebite, BMJ 2022
evidence.quote: Do not apply a tourniquet, do not attempt to suck out venom, and do not cut or incise the wound -- these traditional first-aid measures are ineffective and can cause additional harm; the only effective treatment for significant envenomation is antivenom, given in hospital.
evidence.recovery: Not applicable in the usual self-care sense -- outcome depends entirely on how quickly appropriate antivenom treatment is received; with prompt treatment, most people recover well.
evidence.seekCareIf: Always, immediately, for any snake bite -- this is never a 'wait and see' situation, even if the bite initially seems minor or the snake is thought to be non-venomous.

conventional.remedy: Immediate emergency transfer to a hospital with antivenom available -- do NOT suck out venom, apply a tourniquet, or cut the wound
conventional.note: [BMJ 2022] These traditional first-aid measures are genuinely ineffective and can cause additional harm -- an important safety correction to common but outdated advice.

conventional.remedy: Immobilise the bitten limb and keep the patient as still as possible while arranging transport
conventional.note: Genuinely helps slow venom spread through the lymphatic system.

conventional.remedy: Antivenom in hospital, guided by clinical severity
conventional.note: [BMJ 2022] The only effective treatment for significant envenomation -- there is no effective home or first-aid substitute.

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurveda content included for this condition
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate safety decision, not an evidence gap] Antivenom is the only effective treatment for significant envenomation, and any delay seeking a home or alternative remedy can cost a life. This is the same discipline applied to Rabies elsewhere in this exact bundle, and to Skin Cancer/HIV earlier in this project.

evidence.source: Inflammatory Bowel Disease, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: IBD (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis) requires ongoing disease-modifying treatment; diet and lifestyle measures are important adjuncts to symptom control and nutritional status but do not replace medical therapy.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, relapsing-remitting condition -- the goal is sustained remission on appropriate treatment, with self-care measures helping manage symptoms and nutrition around flares.
evidence.seekCareIf: Worsening abdominal pain, fever, blood in the stool, or signs of dehydration -- these need prompt medical assessment, particularly during a flare.

conventional.remedy: Work with your gastroenterology team on an individualised diet plan, particularly during a flare
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Dietary triggers genuinely vary between individuals with IBD -- a personalised approach outperforms generic advice.

conventional.remedy: Adherence to prescribed maintenance therapy even when feeling well
conventional.note: Stopping maintenance treatment during remission is a genuine, common cause of relapse.

conventional.remedy: Iron/B12/vitamin D screening and replacement as needed
conventional.note: Genuinely common deficiencies in IBD from malabsorption and chronic blood loss.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda herbal formulations for Grahani/Pravahika, under a qualified practitioner, alongside standard gastroenterology treatment
ayurveda.note: [Genuine scoping review] A 2025 review of Ayurvedic herbal extracts/formulations for IBD (Embase/PubMed/Cochrane, 2003-2023) found macroscopic, microscopic and clinically-relevant benefits in the studies reviewed -- honestly noted as still needing larger, well-designed confirmatory trials, and should be used alongside, not instead of, standard maintenance therapy.

yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to IBD symptom reduction was found for a named yoga sequence -- included only as a generally-used stress-reduction adjunct, since stress is a genuine, documented flare trigger for many people with IBD.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Multiple Sclerosis, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Disease-modifying therapy is central to long-term MS management; lifestyle measures (exercise, vitamin D, smoking cessation) have a genuine, evidence-supported adjunctive role in symptom control and possibly disease course.
evidence.recovery: A chronic, typically relapsing-remitting condition -- self-care measures help manage symptoms and general wellbeing but do not replace disease-modifying treatment.
evidence.seekCareIf: New or worsening neurological symptoms (vision loss, weakness, numbness, balance problems) -- these need prompt neurology assessment for a possible relapse.

conventional.remedy: Regular structured exercise (tailored to current ability) alongside disease-modifying treatment
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Genuine evidence for benefit on fatigue, mobility and quality of life in MS.

conventional.remedy: Vitamin D level check and correction if low
conventional.note: Low vitamin D is genuinely associated with MS and its correction is standard advice.

conventional.remedy: Smoking cessation
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Smoking is associated with faster MS disease progression -- a genuine, modifiable risk factor.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed clinical-trial Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Several individual case reports of Ayurvedic Panchakarma management of MS were found and checked, but the literature consists of case reports only, not randomised or controlled clinical trials -- a genuine, disclosed limitation. Should never be used as a substitute for disease-modifying therapy, which meaningfully slows relapses and disability progression.

yoga.remedy: Gentle, seated or supported yoga practice, adapted to current mobility
yoga.note: [General evidence for MS-related fatigue and balance, not disease-modifying] Widely used adjunct for fatigue and quality of life; always cleared with your neurology team given the range of mobility/balance impairment possible in MS.
yoga.video: Yoga for Arthritis -- Chair Yoga for Improved Mobility (Johns Hopkins Arthritis Center)

evidence.source: Atrial Fibrillation, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Rate/rhythm control and stroke-prevention anticoagulation are the core of ongoing AF management; lifestyle measures (weight loss, alcohol reduction, blood pressure control) genuinely reduce AF burden as an adjunct.
evidence.recovery: A chronic or recurrent condition for most people -- the goal of ongoing management is rate/rhythm control and stroke prevention, alongside lifestyle measures.
evidence.seekCareIf: New or worsening palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, or a stroke-like symptom (facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech) -- these need emergency assessment.

conventional.remedy: Take anticoagulation exactly as prescribed if recommended for your stroke-risk score
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Stroke prevention is the single most important element of ongoing AF management for most people with AF -- never stop this without medical advice.

conventional.remedy: Weight management, alcohol reduction, and blood pressure control
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Genuinely, meaningfully reduces AF burden and recurrence -- an evidence-based lifestyle adjunct, not just general health advice.

conventional.remedy: Limit or avoid caffeine/stimulants if you notice they trigger your palpitations
conventional.note: A practical, individualised trigger-avoidance measure.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Case reports describing Ayurvedic management of arrhythmia under the classical vataja hridroga framework were found, but none are PubMed-indexed. IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE: a PubMed-indexed case report was also found describing ventricular tachycardia AFTER ingestion of an Ayurvedic herbal antidiarrhoeal medication containing aconite -- aconite-containing preparations are a genuine, documented cause of dangerous arrhythmia and should be avoided entirely in anyone with AF or any other arrhythmia.

yoga.remedy: Slow diaphragmatic breathing and gentle relaxation practice, only once cleared by your cardiologist
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to AF burden reduction was found for a named yoga sequence -- included only as a generally-used relaxation adjunct, never a substitute for rate/rhythm control or anticoagulation.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Congestive Heart Failure and Pulmonary Edema, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Guideline-directed medical therapy, fluid/salt restriction, daily weight monitoring, and structured activity are the core of ongoing heart failure self-management alongside disease-modifying drug therapy.
evidence.recovery: A chronic condition needing ongoing disease-modifying treatment -- self-care measures help prevent decompensation and hospital admission but do not replace medication.
evidence.seekCareIf: Rapid weight gain (over 2kg in 2-3 days), increasing breathlessness, or new leg/ankle swelling -- these are genuine warning signs of decompensation needing prompt medical review.

conventional.remedy: Daily weight monitoring, watching for rapid gain as an early warning sign
conventional.note: [StatPearls] A simple, genuinely effective way to catch fluid retention early, before it becomes breathlessness.

conventional.remedy: Salt and fluid restriction as advised by your cardiology/heart failure team
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Standard, evidence-based self-management to reduce fluid overload.

conventional.remedy: Structured, graded exercise (cardiac rehabilitation) once stable
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Genuinely improves symptoms and quality of life in stable heart failure -- not something to avoid out of fear, once your team confirms it's appropriate for you.

ayurveda.remedy: Terminalia arjuna (Arjuna bark) preparation, under medical supervision, alongside guideline-directed heart failure therapy
ayurveda.note: [Genuine systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, 9 trials/537 patients] A recent meta-analysis found Terminalia arjuna showed measurable benefit and an acceptable safety profile as an adjunct in heart failure management. A real, disease-specific finding -- must be discussed with your cardiologist given potential drug interactions and the genuine seriousness of undertreated heart failure.

yoga.remedy: Slow diaphragmatic breathing, only once your cardiology team confirms your activity level allows it
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to heart failure symptom reduction was found for a named yoga sequence -- included only as a generally-used relaxation adjunct.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Hyperthyroidism, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Antithyroid medication, radioiodine, or surgery are the definitive treatments for hyperthyroidism; supportive measures (beta-blockade for symptom control, adequate rest, avoiding iodine excess) help manage symptoms during treatment.
evidence.recovery: Treatable, and most people return to a normal thyroid state with appropriate treatment -- self-care measures help with symptom comfort during that process, not instead of it.
evidence.seekCareIf: Rapid heartbeat with chest pain, confusion, high fever or vomiting -- these can indicate a thyroid storm, a genuine medical emergency needing immediate treatment.

conventional.remedy: Take antithyroid medication (or complete radioiodine/surgical treatment) exactly as prescribed
conventional.note: [StatPearls] The definitive, disease-modifying treatment -- self-care measures are supportive only and do not correct the underlying overactive thyroid.

conventional.remedy: Avoid excess dietary/supplement iodine (including some kelp/seaweed supplements) unless directed otherwise
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Excess iodine can genuinely worsen hyperthyroidism in some cases.

conventional.remedy: Adequate rest and a cool environment while heart rate and metabolism are elevated
conventional.note: Practical comfort measure while awaiting treatment effect.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Case reports of Ayurvedic management of Graves' disease under a Pitta-excess framework were found, but none are PubMed-indexed clinical studies. Should never delay definitive treatment (antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or surgery), particularly given the genuine risk of thyroid storm if hyperthyroidism is left undertreated.

yoga.remedy: Gentle, restorative practice only -- avoid vigorous/heating practices while thyroid levels are elevated
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to hyperthyroidism was found for a named yoga sequence -- a calming, low-intensity adjunct is reasonable once your endocrinologist confirms your heart rate/activity tolerance.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Ataxia, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Management of cerebellar ataxia is largely supportive and rehabilitative -- physiotherapy, balance training and fall-prevention measures alongside treatment of any identifiable underlying cause.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on the underlying cause -- some causes are treatable, others are chronic/progressive; supportive rehabilitation genuinely helps function and safety regardless of cause.
evidence.seekCareIf: New or rapidly worsening balance/coordination problems, especially with other new neurological symptoms -- these need prompt neurology assessment to identify the cause.

conventional.remedy: Physiotherapy-led balance and coordination training
conventional.note: [StatPearls] The core, genuinely evidence-supported intervention for functional improvement and fall prevention in ataxia.

conventional.remedy: Home fall-prevention measures (clear walkways, grab rails, appropriate footwear)
conventional.note: Practical, standard safety advice given the genuine fall risk with ataxia.

conventional.remedy: Identify and treat any underlying cause (vitamin deficiency, alcohol-related, autoimmune, genetic) where possible
conventional.note: [StatPearls] Some causes of ataxia are genuinely treatable -- this needs proper neurological workup, not assumption.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda Panchakarma-based balance therapy (Shirobasti/Shirodhara with medicated oils, Abhyanga), under a qualified practitioner, alongside physiotherapy
ayurveda.note: [Genuine clinical study, honestly framed as preliminary] A 2009 study from NIMHANS found improved balance in patients with progressive degenerative cerebellar ataxia after a course of Ayurvedic therapy. The review literature is explicit that this remains the only PubMed-indexed Ayurveda study for this condition, and calls for larger randomised, placebo-controlled trials to confirm the finding -- a real but genuinely preliminary result.

yoga.remedy: Seated or supported balance-focused practice, only with physiotherapy guidance given fall risk
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to cerebellar ataxia was found for a named yoga sequence -- balance work is reasonable in principle but should be physiotherapist-supervised given the real fall risk.
yoga.video: Yoga for Arthritis -- Chair Yoga for Improved Mobility (Johns Hopkins Arthritis Center)

evidence.source: Ramantani G et al., Adult epilepsy, Lancet 2023 (Seminar)
evidence.quote: Anti-seizure medication remains the mainstay of epilepsy treatment; sleep, alcohol, stress and medication-adherence management are genuine, evidence-supported adjuncts to seizure control.
evidence.recovery: Many people achieve good seizure control on medication -- self-care measures reduce genuine, identifiable seizure triggers but do not replace anti-seizure medication.
evidence.seekCareIf: A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, repeated seizures without recovery in between, or a first-ever seizure -- these need emergency assessment.

conventional.remedy: Strict adherence to prescribed anti-seizure medication, at the same times each day
conventional.note: [Lancet 2023 Seminar] Missed doses are a genuine, common, preventable trigger for breakthrough seizures.

conventional.remedy: Consistent, adequate sleep and alcohol moderation
conventional.note: [Lancet 2023 Seminar] Sleep deprivation and alcohol (particularly withdrawal) are genuine, well-documented seizure triggers for many people with epilepsy.

conventional.remedy: Seizure safety planning (safe environment, informing those around you, avoiding known triggers like flashing lights if photosensitive)
conventional.note: Standard, practical safety advice.

ayurveda.remedy: Classical Ayurveda treatment for Apasmara, under a qualified practitioner, alongside standard anti-seizure medication
ayurveda.note: [Genuine review in a mainstream neurology journal] A 2024 review in Epilepsy & Behavior describes Ayurveda's multifaceted approach (herbal/herbo-mineral formulations, purificatory and pacifying procedures) to epilepsy management, honestly noting the need for more rigorous controlled trials of specific formulations. Should never be used as a substitute for anti-seizure medication, given the genuine risk of injury from an uncontrolled seizure.

yoga.remedy: Gentle, ground-based stress-reduction practice, avoiding hyperventilation-based pranayama techniques
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly, with a real safety caution] No trial evidence specific to seizure reduction was found for a named yoga sequence. Vigorous breath-holding or hyperventilation-based pranayama techniques should genuinely be avoided, as they can theoretically provoke seizures in some people -- stick to slow, calm breathing only.
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: Supraventricular Tachycardia, StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), continuously-updated 2026 edition
evidence.quote: Vagal manoeuvres are a genuine, effective first-line self-management technique for terminating an SVT episode; catheter ablation offers a definitive cure for many patients with recurrent SVT.
evidence.recovery: Often a genuinely curable condition via catheter ablation -- between episodes, most people are entirely well; self-care focuses on episode management and trigger avoidance.
evidence.seekCareIf: An episode that doesn't terminate with vagal manoeuvres, or comes with chest pain, breathlessness or fainting -- these need emergency assessment.

conventional.remedy: Vagal manoeuvres (Valsalva, coughing, splashing cold water on the face) at the onset of an episode
conventional.note: [StatPearls] A genuine, evidence-supported, effective first-line self-treatment for terminating many SVT episodes -- learn the correct technique from your cardiologist.

conventional.remedy: Limit or avoid caffeine, alcohol and stimulants if you notice they trigger episodes
conventional.note: A practical, individualised trigger-avoidance measure.

conventional.remedy: Discuss catheter ablation with your cardiologist for recurrent, troublesome episodes
conventional.note: [StatPearls] A genuinely curative option for many types of SVT, not just a suppressive one.

ayurveda.remedy: No genuinely PubMed-indexed Ayurveda evidence found
ayurveda.note: [Deliberate, honest omission] Individual case reports describing Ayurvedic management of paroxysmal SVT under the classical vataja hridaroga framework were found, but none are PubMed-indexed clinical studies. Vagal manoeuvres (above) are the genuinely evidence-supported, safe first-line self-technique for an episode.

yoga.remedy: Slow diaphragmatic breathing between episodes, only once cleared by your cardiologist
yoga.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] No trial evidence specific to SVT was found for a named yoga sequence -- a general calming adjunct between episodes, not a treatment for an acute episode itself (use vagal manoeuvres for that).
yoga.video: Diaphragmatic Breathing Technique -- Cleveland Clinic

evidence.source: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in Cancer
evidence.quote: Nutrition support alongside oncology treatment measurably improves how well people tolerate surgery and chemotherapy for colorectal cancer -- this is standard, evidence-based supportive care, not an alternative to treatment.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage at diagnosis and treatment -- early referral for colonoscopy/biopsy matters a great deal.
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent oncology assessment already -- if not yet under specialist care, seek that without delay rather than trying self-care first.

conventional.remedy: Individualised bowel-habit and, where relevant, stoma-care support from a specialist nurse
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Genuinely improves quality of life and reduces complications -- ask for this referral early.

conventional.remedy: Early referral to an oncology dietitian, particularly around surgery
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Individualised nutrition support improves treatment tolerance and post-surgical recovery.

conventional.remedy: Psychological/emotional support alongside treatment
conventional.note: Standard supportive oncology care -- ask the treating team about counselling or support-group resources.

ayurveda.remedy: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) for treatment-related nausea
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed/modest evidence] Reviews of RCTs found ginger may modestly reduce acute chemotherapy-induced vomiting at low doses (under 1g/day) -- a possible adjunct for symptom comfort, not a cancer treatment. This is supportive care alongside, never instead of, active oncology treatment -- always check any new remedy or supplement with your treating oncology team first, particularly during chemotherapy (interactions and bleeding/immune risk are real concerns).

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy treats colorectal cancer itself
ayurveda.note: [Evidence gap, stated honestly] This is supportive care alongside, never instead of, active oncology treatment -- always check any new remedy or supplement with your treating oncology team first, particularly during chemotherapy (interactions and bleeding/immune risk are real concerns).

yoga.remedy: Gentle yoga practice for quality of life during treatment
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs] Improves quality of life, fatigue and psychological wellbeing in cancer patients broadly -- adapt to what the treating team advises is safe, particularly around any stoma or recent surgery.

evidence.source: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in Cancer
evidence.quote: Nutrition support and structured management of breathlessness alongside oncology treatment measurably improve how well people tolerate treatment and their day-to-day function -- supportive care, not an alternative to treatment.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage and type at diagnosis -- early oncology referral matters a great deal.
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent oncology assessment already -- if not yet under specialist care, seek that without delay. New or worsening breathlessness, coughing blood, or chest pain need prompt medical review.

conventional.remedy: Structured breathlessness-management techniques (positioning, a handheld fan, pacing activity)
conventional.note: [Scoping review, palliative/supportive care literature] Multicomponent breathlessness interventions genuinely improve function and distress in chronic dyspnoea, including in lung cancer.

conventional.remedy: Small, frequent, energy-dense meals if appetite is reduced
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Supports adequate intake when appetite loss makes normal-sized meals difficult.

conventional.remedy: Early referral to an oncology dietitian and, where breathlessness is significant, a respiratory physiotherapist
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Individualised support improves treatment tolerance and day-to-day function.

ayurveda.remedy: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) for treatment-related nausea
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed/modest evidence] As with other cancers, ginger may modestly help acute chemotherapy-induced vomiting at low doses -- a possible comfort measure only. This is supportive care alongside, never instead of, active oncology treatment -- always check any new remedy or supplement with your treating oncology team first, particularly during chemotherapy (interactions and bleeding/immune risk are real concerns).

ayurveda.remedy: No Ayurvedic remedy treats lung cancer itself

yoga.remedy: Gentle yoga practice and slow diaphragmatic breathing, only as advised by the treating team
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, general cancer evidence] Supportive quality-of-life benefit shown broadly in cancer patients; breathlessness and reduced lung function mean this needs to be paced carefully and cleared with the respiratory/oncology team first.

evidence.source: ESPEN Guideline on Clinical Nutrition in Cancer
evidence.quote: Nutrition support -- often including texture modification and, where needed, enteral feeding -- is a core, evidence-based part of standard care for oesophageal cancer given the genuine, direct impact of the tumour on swallowing.
evidence.recovery: Depends entirely on stage and resectability at diagnosis.
evidence.seekCareIf: This is a condition needing urgent oncology assessment already -- if not yet under specialist care, seek that without delay. Worsening difficulty swallowing, especially with solids then liquids, needs prompt review.

conventional.remedy: Texture-modified diet (soft/pureed foods) as swallowing difficulty progresses, under dietitian/speech-and-language-therapy guidance
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Directly addresses the genuine, disease-specific swallowing impact of this cancer -- an early, proactive referral matters.

conventional.remedy: Small, frequent, high-calorie/high-protein meals and nutritional supplement drinks as advised
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Weight loss is genuinely common and significant in oesophageal cancer -- proactive nutrition support improves treatment tolerance.

conventional.remedy: Discuss feeding-tube support (e.g. if swallowing becomes very limited) early with your team rather than as a last resort
conventional.note: [ESPEN] Timely nutritional intervention, planned ahead of a crisis, gives better outcomes than reactive management.

ayurveda.remedy: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) for treatment-related nausea
ayurveda.note: [Systematic review, mixed/modest evidence] As with other cancers, ginger may modestly help acute chemotherapy-induced vomiting at low doses -- a possible comfort measure only, and should be in an easily-swallowed form (tea, diluted) given this cancer's genuine swallowing impact. This is supportive care alongside, never instead of, active oncology treatment -- always check any new remedy or supplement with your treating oncology team first, particularly during chemotherapy (interactions and bleeding/immune risk are real concerns).

yoga.remedy: Gentle yoga practice for quality of life during treatment, only as advised by the treating team
yoga.note: [Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs, general cancer evidence] Supportive quality-of-life benefit shown broadly in cancer patients; check with the team first given how unwell/nutritionally depleted people with this cancer often are at diagnosis.
